citations.quote:
Adopt, as the **central-force model** for the two-body part of this page, the
following restricted model class inside the force and interaction branches of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]].

**(i) The two-label central model.** A model of class (i) is a force model of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$ labels, fixed masses
$m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_0$, the
collision-excluded configuration domain
$$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$
for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and the force map presented through the
time-independent **static central pair potential**
$$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),\qquad u:J_0\to\mathbb R\ \text{of class }C^2,$$
so that $F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain (clauses (iii)
and (iv) of [[post-cm02-interactions]]; $U$ is of class $C^2$ on the open
$Q$ by [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). In the external-plus-pair
presentation of clause (i) of that postulate the model has
$F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$: no external forces act on the labels of a model
of class (i).

**(ii) The reduced one-label problem.** For a model of class (i) put
$\mu:=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)>0$ of dimension $\mu$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). The
**reduced problem** of the model is the one-label problem of mass $\mu$ whose
unknown is the relative coordinate $r=x_1-x_2$ and whose equation is
$$\mu\,r''=-\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r;$$
by [[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]] the relative coordinate of every motion
of a model of class (i) solves this equation, and every pair of a uniform
centre-of-mass motion and a solution of the reduced equation on a common
interval reconstructs a motion of the model. Adopt the reduced problem as the
object that the central-force statements of this page describe, and the
central-force-trajectory vocabulary of
[[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]] (attached angular momentum
$j=\mu\,r\times r'$ and energy $E=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+u(\lvert
r\rvert)$) as the vocabulary in which those statements are phrased.

**(iii) The one-label fixed-centre idealization.** A **one-label central
model** is a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=1$,
mass $\mu>0$, time window $I_0$, a fixed **centre** $c\in\mathbb R^3$, the
configuration domain $Q_c=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lvert x-c\rvert\in J_0\}$, and
the external force map
$$F(t,x,v)=-\frac{u'(\lvert x-c\rvert)}{\lvert x-c\rvert}\,(x-c),$$
presented through the potential $u(\lvert x-c\rvert)$ with the same function
$u\in C^2(J_0)$. This model is the **fixed-centre idealization** of the
reduced problem: it drops the centre-of-mass degree of freedom and holds the
force centre fixed. It is a separate adopted model class, not a consequence
of class (i), and every use of it must state that the idealization is
intended.

**(iv) Reading conventions.** In the statements of this page: the **force
centre** of the reduced problem is the origin of the relative coordinate
$r$; an **orbit** is the trajectory $t\mapsto r(t)$ of the reduced problem
(equivalently, by [[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]], the trajectory of either
label relative to the centre of mass, up to the mass ratio); "circular" and
"elliptic" name properties of that trajectory; and the words "planet",
"satellite", "central body" and "test particle" name labels of a model of
class (i) or (iii). These words carry no empirical claim about nature.

**(v) Exclusions and status.** The class excludes: velocity-dependent and
explicitly time-dependent central forces; non-central and non-potential
forces; constraints and reaction forces; colliding configurations
$x_1=x_2$ (equivalently $r=0$); external forces on the labels; and models
with more than two labels. Finite-size, rotational, deformational, dissipative
and relativistic effects are outside the class. The masses, the interval
$J_0$ and the function $u$ (including any parameters it carries) are model
data, not measured values ([[def-cm01-units]]); quantitative empirical use
requires separately stated measured inputs with their uncertainties, and no
statement of this page asserts that any physical system is exactly a model
of this class.

Adopt the force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$
labels, masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time
window $I_0$, and the collision-excluded configuration domain
$$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$
for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]). Suppose the model presents its force map
through the time-independent potential
$$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),$$
where $u:J_0\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that
$F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain ([[post-cm02-interactions]],
clauses (iii) and (iv), [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). Let
$x:J\to Q$ be a **motion** of the model on an interval $J$ with nonempty
interior ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]) and write
$$M:=m_1+m_2,\quad \mu:=\frac{m_1m_2}{M},\quad X:=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{M},\quad V:=X',\quad P:=m_1x_1'+m_2x_2',\quad r:=x_1-x_2,$$
with $\lvert\cdot\rvert=\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ the Euclidean norm
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and dimensions as in [[def-cm01-units]]
($[M]=[\mu]=\mu$, $[X]=[r]=\ell$, $[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$). Then:

1. **(Pair forces.)** On $J$ the evaluated forces are
   $$F_1\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=-\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r,\qquad F_2\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=+\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r;$$
   thus the force map admits the external-plus-pair decomposition of
   [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (i) with
   $F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$ and the single pair force
   $F_{12}=-u'(\lvert r\rvert)r/\lvert r\rvert=-F_{21}$, which is central
   and antisymmetric in the sense of clause (ii). This identity does not
   assert that a separate decomposition was declared as model data.
2. **(Centre of mass.)** $P$ is constant on $J$ and $X$ is affine: for all
   $t,t_0\in J$, $X(t)=X(t_0)+(t-t_0)V$ with the constant
   $V=X'=M^{-1}P$.
3. **(Relative motion.)** $r$ is of class $C^2$ on $J$, satisfies
   $$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{u'(\lvert r(t)\rvert)}{\lvert r(t)\rvert}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
   and is therefore a **central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$** in the
   sense of [[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]; its angular momentum vector
   $j=\mu\,r\times r'$ and energy $E=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+
   u(\lvert r\rvert)$ are the attached objects of that definition.
4. **(Reconstruction and bijection.)** The identities
   $x_1=X+\frac{m_2}{M}r$ and $x_2=X-\frac{m_1}{M}r$ hold on $J$.
   Conversely, if $X^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is affine with
   $(X^{\circ})''=0$ and $r^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is a $C^2$ curve with
   $\lvert r^{\circ}(t)\rvert\in J_0$ and
   $\mu(r^{\circ})''=-u'(\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert)r^{\circ}/\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert$
   on $J$, then
   $$x_1^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}+\frac{m_2}{M}r^{\circ},\qquad x_2^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}-\frac{m_1}{M}r^{\circ}$$
   define a motion $x^{\circ}:J\to Q$ of the model whose centre of mass is
   $X^{\circ}$ and whose relative coordinate is $r^{\circ}$. Consequently
   the assignment $x\mapsto(X,r)$ is a bijection from the motions of the
   model on $J$ onto the pairs (affine curve $X^{\circ}$ with
   $(X^{\circ})''=0$\!, central-force trajectory $r^{\circ}$ for $(\mu,u)$
   with values in $J_0$) on $J$.

Let $\mu>0$ be a real number, let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval,
let $U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be
an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), and let
$r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be twice differentiable with $|r(t)|\in J_0$ for every
$t\in I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The curve $r$ is a
**central-force trajectory for** $(\mu,U)$ when

$$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{U'(|r(t)|)}{|r(t)|}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

where $|x|:=\lVert x\rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and $U'$ is the derivative of $U$ on the
open interval $J_0$.

**Attached objects.** The **angular momentum vector** of such a trajectory is
the curve $j:I\to\mathbb R^3$,

$$j(t):=\mu\,r(t)\times r'(t),$$

with $\times$ the cross product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]);
its **energy** is the function $E:I\to\mathbb R$,

$$E(t):=\tfrac12\mu\,\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2+U(|r(t)|);$$

and for every $J\ge0$ the **effective potential of momentum magnitude** $J$ is
the function $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J:J_0\to\mathbb R$,

$$U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho):=U(\rho)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu\,\rho^2}.$$

**Why the objects are defined.** Since $\rho>0$ throughout $J_0$, the right-hand
side of the central-force equation is defined, the map
$\rho\mapsto J^2/(2\mu\rho^2)$ is $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$ (a quotient of $C^2$
functions with nowhere vanishing denominator), and $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ is
again $C^2$; in particular second derivatives of $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ are
available. The vector $j(t)$ is defined for every $t\in I$ because $r$ is
differentiable there.

**Mathematical status.** The data $\mu$, $U$ and $J$ are real numbers and
functions; the equation and the attached objects are mathematical statements
about curves. Nothing here asserts that the equation describes a physical
interaction, and the names are conventional labels for the mathematical
objects only.

**(a) Unconstrained branch.** The **unconstrained configuration domain** is an
open set $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, chosen as part of the model. A tuple
$x\in Q$ is an **admissible configuration**: an assignment of one position to
each label at one time. A **singular-force exclusion** is the removal of the
**collision set**

$$\Delta:=\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:\ \text{there are }i\ne j\text{ with }x_{i}=x_{j}\Bigr\}$$

from the domain, which is done when the model's force law is not defined at
coincident positions: $\Delta$ is closed (it is the union of the finitely many
closed sets $\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}$, each the zero set of the continuous map
$x\mapsto x_{i}-x_{j}$), so $Q:=\mathbb R^{3N}\setminus\Delta$ is open and is a
legitimate configuration domain. Whether the exclusion is part of the model is
a modelling decision recorded with the force law; the framework itself only
requires $Q$ to be open and stated.

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $(t,z(t))\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $(t,z(t))\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

Let $\mu>0$ be a real number, let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval,
let $U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be
an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), and let
$r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be twice differentiable with $|r(t)|\in J_0$ for every
$t\in I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The curve $r$ is a
**central-force trajectory for** $(\mu,U)$ when

$$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{U'(|r(t)|)}{|r(t)|}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

where $|x|:=\lVert x\rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and $U'$ is the derivative of $U$ on the
open interval $J_0$.

**Attached objects.** The **angular momentum vector** of such a trajectory is
the curve $j:I\to\mathbb R^3$,

$$j(t):=\mu\,r(t)\times r'(t),$$

with $\times$ the cross product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]);
its **energy** is the function $E:I\to\mathbb R$,

$$E(t):=\tfrac12\mu\,\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2+U(|r(t)|);$$

and for every $J\ge0$ the **effective potential of momentum magnitude** $J$ is
the function $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J:J_0\to\mathbb R$,

$$U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho):=U(\rho)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu\,\rho^2}.$$

**Why the objects are defined.** Since $\rho>0$ throughout $J_0$, the right-hand
side of the central-force equation is defined, the map
$\rho\mapsto J^2/(2\mu\rho^2)$ is $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$ (a quotient of $C^2$
functions with nowhere vanishing denominator), and $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ is
again $C^2$; in particular second derivatives of $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ are
available. The vector $j(t)$ is defined for every $t\in I$ because $r$ is
differentiable there.

**Mathematical status.** The data $\mu$, $U$ and $J$ are real numbers and
functions; the equation and the attached objects are mathematical statements
about curves. Nothing here asserts that the equation describes a physical
interaction, and the names are conventional labels for the mathematical
objects only.

Let $\mu>0$, let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval, let
$U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
with at least two points, and let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force
trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ whose angular momentum $j=\mu\,r\times r'$ is a nonzero
constant vector ([[thm-cm-central-force-angular-momentum-conservation]]); write
$J:=|j|>0$. Let $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an oriented orthonormal triad with
$e_3=j/J$ ([[lem-cm-oriented-orthonormal-triads]]).

Then there are twice differentiable $\rho:I\to(0,\infty)$ and
$\theta:I\to\mathbb R$ with

$$r(t)=\rho(t)\bigl(\cos\theta(t)\,e_1+\sin\theta(t)\,e_2\bigr)\qquad(t\in I),$$

and for **every** such pair $(\rho,\theta)$:

1. $\rho(t)=|r(t)|$ for all $t$;
2. $\rho^2\theta'=J/\mu$ on $I$, so $\theta'>0$;
3. the effective-potential equation $\mu\rho''=-\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)'(\rho)$
   holds on $I$, with $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J=U+J^2/(2\mu\rho^2)$
   ([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]);
4. $E:=\frac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+U(|r|)$ equals
   $\frac12\mu\rho'^2+U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho)$ and is constant on $I$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(\theta_1,\theta_2)\subseteq(0,\pi)$ be a deflection
branch of [[def-cm-scattering-data]], with inverse $b(\theta)$, and set
$D=(a_1,a_2)\times(0,2\pi)$, $H=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\times(0,2\pi)$ and
$T(b,\varphi)=(\theta(b),\varphi)$. Restrict the incident measure $\nu$ to
$D$. Its pushforward, defined by $T_*\nu(B)=\nu(T^{-1}(B))$ for Borel
$B\subseteq H$, satisfies
$$T_*\nu(B)=\int_B b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|\,d\lambda_2(\theta,\varphi).$$
For every nonnegative Borel $g:H\to[0,+\infty]$, and for every real Borel
$g$ with either side's integral of $|g|$ finite, consequently
$$\int_D g(\theta(b),\varphi)b\,d\lambda_2(b,\varphi)=\int_H g(\theta,\varphi)b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|\,d\lambda_2(\theta,\varphi).$$
The nonnegative equality allows $+\infty$; in the real case both sides are
finite and absolute integrability on one side is equivalent to that on the
other. In particular it applies to continuous periodic test functions that
are nonnegative or absolutely integrable, and to compactly supported
continuous test functions. No equality of undefined signed improper
integrals is asserted. Nonnegative double-integral notation denotes the
corresponding Lebesgue integrals, with iterated integrals justified by Tonelli.

Thus the outgoing angular measure has density $b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|$
against $d\theta\,d\varphi$ and density
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(\theta)=\frac{b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|}{\sin\theta}=\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,|\theta'(b(\theta))|}$$
against the solid-angle measure. For finitely many branches on disjoint
incident intervals the measures add, including on overlapping image
intervals; in particular contributions with pairwise disjoint images add.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Borel/Lebesgue measure foundation below.

**Data.** Let $\mu>0$, let $U:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $R>0$ satisfy $U(r)=0$
for every $r\ge R$ (a **finite-range potential**), and let $E>0$ and $J>0$ be
reals. Write

$$V(r):=U(r)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2}\qquad(r>0).$$

**Incident flux measure.** Let $\nu$ be the Borel measure on the open rectangle
$(0,\infty)\times(0,2\pi)$ given by the density $b$ against Lebesgue measure
$\lambda_2$,

$$\nu(A):=\int_A b\,d\lambda_2(b,\varphi)\qquad(A\subseteq(0,\infty)\times(0,2\pi)\ \text{Borel}),$$

the integral being that of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]; the
nonnegative Borel function $(b,\varphi)\mapsto b$ defines a measure by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]
([[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]]). In the model this
measure records a uniform incident beam: an annulus of impact parameters
$[b_1,b_2)$ contributes $\pi(b_2^2-b_1^2)$ over the full azimuth range, or
$\tfrac12(b_2^2-b_1^2)$ per unit azimuth.

**Solid-angle element.** Let $\Omega$ be the Borel measure on
$(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$ with density $\sin$ against $\lambda_2$,

$$\Omega(B):=\int_B\sin\theta\,d\lambda_2(\theta,\varphi)\qquad(B\subseteq(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\ \text{Borel}),$$

where $\sin$ is the function of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]].
It is continuous, being differentiable by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]].
Also $\sin0=\sin\pi=0$ by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]];
strict increase on $[0,\pi/2]$ and strict decrease on $[\pi/2,\pi]$
([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]]) give $\sin\theta>0$ for
$0<\theta<\pi$. Thus $(\theta,\varphi)\mapsto\sin\theta$ is a nonnegative
Borel function (continuous preimages of Borel sets are Borel,
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), and
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]
establishes that $\Omega$ is a measure. This
is the standard solid-angle element written $\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi$
(the surface measure of the unit sphere in spherical coordinates, restricted
to the open chart).

**Deflection branch.** A **deflection branch** is an interval
$(a_1,a_2)\subseteq(0,\infty)$ with at least two points together with a
function $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ that is of class $C^1$ and satisfies
$\theta'(b)\ne0$ for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$. Such a $\theta$ is strictly
monotone (the continuous nonvanishing derivative has constant sign, and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]] gives strict monotonicity) and its image is an interval with endpoints $\theta_1<\theta_2$
([[def-interval]]); its inverse $b:(\theta_1,\theta_2)\to(a_1,a_2)$ is
differentiable with $b'(\theta)=1/\theta'(b(\theta))$, by the
derivative-of-an-inverse theorem [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]] applied to
the continuous injective $\theta$ (every point of $(a_1,a_2)$ is a limit point
of it, [[def-limit-point-r]], [[def-derivative]]).

**Cross-section density.** The **cross-section density of the branch** is the
function

$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(\theta):=\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'\bigl(b(\theta)\bigr)\bigr|} \qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2).$$

**Mathematical status.** The measures, branches and density are abstract data
independent of the finite-range trajectory data $(\mu,U,R,E,J)$. A branch is not asserted to arise from any
trajectory; the scattering theorems of this page identify the deflection
angle computed from the central-force equation with the values of such a
function under their hypotheses, and they compute the pushforward of $\nu$ under the induced map. No counting of
detected particles, and no empirical claim, is part of this definition.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Borel measures.

This item fixes the **cross-section** vocabulary of the central scattering
models of [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] relative to the uniform-incident
preparation of that definition.

**(i) The differential cross-section of a branch.** Let a central scattering
model be given, let $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ be a **deflection branch**
in the sense of [[def-cm-scattering-data]] — an interval $(a_1,a_2)$ of
impact parameters with $\theta$ of class $C^1$ and $\theta'(b)\ne0$ — and
suppose the branch **records the deflection** of the model: for every
$b\in(a_1,a_2)$ the scattering motion of the model with impact parameter $b$,
fixed energy $E$ and angular momentum magnitude $J(b)=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b$ has scattering angle
$\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\theta(b)$. Write
$(a_1,a_2)\ni b\mapsto\theta\in(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ for this bijection and
$b(\theta):=\theta^{-1}(\theta)$ for its inverse
([[def-cm-scattering-data]]). The **differential cross-section of the
branch** is the function
$$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta):=\frac{b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|}{\sin\theta} =\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'\bigl(b(\theta)\bigr)\bigr|}\qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2),$$
the cross-section density of [[def-cm-scattering-data]]. Its dimension is
$[\mathrm d\sigma/\mathrm d\Omega]=\ell^2$ (solid angle dimensionless in the
chosen convention, [[def-cm01-units]]), and one says "per steradian" for the
unit of solid angle.

**(ii) Branch sums.** Let $\mathcal B=\{(a_1^{(j)},a_2^{(j)},\theta_j)\}_{j=1}^N$
be a finite family of deflection branches of the same model whose incident
intervals $(a_1^{(j)},a_2^{(j)})$ are pairwise disjoint, with each branch
recording the model's deflections as in clause (i). Write
$A_j:=\theta_j((a_1^{(j)},a_2^{(j)}))$ for its image and
$b_j:=\theta_j^{-1}$ and
$q_j(\theta):=b_j(\theta)|b_j'(\theta)|/\sin\theta$ for its branch density
from clause (i), defined on $A_j$.
Angular images are not required to be disjoint. The **differential
cross-section of the model for this family** is, for
$\theta\in A:=\bigcup_{j=1}^N A_j$,
$$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma_{\mathcal B}}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta) :=\sum_{\{j:\,\theta\in A_j\}}q_j(\theta).$$
Thus $q_j$ is the contribution of branch $j$, and contributions add at every
angle belonging to more than one image. The total density for this family is
left undefined at angles belonging to no branch image. No claim is made that
the branch images cover $(0,\pi)$ or that the family includes every
deflection of the model.

**(iii) Cross-section measure and truncated totals.** For one branch $j$ with image $A_j$, and a Borel angular window $Y\subseteq A_j$, define
$$\sigma_j(Y):=\int_Yq_j(\theta)\,2\pi\sin\theta\,d\lambda_1(\theta)=\int_{Y\times(0,2\pi)}b_j(\theta)|b_j'(\theta)|\,d\lambda_2.$$
When only one branch is under discussion, write $\sigma(Y)$ for this
branch-specific measure.
For the finite family $\mathcal B$ of clause (ii), define
$$\sigma_{\mathcal B}(Y):=\sum_{j=1}^N\sigma_j(Y\cap A_j)=\int_{Y\cap A}\frac{\mathrm d\sigma_{\mathcal B}}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta)\,2\pi\sin\theta\,d\lambda_1(\theta)$$
for every Borel $Y\subseteq(0,\pi)$. These are nonnegative Lebesgue integrals over measurable sets in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], with extended value $+\infty$ allowed. The measure-level identity of [[thm-cm-differential-cross-section-density]] identifies each branch integral with the area of that branch's incident preimage; finite additivity gives the family formula, including where angular images overlap. On a compact interior interval each branch integral equals the ordinary Riemann integral; on an open interval its value is the monotone limit over compact interior truncations, equivalently the nonnegative improper integral when finite. General Borel windows use the Lebesgue integral, not a two-piece interval improper integral.
The **ideal total cross-section** of a branch is $\sigma_j(A_j)$; for a family it is $\sigma_{\mathcal B}(A)$. If infinite, there is no finite ideal total. Every compact interior angular window in a branch image has finite branch cross-section; more generally a cutoff whose incident preimage is bounded has finite cross-section. An arbitrary positive angular cutoff need not suffice for an arbitrary branch.

**(iv) The uniform-incident reading.** Under the uniform-incident preparation
of [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] clause (iv) with cutoff $b_{\max}$ and flux
$\Phi$, the model predicts the expected rate of scattered labels into a
Borel angular window $Y$ from one branch to be the flux times its cutoff
cross-section for the portion of that branch with $b<b_{\max}$. Writing
$T_j(b,\varphi)=(\theta_j(b),\varphi)$ on the branch rectangle and
$D_{\max}=(0,b_{\max})\times(0,2\pi)$, the branch cutoff measure is
$$\sigma_{j,b_{\max}}(Y):=\nu\!\left(T_j^{-1}(Y\times(0,2\pi))\cap ((a_1^{(j)},a_2^{(j)})\times(0,2\pi))\cap D_{\max}\right),$$
and its expected rate is $\Phi\sigma_{j,b_{\max}}(Y)$. For a finite family
with pairwise disjoint incident intervals, define
$\sigma_{\mathcal B,b_{\max}}(Y):=\sum_{j=1}^N\sigma_{j,b_{\max}}(Y)$;
the expected rate is $\Phi\sigma_{\mathcal B,b_{\max}}(Y)$, including when
the angular images overlap. If the entire incident preimage of $Y$ lies
below the cutoff, this sum is $\Phi\sigma_{\mathcal B}(Y)$. This is a
prediction of the model under the adopted preparation. In particular:

- $\sigma_j(Y)$ and $\sigma_{\mathcal B}(Y)$ are **not** probabilities per
  incident label, **not** counts of detected events, and **not** apparatus
  properties;
- a comparison with data requires a separately specified experiment: an
  apparatus model, a detector with finite angular resolution and acceptance,
  a sampling model and uncertainties, and a statistical analysis, none of
  which is supplied by this page;
- an ideal branch cross-section may diverge at a forward angle, while
  the adopted finite incident cutoff gives
  $\sigma_{\mathcal B,b_{\max}}(Y)\le\pi b_{\max}^{2}$ for every
  window $Y$, because the branch incident intervals are disjoint. Thus
  these cutoff rates are finite even if the ideal window cross-section
  is infinite. Without an incident cutoff, the rate $\Phi\sigma_{\mathcal B}(Y)$
  is finite exactly when that ideal window cross-section is finite.
  A finite measured rate constrains the model jointly with its incident
  preparation and apparatus acceptance;
- finite samples fluctuate: an observed angular distribution can miss a
  branch's features with positive probability under ordinary sampling models,
  and agreement is evidence about the model-plus-apparatus assumptions, not a
  proof of the model.

**(v) Status and exclusions.** The branch hypothesis includes
$\theta'\ne0$: the definition excludes angles at which
$\theta'(b)=0$ (rainbow-type stationary deflections) and leaves them to
separate limiting measures. It also excludes, at the level of this page,
friction and tangential contact laws, attractive capture, screening,
radiation, relativistic and quantum modifications, and any identification of
the model parameters with measured electromagnetic quantities; those require
separate models or cross-framework items. The functions $\theta$, $b$ and the
data $E$, $J$, $u$, $b_{\max}$, $\Phi$ are model data
([[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] clause (vi)).

**Why the objects are defined.** The inverse $b$ is $C^1$ with
$b'(\theta)=1/\theta'(b(\theta))$ because a $C^1$ function on an interval with
nowhere vanishing derivative is strictly monotone and has a differentiable
inverse ([[def-cm-scattering-data]]); $\sin\theta>0$ on $(0,\pi)$; hence the
denominators do not vanish and the density is finite at every interior point
of the branch image. The pushforward identity that justifies the reading
"density carried by the branch" is
[[thm-cm-differential-cross-section-density]], a theorem of this page's
mathematical suppliers.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the preparation and cross-section measures.

This item fixes the **scattering data** of the restricted model class of
[[post-cm05-central-model]] and the preparation conventions in which the
scattering statements of this page are phrased. All objects are model data;
nothing here is a measured value.

**(i) The scattering model.** A **central scattering model** is a model of
class (i) of [[post-cm05-central-model]] with $N=2$ labels, masses
$m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), no external forces, and a
static central pair potential $u\in C^2(J_0)$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]])
whose collision-excluded interval satisfies $(0,\infty)\subseteq J_0$, so
that the only forbidden configuration is the collision $r=0$. Its **reduced
problem** is the one-label problem of class (ii) with reduced mass
$\mu:=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ ([[def-cm01-units]]: $[\mu]=\mu$) and the same
potential, presented through the relative coordinate $r=x_1-x_2$; by
[[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]] the relative coordinate of every motion of
the model is a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ and every pair of an
affine centre-of-mass motion and a solution of the reduced equation on a
common interval reconstructs a motion of the model.

**(ii) Scattering motions and their data.** Let $r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$
be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ defined on all of $\mathbb R$
with values $|r(t)|\in J_0$ and with constant angular momentum
$j=\mu\,r\times r'=Je_3\ne0$ for $J>0$ and an oriented orthonormal triad
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ ([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]],
[[thm-cm-central-force-angular-momentum-conservation]],
[[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]],
[[lem-cm-oriented-orthonormal-triads]]). Call $r$ a **scattering motion** when it has a unique apsis $t_*$ with $\rho=|r|$ decreasing strictly before $t_*$, increasing strictly after it, $\rho(t)\to\infty$ as $t\to\pm\infty$, and the nonzero limits below exist with the stated speed, equal finite impact-distance limits and finite equal half-advances. These are defining conditions, not deductions for arbitrary $C^2$ potentials. The finite-range theorem requires $u=0$ beyond some $R$, $E,J>0$, a simple outer turning point $V(r_*)=E$, $V'(r_*)<0$, $V(r)<E$ for $r>r_*$, and a trajectory staying above and attaining $r_*$. The repulsive Coulomb theorem instead requires $u=\kappa/\rho$, $\kappa,E,J>0$ and a trajectory attaining its turning radius. Each theorem proves the defining conditions in its own scope. Its **energy** is the constant
$$E:=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+u(\lvert r\rvert)>0$$
of [[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]] (constant by
[[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]] clause 4), its **asymptotic
velocities** are the limits
$$v_-:=\lim_{t\to-\infty}r'(t),\qquad v_+:=\lim_{t\to+\infty}r'(t),$$
taken in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]
(their existence under the hypotheses is a theorem, not a convention), and
its **scattering speed** is
$$v_\infty:=\lVert v_-\rVert_2=\lVert v_+\rVert_2=\sqrt{2E/\mu},$$
the equality being part of the scattering theorems. The **incoming branch**
is the trajectory restricted to times before its apsis. The **impact parameter** is the asymptotic perpendicular-distance limit
$$b:=\lim_{t\to-\infty}\frac{\lVert r(t)\times v_-\rVert_2}{\lVert v_-\rVert_2}=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{\lVert r(t)\times v_+\rVert_2}{\lVert v_+\rVert_2}=\frac{J}{\mu v_\infty}>0.$$
Here the distance at each time is to the line through the origin in the limiting velocity direction, not to an exact affine trajectory line. For a finite-range potential, the sufficiently early incoming tail is a straight half-line whose affine extension has this distance; for Coulomb these are only limits, with no exact free tail or finite longitudinal intercept claimed. The dimension is $[b]=\ell$.

**(iii) Polar advance and deflection conventions.** Fix polar data
$(\rho,\theta)$ of the scattering motion in the triad, $r=\rho\,n(\theta)$,
$n(\varphi):=\cos\varphi\,e_1+\sin\varphi\,e_2$
([[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]), and let $t_*$ be an apsis time,
$|r(t_*)|=\min_t|r(t)|$. The **polar advance of one half** is
$$\Delta:=\theta(+\infty)-\theta(t_*)=\theta(t_*)-\theta(-\infty),$$
defined by the limits asserted in the scattering theorems, and the
**polar advance of the motion** is $2\Delta$. The **scattering angle** is the
undirected angle between the asymptotic velocity directions,
$$\theta_{\mathrm{s}}:=\arccos\!\left(\frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{\lVert v_-\rVert_2\,\lVert v_+\rVert_2}\right)\in[0,\pi],$$
the incoming and outgoing velocity directions are oriented, so this is not the smaller unoriented angle between two lines;
the **signed velocity rotation** is the continuous rotation angle of
$r'(t)$, measured counterclockwise about $e_3$ relative to the incoming
direction, so that a positive value is a counterclockwise turn. The scattering
theorems give $\cos\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\cos(\pi-2\Delta)$ and the signed
rotation $2\Delta-\pi$; in particular, when $0<\Delta<\pi/2$ the scattering
angle is
$$\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi),$$
while outside that range $\theta_{\mathrm{s}}$ is the wrapped value $\arccos(\cos(\pi-2\Delta))$.
The **deflection map** at fixed model potential $u$, reduced mass $\mu$ and energy $E>0$ is the partial map $b\mapsto\theta_{\mathrm s}(b)$ on those $b>0$ for which a scattering motion exists and all such motions have the same angle. Its corresponding angular momentum magnitude varies as
$$J(b)=\mu b v_\infty=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b.$$
Time translation and rotation of a motion do not change its angle. **Deflection branches** are $C^1$ branches of this partial map as defined in [[def-cm-scattering-data]].

**(iv) The uniform-incident preparation (adopted model datum).** The
**uniform-incident preparation** of a central scattering model with cutoff
$b_{\max}>0$ and flux $\Phi>0$ is the following adopted model of a scattering
experiment for the reduced problem: independent incident reduced labels with common energy $E>0$ and impact-azimuth probability measure
$$P(A)=\frac{\nu(A\cap D_{\max})}{\pi b_{\max}^2},\qquad D_{\max}=(0,b_{\max})\times(0,2\pi).$$
Its density is $b/(\pi b_{\max}^2)$, and its total mass is one since $\nu(D_{\max})=\pi b_{\max}^2$. Angular momentum magnitude is $J(b)=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b$; its plane orientation may vary with azimuth. The **incident flux** $\Phi$ is the expected number of incident labels per unit area per unit time, with $[\Phi]=\ell^{-2}\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). The adopted total arrival rate is $\Phi\pi b_{\max}^2$, so for a Borel set $A\subseteq D_{\max}$ the expected incident rate is
$$\dot N(A)=\Phi\pi b_{\max}^2 P(A)=\Phi\nu(A).$$
Here $\nu$ is the incident area measure of [[def-cm-scattering-data]]. For a
specified deflection branch $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ and a
Borel scattering-angle window $Y\subseteq(\theta_1,\theta_2)$, the predicted
rate from that branch under this cutoff preparation is
$$\dot N_{\mathrm{br}}(Y):=\Phi\,\nu\!\left(\left\{(b,\varphi)\in D_{\max}:a_1<b<a_2,\ \theta(b)\in Y\right\}\right).$$
The preimage is Borel because $\theta$ is continuous on its branch. For a
finite family of branches with pairwise disjoint incident intervals, branch
rates add, including when their angular images overlap. Incidences outside
recorded scattering branches are not assigned an outgoing scattering angle
by this definition. The rate above integrates over the full impact-azimuth
range; it is a model prediction, not a detected count. Comparing it with data
requires a separately specified experiment, apparatus model, sampling model
and statistical analysis.

**(v) Reading conventions.** All angles and lengths above are data of the
**relative** problem: angles are computed from the relative coordinate
$r=x_1-x_2$ and its asymptotic velocities $v_\pm$, not from either label's
trajectory. The centre of mass $X$ and the reconstruction formulas
$x_1=X+\frac{m_2}{M}r$ and $x_2=X-\frac{m_1}{M}r$, with $M=m_1+m_2$, are
those of clause (i), [[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]] and
[[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]] clause 4. They show that individual-label
directions generally differ from the relative direction and from each
other. "Target", "projectile" and "detector" are names for model components
and carry no empirical claim.

**(vi) Exclusions and status.** The class excludes velocity- or
time-dependent, non-central and non-potential forces; constraints and
reaction forces; collisions $r=0$; external forces; and models with more than
two labels, exactly as in [[post-cm05-central-model]] clause (v). The
preparation of clause (iv) is one adopted idealisation among many; the
scattering theorems state separately which potentials, energies and angular
momenta produce the data of clauses (ii)-(iii). The quantities $\mu$, $u$
(with any parameters it carries), $E$, $J$, $b$, $b_{\max}$, $\Phi$ are model
data; quantitative empirical use requires separately stated measured inputs
with uncertainties, and no statement of this page asserts that any physical
system is exactly a central scattering model or that any beam is exactly
uniform.

**Why the objects are defined.** The relative coordinate is a central-force
trajectory by the cited reduction theorem; the attached energy and angular
momentum are defined by [[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]] and are constant
on the trajectory by [[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]] clause 4 and
[[thm-cm-central-force-angular-momentum-conservation]]; the impact parameter is defined by its limiting distance, with existence and equality proved under the theorem-specific hypotheses; and the
preparation measure of clause (iv) is the measure $\nu$ of
[[def-cm-scattering-data]]. The arccosine of clause (iii) is defined because
the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives
$|\langle v_-,v_+\rangle|/(\lVert v_-\rVert_2\lVert v_+\rVert_2)\le1$
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

**Mathematical status.** The vocabulary is attached to the adopted model
class of [[post-cm05-central-model]]; the existence of the limits, the
identities for $v_\infty$, $b$, $\Delta$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{s}}$, and the
form of the deflection map under explicit potential hypotheses are the
content of the mathematics and physics theorems of this page, not of this
definition.

Let $\mu>0$, let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval, let
$U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
with at least two points, and let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force
trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with angular momentum vector
$j=\mu\,r\times r'$ ([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]). Then:

1. $j$ is differentiable on $I$ with $j'(t)=0$ for every $t\in I$; hence $j$ is
   constant on $I$;
2. for every $t\in I$, $\langle r(t),j(t)\rangle=0$ and
   $\langle r'(t),j(t)\rangle=0$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\det G(u,v)$, and this value is positive exactly when $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent.

Equivalently,
$$\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2.$$

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ carries the
Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
[[def-p-norms-on-rn]], whose induced metric is the published $d_2$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]],
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). A function into $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is called
**vector-valued**.

### Continuity

Let $(X, d_X)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$
carry the restricted metric $d_A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]), let
$f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $a \in A$. Then $f$ is **continuous at $a$**
when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ d_X(x,a) < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ \lVert f(x) - f(a)\rVert_2 < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon, \delta$ ranging over the positive reals, and **continuous on
$A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**This is not a new notion, and that is the point of writing it down.** Since
$\lVert f(x)-f(a)\rVert_2 = d_2\bigl(f(x),f(a)\bigr)$ and $d_A$ is the
restriction of $d_X$, the displayed condition is **verbatim** the condition of
[[def-metric-continuity]] for the map of metric spaces
$f : (A,d_A) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$. So every theorem about continuous maps
of metric spaces applies to vector-valued functions with no translation, and
this library has exactly one notion of continuity here. The same move was made
once before, between the $\mathbb{R}$-native and the metric notions, in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]]; this item is that move one dimension up in
the codomain.

The two cases used below are $X = \mathbb{R}$ with $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) and $X = \mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $d_2$, for
$n \ge 1$.

### Limits, for a real domain

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$, let $c$ be a limit
point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) and let $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. We say
$f(x)$ **tends to $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$**, and write
$\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$, when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ 0 < |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ \lVert f(x) - L\rVert_2 < \varepsilon\ \bigr].$$

This is the condition of [[def-function-limit]] with the absolute value in the
codomain replaced by $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$; as there, the puncture $0 < |x-c|$ is
what makes $c$ a point the function need not be defined at, and the hypothesis
that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is what stops the condition from being satisfied
vacuously.

**The notation denotes: at most one $L$ satisfies the condition.** Suppose $L$
and $L'$ both do and $L \ne L'$. Then $\varepsilon := \lVert L-L'\rVert_2 / 2 > 0$
by (N1) for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). Take $\delta$
and $\delta'$ for this $\varepsilon$ and put $\eta := \min\{\delta,\delta'\} > 0$.
Since $c$ is a limit point of $A$ there is $x \in A$ with $0 < |x-c| < \eta$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), and then

$$\lVert L - L'\rVert_2 \;\le\; \lVert L - f(x)\rVert_2 + \lVert f(x) - L'\rVert_2 \;<\; \varepsilon + \varepsilon \;=\; \lVert L-L'\rVert_2$$

by (N3) and (N2), which trichotomy forbids. So $L = L'$.

### Components

For $i < m$ define the $i$-th **coordinate projection**
$\pi_i : \mathbb{R}^{m} \to \mathbb{R}$ by $\pi_i(y) := y_i = y(i)$, and for
$f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ the $i$-th **component** $f_i := \pi_i \circ f$, a
real-valued function on $A$.

**Each $\pi_i$ is $1$-Lipschitz** ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]): for
$y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$,

$$\bigl|\pi_i(y) - \pi_i(z)\bigr| \;=\; |y_i - z_i| \;\le\; \lVert y - z\rVert_2 \;=\; d_2(y,z),$$

the middle inequality being $|w_i| \le \lVert w\rVert_2$ at $w := y-z$
([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]] clause 3, or
directly because $w_i^{2}$ is one term of the sum $\sum_{k<m}w_k^{2}$). Written
in coordinates, $f(x)$ is the vector whose $i$-th coordinate is $f_i(x)$, and
$f(x) = \sum_{i<m} f_i(x)\,e_i$ in the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]).

Let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval
([[def-interval]]), let $u:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^k$ for some
$k\ge1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and put
$$A:=\{\,x\in\mathbb R^3:\lvert x\rvert\in J_0\,\},\qquad \lvert x\rvert:=\lVert x\rVert_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle},$$
the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. $A$ is open in $\mathbb R^3$ and $0\notin A$;
2. the function $N:A\to(0,\infty)$, $N(x):=\lvert x\rvert$, is of class
   $C^\infty$ on $A$; it is totally differentiable at every $x\in A$
   ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]) with
   $$DN(x)h=\frac{\langle x,h\rangle}{\lvert x\rvert}\qquad(h\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad\text{so}\qquad\nabla N(x)=\frac{x}{\lvert x\rvert}$$
   ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]);
3. the radial composite $U:=u\circ N:A\to\mathbb R$, $U(x)=u(\lvert x\rvert)$,
   is of class $C^k$ on $A$ and totally differentiable at every $x\in A$
   with
   $$DU(x)h=u'(\lvert x\rvert)\,\frac{\langle x,h\rangle}{\lvert x\rvert}=\Bigl\langle u'(\lvert x\rvert)\frac{x}{\lvert x\rvert},\,h\Bigr\rangle\qquad(h\in\mathbb R^3),$$
   that is, $\nabla U(x)=u'(\lvert x\rvert)\,x/\lvert x\rvert$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $F$ is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time**, if every compact time-state cylinder $C\subseteq D$ has a finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x),(t,y)\in C$ have the same time coordinate.

On every compact time-state cylinder the state-variable inequality holds with one finite constant $L$. More generally, let $p\ge1$, let $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, let $D_\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\Lambda$ be open in its relative Euclidean topology, and let $F:D_\Lambda\to\mathbb R^n$. The parameter family is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniform in time and parameters** when every compact time-state-parameter cylinder $C\subseteq D_\Lambda$ has one finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x,\lambda)-F(t,y,\lambda)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x,\lambda),(t,y,\lambda)\in C$ have the same time and parameter coordinates.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]. Let $t_0<b$ be reals, let $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ with $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, and let $x:[t_0,b)\to\mathbb R^n$ be a solution of the initial value problem

$$x'(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad x(t_0)=x_0$$

on $[t_0,b)$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). Suppose there is a compact set $K\subseteq D$ and a real $\delta>0$ such that

$$\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\in K\qquad\text{for every }t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b).$$

Then:

1. there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a solution $\tilde x:[t_0,b+\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R^n$ of the same initial value problem with $\tilde x(t)=x(t)$ for all $t\in[t_0,b)$; in particular $\tilde x(b)=\lim_{t\uparrow b}x(t)$ exists and lies in the state projection of $K$;
2. if moreover $D=\mathbb R\times U$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $F$ is autonomous, $F(t,z)=G(z)$ with $G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and if there is a compact $K_0\subseteq U$ with $x(t)\in K_0$ for every $t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b)$, then the extension conclusion of clause 1 holds as well.

Let $c < d$ be reals and let $\varphi : [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable
at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ ([[def-derivative]]), with
$\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to
\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is
exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may
lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times.
The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse
function is ever formed.

**Continuity of $f$ is a hypothesis and cannot be weakened to integrability.**
With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be
integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is
the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Call $G : I \to \mathbb{R}$ a **primitive of $f$ on
$I$** when $G$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ as a function on $I$ with
$G' = f$ there ([[def-derivative]]). Then:

1. **Existence.** Fix $c_0 \in I$. The function
   $$F : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad F(x) \;:=\; \int_{c_0}^x f$$
   is defined at every $x \in I$ ([[def-oriented-integral]],
   [[def-the-integral-function]]) and is a primitive of $f$ on $I$.
2. **Uniqueness up to a constant.** If $G_1$ and $G_2$ are primitives of $f$ on
   $I$ then there is a real $k$ with $G_1(x) = G_2(x) + k$ for every $x \in I$.
3. **Evaluation.** If $a, b \in I$ with $a < b$ and $G$ is any primitive of $f$
   on $I$, then
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**The scope is exactly the continuous case, and that is not a limitation of the
proof.** An integrable function need not have a primitive, and a function with a
primitive need not be integrable; this corollary is precisely the intersection
where both fundamental theorems apply, and both witnesses are on the companion
page.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
injective ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). Then:

1. $f$ is strictly monotone ([[def-monotone-function]]);
2. $f[I]$ is order-convex;
3. the map $f : I \to f[I]$ is a bijection, so there is exactly one
   $g : f[I] \to I$ with $g(f(x)) = x$ for every $x \in I$ and $f(g(u)) = u$ for
   every $u \in f[I]$;
4. $g$ is strictly monotone in the same sense as $f$: increasing if $f$ is
   increasing, decreasing if $f$ is decreasing;
5. $g$ is continuous on $f[I]$.

**"Interval" means "order-convex" here**, as throughout this library
([[thm-connected-subsets-of-r-are-intervals]] is what licenses the word and
[[def-interval]] records that the classification of order-convex sets into the
nine written forms is not proved here). No compactness and no boundedness is
assumed: $I$ may be open, half-open, unbounded, or a single point.

derivations.claim: By [L1], the relative coordinate is a $C^2$ central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ with attached angular momentum $j=Je_3$ and energy $E$, and $|r(t)|\in(0,\infty)$. The potential and turning-point conditions are exactly (H1)-(H2), and the trajectory attains $r_*$ at $t_*$ while satisfying $|r|\ge r_*$.

Global branches and extension: the first-order Cartesian central-force field of [L6] has a unique maximal solution through $(r(t_*),r'(t_*))$ by [L7], and the given trajectory on $I$ is its restriction; write the maximal curve as $\bar r$ and $\rho=|\bar r|$. By [L2], $\rho'(t_*)=0$ and $\rho''(t_*)=-V'(r_*)/\mu>0$, so $\rho>r_*$ immediately on both sides of $t_*$. Whenever $\rho>r_*$, the energy identity and (H2) give $\rho'\ne0$, hence $\rho'$ has constant sign on each connected interval where $\rho>r_*$. On the outgoing interval adjacent to $t_*$ that sign is positive. If the interval had a finite right endpoint $T$ inside the maximal domain, continuity would give $\rho(T)=r_*$; then the radial equation in [L2] gives $\rho''(T)>0$, so $\rho'<0$ immediately before $T$, contradicting the positive sign on that interval. Thus the outgoing interval reaches the maximal right endpoint, with $\rho>r_*$ and $\rho'>0$ throughout. The symmetric argument gives $\rho>r_*$ and $\rho'<0$ on the incoming interval. In particular $\rho\ge r_*$ throughout the maximal interval. Since $u$ is continuous on $[r_*,R]$ when this interval is nonempty and vanishes for $r\ge R$, it is bounded below on $[r_*,\infty)$; the energy identity therefore bounds $|\bar r'|$. On any finite endpoint, $\bar r$ is bounded by this speed bound and remains at distance at least $r_*>0$ from the origin. Its state consequently lies in a compact subset of $\{(r,v):r\ne0\}$ near that endpoint, so [L7] continues it past every finite endpoint. The maximal interval is therefore all of $\mathbb R$, and uniqueness is from [L6]. The global branches and radial energy identity established here supply the hypotheses for the direct quadrature and angle calculation below. For the model statement, let $X$ be the centre of mass of the original motion, affine on $I$ with $X''=0$ by [L1] clause 2, and let $\bar X$ be its affine extension to $\mathbb R$; then by [L1] clause 4 the pair $(\bar X,\bar r)$ reconstructs a motion of the model with its autonomous force law extended to time window $\mathbb R$, because $|\bar r(t)|\in(0,\infty)$ keeps the configuration admissible. This is clause 1.

Time quadrature in clause 1: for $s>r_*$ the integrand in the displayed $\tau(s)$ is positive and continuous. The derivative definition gives $(E-V(s))/(s-r_*)\to -V'(r_*)>0$ as $s\downarrow r_*$, so near $r_*$ the integrand is bounded by a constant times $(s-r_*)^{-1/2}$, which has a finite integral on every bounded interval starting at $r_*$. Thus $\tau(s)<\infty$ for every finite $s\ge r_*$. Since $V(s)=J^2/(2\mu s^2)\to0$ for $s\ge R$, the integrand tends to $1/\sqrt{2E/\mu}>0$ and $\tau(s)\to\infty$; it is strictly increasing from $\tau(r_*)=0$. On either monotone branch, the fundamental theorem gives $\tau'(s)=1/\sqrt{(2/\mu)(E-V(s))}$ for $s>r_*$. By the chain rule and the radial energy identity, $(\tau\circ\rho)'=1$ on the outgoing branch and $(\tau\circ\rho)'=-1$ on the incoming branch. Taking the limits at $t_*$ gives $\tau(\rho(t))=|t-t_*|$, and strict increase and unboundedness of $\tau$ yield $\rho(t_*\pm\tau(s))=s$ for every $s\ge r_*$. This proves the quadrature assertion and also $\rho(t)\to\infty$ on both tails.

Free tails and asymptotic velocities: on the outgoing branch $\rho$ is increasing. It is unbounded: if it had a finite limit $L>r_*$, the energy identity and (H2) would imply $\rho'(t)\to\sqrt{(2/\mu)(E-V(L))}>0$, contradicting convergence to $L$. Thus $\rho(t)\to\infty$, and after it passes $R$ it remains there; since $u'(r)=0$ for $r\ge R$, the Cartesian equation gives $\bar r''=0$ on that tail. The incoming branch is symmetric. Now let $t_1\ge t_*$ with $\rho(t_1)>R$; the motion is free for all later times and its constant velocity is $v_+:=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\bar r'(t)$. At any such free point $u=0$, so energy gives $|v_+|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}=:v_\infty>0$. If instead $\rho(t_1)=R$, define $q_+(t):=\bar r(t_1)+(t-t_1)\bar r'(t_1)$ for $t\ge t_1$. Differentiating $\rho^2=\langle\bar r,\bar r\rangle$ gives $\langle\bar r,\bar r'\rangle=\rho\rho'$; since $\rho$ is nondecreasing on this branch, $\langle\bar r(t_1),\bar r'(t_1)\rangle=R\rho'(t_1)\ge0$. Also $|\bar r'(t_1)|^2=2E/\mu>0$ because $u(R)=0$, so $|q_+(t)|^2=R^2+2(t-t_1)\langle\bar r(t_1),\bar r'(t_1)\rangle+(t-t_1)^2|\bar r'(t_1)|^2\ge R^2$. Since $u'(r)=0$ for all $r\ge R$, including $R$, $q_+$ and $\bar r$ solve the same Cartesian equation with the same state at $t_1$; [L6] gives $\bar r=q_+$ for all $t\ge t_1$. Thus its constant velocity is again $v_+$ and has norm $v_\infty$. The incoming equality case is identical with $q_-(t):=\bar r(t_2)+(t-t_2)\bar r'(t_2)$ for $t\le t_2$: $\rho'(t_2)\le0$ and $t-t_2\le0$ give $|q_-(t)|\ge R$, so [L6] gives the incoming free formula and $v_-:=\lim_{t\to-\infty}\bar r'(t)$ with $|v_-|=v_\infty$. This proves clause 2's free-motion and velocity claims.
