Clause 3, polar advance: apply [[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]] to the global trajectory $\bar r$ of step 2.1, giving polar data $(\rho,\theta)$ on all of $\mathbb R$. Let $n(\varphi)=\cos\varphi\,e_1+\sin\varphi\,e_2$ be its unit radial direction. On the outgoing branch, $\theta'=J/(\mu\rho^2)>0$ and $\rho'=\sqrt{(2/\mu)(E-V(\rho))}$; substitution on compact subintervals away from $t_*$ gives $$\theta(+\infty)-\theta(t_*)=\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{J\,\mathrm dr}{r^2\sqrt{2\mu(E-V(r))}}=:\Delta.$$ The integral converges at $r_*$ because $E-V(r)\sim -V'(r_*)(r-r_*)$ as $r\downarrow r_*$, and at infinity because $V(r)=J^2/(2\mu r^2)$ for $r\ge R$; it is positive. The same substitution on the incoming branch, where $\rho'<0$ and $\theta'>0$, gives $\theta(t_*)-\theta(-\infty)=\Delta$. Thus $\theta_\pm:=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}\theta(t)$ exist and $\theta_+-\theta_-=2\Delta$. By the free tails of step 3.2, $\bar r(t)/\rho(t)\to v_+/|v_+|$ as $t\to+\infty$ and $\bar r(t)/\rho(t)\to-v_-/|v_-|$ as $t\to-\infty$. Since $\bar r/\rho=n(\theta)$, continuity gives $n(\theta_+)=v_+/|v_+|$ and $n(\theta_-)=-v_-/|v_-|$. The addition formulas imply $n(\theta_+)=R_{2\Delta}n(\theta_-)$, hence $$\frac{v_+}{|v_+|}=-R_{2\Delta}\Bigl(\frac{v_-}{|v_-|}\Bigr).$$ For any unit $q$ in the plane, $\langle q,e_3\times q\rangle=0$, so this identity gives $\langle v_-,v_+\rangle/(|v_-||v_+|)=-\cos(2\Delta)=\cos(\pi-2\Delta)$. Therefore $\theta_{\mathrm s}=\arccos(\cos(\pi-2\Delta))$ by clause (iii) of [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]]; when $0<\Delta<\pi/2$, $\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi)$ is that angle. To identify the continuous signed rotation, differentiate $\bar r=\rho n(\theta)$: $\bar r'=\rho'n(\theta)+J/(\mu\rho)(e_3\times n(\theta))$, whose positive tangential component ensures $|\bar r'|>0$. Put $\psi(t)=\arccos(\rho'(t)/|\bar r'(t)|)\in(0,\pi)$ using [L9]. The Pythagorean identity and positivity give $\bar r'/|\bar r'|=n(\theta+\psi)$, so $\theta+\psi$ is a continuous real angle for the velocity direction. On the free tails, $|\bar r'|=v_\infty$ and the radial energy equation gives $\rho'\to-v_\infty$ incoming and $\rho'\to v_\infty$ outgoing. Thus $\psi\to\pi$ incoming and $\psi\to0$ outgoing; the net continuous rotation is $\theta_+-(\theta_-+\pi)=2\Delta-\pi$. This is clause 3.

Clause 2, impact parameter: on the incoming branch choose $t_2\le t_*$ with $\rho(t_2)\ge R$; the affine extension of the incoming free tail is $\{\bar r(t_2)+s\,v_-:s\in\mathbb R\}$ and its perpendicular distance from the origin is $|\bar r(t_2)\times v_-|/|v_-|=|j|/(\mu|v_-|)=J/(\mu v_\infty)$ by step 3.2 and [L4]. For the outgoing line $\{\bar r(t_1)+s\,v_+:s\in\mathbb R\}$, the same computation with [L4] gives distance $|\bar r(t_1)\times v_+|/|v_+|=|j|/(\mu|v_+|)=J/(\mu v_\infty)$; since $J/(\mu\sqrt{2E/\mu})=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}$, both distances equal $b=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}$ as displayed, and multiplying by $v_\infty$ gives $J=\mu b v_\infty$.

Clause 4: the assumed family uses the same $\mu,u,E$ and varying $J(b)=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b$, with (H2) and the trajectory conditions for each member. By the branch hypothesis its scattering angle is $\theta(b)$; [L3] gives the measure and test-function identity on the entire open branch with the stated nonnegative or absolute-integrability condition. Under the preparation the probability law is $P=\nu|_{D_{\max}}/(\pi b_{\max}^2)$ and the total arrival rate is $\Phi\pi b_{\max}^2$. Hence the branch portion $(a_1,c)\times(0,2\pi)$ has expected rate $\Phi\nu((a_1,c)\times(0,2\pi))$. Its pushforward is supported in $Y=\theta((a_1,c))$, so [L3] identifies that area with this branch's contribution $\sigma_{\mathrm{br}}(Y)=2\pi\int_{a_1}^c b\,db=\pi(c^2-a_1^2)$. Other branches with overlapping images contribute separately by finite addition as defined in [[def-cm15-cross-section]] clause (ii). This proves the rate regardless of whether the branch increases or decreases.

Clause 5 is the statement of the scope: the branch hypothesis of clause 4 is an explicit assumption, not a consequence of (H1)-(H2); no monotonicity or nonvanishing of $\theta'$ off the branch is used or claimed; and the exclusions are those of [[post-cm05-central-model]] clause (v) together with (H1). This completes the proof.

citations.quote:
Let $\mu>0$, let $\kappa>0$ and $U(r)=\kappa/r$ on $(0,\infty)$ (the repulsive
Coulomb potential, of class $C^2$), let $E>0$ and $J>0$, and put
$$V(r):=\frac{\kappa}{r}+\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2},\qquad b:=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}>0,\qquad \alpha:=\frac{\kappa}{Eb}>0.$$
Then:

1. $V$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, with $V(r)\to\infty$ as $r\downarrow0$
   and $V(r)\to0$ as $r\to\infty$; hence there is exactly one $r_*>0$ with
   $V(r_*)=E$, it is simple ($V'(r_*)<0$), and $V(r)<E$ for all $r>r_*$.
2. Let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with
   constant angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, energy $E$, with $|r(t)|\ge r_*$
   for all $t\in I$ and with $|r(t_*)|=r_*$ for some $t_*\in I$. Then $r$
   extends uniquely to all of $\mathbb R$; along the extension $\rho=|r|\ge r_*>0$
   (no collision), $\rho$ is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and
   strictly increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$, and the asymptotic velocities
   $v_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r'(t)$ exist with $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}$.
   Moreover the asymptotic perpendicular distance of each branch to its
   limiting direction exists and equals
   $$b=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}=\frac{J}{\mu|v_\pm|}, \qquad\text{so that}\qquad J=\mu b|v_\pm| .$$
The distance in clause 2 means the limit of $|r(t)\times v_\pm|/|v_\pm|$ as $t\to\pm\infty$, the distance to the line through the origin in the limiting velocity direction; it does not assert a free tail or a finite longitudinal intercept.

3. For the polar angle, with $u_*:=1/r_*$,
   $$\Delta:=\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{J\,\mathrm dr}{r^2\sqrt{2\mu\,(E-V(r))}} =\int_0^{u_*}\frac{b\,\mathrm du}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{\kappa}{E}u-b^2u^2}} =\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$

4. Write $n_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r(t)/|r(t)|$. Then
   $n_+=v_+/|v_+|$, $n_-=-v_-/|v_-|$, and in an oriented polar plane
   the outgoing velocity direction is the incoming direction rotated by
   $2\Delta-\pi\in(-\pi,0)$. In particular
   $$\frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{|v_-||v_+|}=\cos(\pi-2\Delta),\qquad \theta_{\mathrm s}=\pi-2\Delta=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$
   For fixed $\mu,\kappa,E$ this gives an actual family for every $b>0$,
   with angular momentum $J(b)=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b$: choose its unique turning
   radius and initial data $r(0)=r_*e_1$, $r'(0)=J(b)e_2/(\mu r_*)$.
   Local existence and the extension in clause 2 give a member of the family
   for every $b$, unique up to apsis time and oriented plane placement.

Adopt, as the **central-force model** for the two-body part of this page, the
following restricted model class inside the force and interaction branches of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]].

**(i) The two-label central model.** A model of class (i) is a force model of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$ labels, fixed masses
$m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_0$, the
collision-excluded configuration domain
$$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$
for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and the force map presented through the
time-independent **static central pair potential**
$$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),\qquad u:J_0\to\mathbb R\ \text{of class }C^2,$$
so that $F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain (clauses (iii)
and (iv) of [[post-cm02-interactions]]; $U$ is of class $C^2$ on the open
$Q$ by [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). In the external-plus-pair
presentation of clause (i) of that postulate the model has
$F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$: no external forces act on the labels of a model
of class (i).

**(ii) The reduced one-label problem.** For a model of class (i) put
$\mu:=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)>0$ of dimension $\mu$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). The
**reduced problem** of the model is the one-label problem of mass $\mu$ whose
unknown is the relative coordinate $r=x_1-x_2$ and whose equation is
$$\mu\,r''=-\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r;$$
by [[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]] the relative coordinate of every motion
of a model of class (i) solves this equation, and every pair of a uniform
centre-of-mass motion and a solution of the reduced equation on a common
interval reconstructs a motion of the model. Adopt the reduced problem as the
object that the central-force statements of this page describe, and the
central-force-trajectory vocabulary of
[[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]] (attached angular momentum
$j=\mu\,r\times r'$ and energy $E=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+u(\lvert
r\rvert)$) as the vocabulary in which those statements are phrased.

**(iii) The one-label fixed-centre idealization.** A **one-label central
model** is a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=1$,
mass $\mu>0$, time window $I_0$, a fixed **centre** $c\in\mathbb R^3$, the
configuration domain $Q_c=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lvert x-c\rvert\in J_0\}$, and
the external force map
$$F(t,x,v)=-\frac{u'(\lvert x-c\rvert)}{\lvert x-c\rvert}\,(x-c),$$
presented through the potential $u(\lvert x-c\rvert)$ with the same function
$u\in C^2(J_0)$. This model is the **fixed-centre idealization** of the
reduced problem: it drops the centre-of-mass degree of freedom and holds the
force centre fixed. It is a separate adopted model class, not a consequence
of class (i), and every use of it must state that the idealization is
intended.

**(iv) Reading conventions.** In the statements of this page: the **force
centre** of the reduced problem is the origin of the relative coordinate
$r$; an **orbit** is the trajectory $t\mapsto r(t)$ of the reduced problem
(equivalently, by [[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]], the trajectory of either
label relative to the centre of mass, up to the mass ratio); "circular" and
"elliptic" name properties of that trajectory; and the words "planet",
"satellite", "central body" and "test particle" name labels of a model of
class (i) or (iii). These words carry no empirical claim about nature.

**(v) Exclusions and status.** The class excludes: velocity-dependent and
explicitly time-dependent central forces; non-central and non-potential
forces; constraints and reaction forces; colliding configurations
$x_1=x_2$ (equivalently $r=0$); external forces on the labels; and models
with more than two labels. Finite-size, rotational, deformational, dissipative
and relativistic effects are outside the class. The masses, the interval
$J_0$ and the function $u$ (including any parameters it carries) are model
data, not measured values ([[def-cm01-units]]); quantitative empirical use
requires separately stated measured inputs with their uncertainties, and no
statement of this page asserts that any physical system is exactly a model
of this class.

Adopt the force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$
labels, masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time
window $I_0$, and the collision-excluded configuration domain
$$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$
for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]). Suppose the model presents its force map
through the time-independent potential
$$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),$$
where $u:J_0\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that
$F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain ([[post-cm02-interactions]],
clauses (iii) and (iv), [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). Let
$x:J\to Q$ be a **motion** of the model on an interval $J$ with nonempty
interior ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]) and write
$$M:=m_1+m_2,\quad \mu:=\frac{m_1m_2}{M},\quad X:=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{M},\quad V:=X',\quad P:=m_1x_1'+m_2x_2',\quad r:=x_1-x_2,$$
with $\lvert\cdot\rvert=\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ the Euclidean norm
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and dimensions as in [[def-cm01-units]]
($[M]=[\mu]=\mu$, $[X]=[r]=\ell$, $[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$). Then:

1. **(Pair forces.)** On $J$ the evaluated forces are
   $$F_1\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=-\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r,\qquad F_2\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=+\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r;$$
   thus the force map admits the external-plus-pair decomposition of
   [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (i) with
   $F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$ and the single pair force
   $F_{12}=-u'(\lvert r\rvert)r/\lvert r\rvert=-F_{21}$, which is central
   and antisymmetric in the sense of clause (ii). This identity does not
   assert that a separate decomposition was declared as model data.
2. **(Centre of mass.)** $P$ is constant on $J$ and $X$ is affine: for all
   $t,t_0\in J$, $X(t)=X(t_0)+(t-t_0)V$ with the constant
   $V=X'=M^{-1}P$.
3. **(Relative motion.)** $r$ is of class $C^2$ on $J$, satisfies
   $$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{u'(\lvert r(t)\rvert)}{\lvert r(t)\rvert}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
   and is therefore a **central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$** in the
   sense of [[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]; its angular momentum vector
   $j=\mu\,r\times r'$ and energy $E=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+
   u(\lvert r\rvert)$ are the attached objects of that definition.
4. **(Reconstruction and bijection.)** The identities
   $x_1=X+\frac{m_2}{M}r$ and $x_2=X-\frac{m_1}{M}r$ hold on $J$.
   Conversely, if $X^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is affine with
   $(X^{\circ})''=0$ and $r^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is a $C^2$ curve with
   $\lvert r^{\circ}(t)\rvert\in J_0$ and
   $\mu(r^{\circ})''=-u'(\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert)r^{\circ}/\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert$
   on $J$, then
   $$x_1^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}+\frac{m_2}{M}r^{\circ},\qquad x_2^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}-\frac{m_1}{M}r^{\circ}$$
   define a motion $x^{\circ}:J\to Q$ of the model whose centre of mass is
   $X^{\circ}$ and whose relative coordinate is $r^{\circ}$. Consequently
   the assignment $x\mapsto(X,r)$ is a bijection from the motions of the
   model on $J$ onto the pairs (affine curve $X^{\circ}$ with
   $(X^{\circ})''=0$\!, central-force trajectory $r^{\circ}$ for $(\mu,u)$
   with values in $J_0$) on $J$.

Let $\mu>0$ be a real number, let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval,
let $U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be
an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), and let
$r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be twice differentiable with $|r(t)|\in J_0$ for every
$t\in I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The curve $r$ is a
**central-force trajectory for** $(\mu,U)$ when

$$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{U'(|r(t)|)}{|r(t)|}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

where $|x|:=\lVert x\rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and $U'$ is the derivative of $U$ on the
open interval $J_0$.

**Attached objects.** The **angular momentum vector** of such a trajectory is
the curve $j:I\to\mathbb R^3$,

$$j(t):=\mu\,r(t)\times r'(t),$$

with $\times$ the cross product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]);
its **energy** is the function $E:I\to\mathbb R$,

$$E(t):=\tfrac12\mu\,\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2+U(|r(t)|);$$

and for every $J\ge0$ the **effective potential of momentum magnitude** $J$ is
the function $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J:J_0\to\mathbb R$,

$$U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho):=U(\rho)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu\,\rho^2}.$$

**Why the objects are defined.** Since $\rho>0$ throughout $J_0$, the right-hand
side of the central-force equation is defined, the map
$\rho\mapsto J^2/(2\mu\rho^2)$ is $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$ (a quotient of $C^2$
functions with nowhere vanishing denominator), and $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ is
again $C^2$; in particular second derivatives of $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ are
available. The vector $j(t)$ is defined for every $t\in I$ because $r$ is
differentiable there.

**Mathematical status.** The data $\mu$, $U$ and $J$ are real numbers and
functions; the equation and the attached objects are mathematical statements
about curves. Nothing here asserts that the equation describes a physical
interaction, and the names are conventional labels for the mathematical
objects only.

Let $\mu>0$, let $\kappa>0$ and $U(r)=\kappa/r$ on $(0,\infty)$ (the repulsive
Coulomb potential, of class $C^2$), let $E>0$ and $J>0$, and put
$$V(r):=\frac{\kappa}{r}+\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2},\qquad b:=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}>0,\qquad \alpha:=\frac{\kappa}{Eb}>0.$$
Then:

1. $V$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, with $V(r)\to\infty$ as $r\downarrow0$
   and $V(r)\to0$ as $r\to\infty$; hence there is exactly one $r_*>0$ with
   $V(r_*)=E$, it is simple ($V'(r_*)<0$), and $V(r)<E$ for all $r>r_*$.
2. Let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with
   constant angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, energy $E$, with $|r(t)|\ge r_*$
   for all $t\in I$ and with $|r(t_*)|=r_*$ for some $t_*\in I$. Then $r$
   extends uniquely to all of $\mathbb R$; along the extension $\rho=|r|\ge r_*>0$
   (no collision), $\rho$ is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and
   strictly increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$, and the asymptotic velocities
   $v_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r'(t)$ exist with $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}$.
   Moreover the asymptotic perpendicular distance of each branch to its
   limiting direction exists and equals
   $$b=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}=\frac{J}{\mu|v_\pm|}, \qquad\text{so that}\qquad J=\mu b|v_\pm| .$$
The distance in clause 2 means the limit of $|r(t)\times v_\pm|/|v_\pm|$ as $t\to\pm\infty$, the distance to the line through the origin in the limiting velocity direction; it does not assert a free tail or a finite longitudinal intercept.

3. For the polar angle, with $u_*:=1/r_*$,
   $$\Delta:=\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{J\,\mathrm dr}{r^2\sqrt{2\mu\,(E-V(r))}} =\int_0^{u_*}\frac{b\,\mathrm du}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{\kappa}{E}u-b^2u^2}} =\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$

4. Write $n_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r(t)/|r(t)|$. Then
   $n_+=v_+/|v_+|$, $n_-=-v_-/|v_-|$, and in an oriented polar plane
   the outgoing velocity direction is the incoming direction rotated by
   $2\Delta-\pi\in(-\pi,0)$. In particular
   $$\frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{|v_-||v_+|}=\cos(\pi-2\Delta),\qquad \theta_{\mathrm s}=\pi-2\Delta=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$
   For fixed $\mu,\kappa,E$ this gives an actual family for every $b>0$,
   with angular momentum $J(b)=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b$: choose its unique turning
   radius and initial data $r(0)=r_*e_1$, $r'(0)=J(b)e_2/(\mu r_*)$.
   Local existence and the extension in clause 2 give a member of the family
   for every $b$, unique up to apsis time and oriented plane placement.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the cross-section measures. Fix $\mu>0$, $\kappa>0$ and $E>0$. For every $b>0$ put $J(b)=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b$ and use the Coulomb trajectory family of [[thm-cm-coulomb-scattering]] clause 4. Its impact distance is $b$ and its
**deflection map**
$$\theta_{\rm def}:(0,\infty)\to(0,\pi),\qquad \theta_{\rm def}(b):=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$
Then:

1. $\theta_{\rm def}$ is $C^1$ and strictly decreasing, with
   $\theta_{\rm def}(b)\to\pi$ as $b\downarrow0$ and
   $\theta_{\rm def}(b)\to0$ as $b\to\infty$; it is a $C^1$ bijection
   $(0,\infty)\to(0,\pi)$ with inverse
   $$b(\theta)=\frac{\kappa}{2E}\cot\frac{\theta}{2}\qquad(0<\theta<\pi).$$
2. For every interval $(\theta_1,\theta_2)\subseteq(0,\pi)$ the pair
   $(\theta,b)$ is a deflection branch with cross-section density
   $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta) =b(\theta)\Bigl|\frac{\mathrm db}{\mathrm d\theta}(\theta)\Bigr|\frac{1}{\sin\theta} =\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\Bigr)^2\csc^4\frac{\theta}{2},$$
   finite and positive on $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$; and the pushforward of the
   incident flux measure under the branch is described by
   [[thm-cm-differential-cross-section-density]].
3. For every $\theta_0\in(0,\pi)$ the truncated total cross-section
   $$\int_0^{\theta_0}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\Bigr)^2 \csc^4\frac{\theta}{2}\,\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi\,\mathrm d\theta=+\infty,$$
   while for $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi$ the integral over
   $(\theta_1,\theta_2)\times(0,2\pi)$ is finite; in this sense the total
   cross-section of the ideal Coulomb model diverges at forward angles and
   every compact angular acceptance away from $0$ has finite cross-section.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Borel/Lebesgue measure foundation below.

**Data.** Let $\mu>0$, let $U:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $R>0$ satisfy $U(r)=0$
for every $r\ge R$ (a **finite-range potential**), and let $E>0$ and $J>0$ be
reals. Write

$$V(r):=U(r)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2}\qquad(r>0).$$

**Incident flux measure.** Let $\nu$ be the Borel measure on the open rectangle
$(0,\infty)\times(0,2\pi)$ given by the density $b$ against Lebesgue measure
$\lambda_2$,

$$\nu(A):=\int_A b\,d\lambda_2(b,\varphi)\qquad(A\subseteq(0,\infty)\times(0,2\pi)\ \text{Borel}),$$

the integral being that of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]; the
nonnegative Borel function $(b,\varphi)\mapsto b$ defines a measure by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]
([[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]]). In the model this
measure records a uniform incident beam: an annulus of impact parameters
$[b_1,b_2)$ contributes $\pi(b_2^2-b_1^2)$ over the full azimuth range, or
$\tfrac12(b_2^2-b_1^2)$ per unit azimuth.

**Solid-angle element.** Let $\Omega$ be the Borel measure on
$(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$ with density $\sin$ against $\lambda_2$,

$$\Omega(B):=\int_B\sin\theta\,d\lambda_2(\theta,\varphi)\qquad(B\subseteq(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\ \text{Borel}),$$

where $\sin$ is the function of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]].
It is continuous, being differentiable by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]].
Also $\sin0=\sin\pi=0$ by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]];
strict increase on $[0,\pi/2]$ and strict decrease on $[\pi/2,\pi]$
([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]]) give $\sin\theta>0$ for
$0<\theta<\pi$. Thus $(\theta,\varphi)\mapsto\sin\theta$ is a nonnegative
Borel function (continuous preimages of Borel sets are Borel,
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), and
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]
establishes that $\Omega$ is a measure. This
is the standard solid-angle element written $\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi$
(the surface measure of the unit sphere in spherical coordinates, restricted
to the open chart).

**Deflection branch.** A **deflection branch** is an interval
$(a_1,a_2)\subseteq(0,\infty)$ with at least two points together with a
function $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ that is of class $C^1$ and satisfies
$\theta'(b)\ne0$ for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$. Such a $\theta$ is strictly
monotone (the continuous nonvanishing derivative has constant sign, and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]] gives strict monotonicity) and its image is an interval with endpoints $\theta_1<\theta_2$
([[def-interval]]); its inverse $b:(\theta_1,\theta_2)\to(a_1,a_2)$ is
differentiable with $b'(\theta)=1/\theta'(b(\theta))$, by the
derivative-of-an-inverse theorem [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]] applied to
the continuous injective $\theta$ (every point of $(a_1,a_2)$ is a limit point
of it, [[def-limit-point-r]], [[def-derivative]]).

**Cross-section density.** The **cross-section density of the branch** is the
function

$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(\theta):=\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'\bigl(b(\theta)\bigr)\bigr|} \qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2).$$

**Mathematical status.** The measures, branches and density are abstract data
independent of the finite-range trajectory data $(\mu,U,R,E,J)$. A branch is not asserted to arise from any
trajectory; the scattering theorems of this page identify the deflection
angle computed from the central-force equation with the values of such a
function under their hypotheses, and they compute the pushforward of $\nu$ under the induced map. No counting of
detected particles, and no empirical claim, is part of this definition.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Borel measures.

This item fixes the **cross-section** vocabulary of the central scattering
models of [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] relative to the uniform-incident
preparation of that definition.

**(i) The differential cross-section of a branch.** Let a central scattering
model be given, let $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ be a **deflection branch**
in the sense of [[def-cm-scattering-data]] — an interval $(a_1,a_2)$ of
impact parameters with $\theta$ of class $C^1$ and $\theta'(b)\ne0$ — and
suppose the branch **records the deflection** of the model: for every
$b\in(a_1,a_2)$ the scattering motion of the model with impact parameter $b$,
fixed energy $E$ and angular momentum magnitude $J(b)=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b$ has scattering angle
$\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\theta(b)$. Write
$(a_1,a_2)\ni b\mapsto\theta\in(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ for this bijection and
$b(\theta):=\theta^{-1}(\theta)$ for its inverse
([[def-cm-scattering-data]]). The **differential cross-section of the
branch** is the function
$$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta):=\frac{b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|}{\sin\theta} =\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'\bigl(b(\theta)\bigr)\bigr|}\qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2),$$
the cross-section density of [[def-cm-scattering-data]]. Its dimension is
$[\mathrm d\sigma/\mathrm d\Omega]=\ell^2$ (solid angle dimensionless in the
chosen convention, [[def-cm01-units]]), and one says "per steradian" for the
unit of solid angle.

**(ii) Branch sums.** Let $\mathcal B=\{(a_1^{(j)},a_2^{(j)},\theta_j)\}_{j=1}^N$
be a finite family of deflection branches of the same model whose incident
intervals $(a_1^{(j)},a_2^{(j)})$ are pairwise disjoint, with each branch
recording the model's deflections as in clause (i). Write
$A_j:=\theta_j((a_1^{(j)},a_2^{(j)}))$ for its image and
$b_j:=\theta_j^{-1}$ and
$q_j(\theta):=b_j(\theta)|b_j'(\theta)|/\sin\theta$ for its branch density
from clause (i), defined on $A_j$.
Angular images are not required to be disjoint. The **differential
cross-section of the model for this family** is, for
$\theta\in A:=\bigcup_{j=1}^N A_j$,
$$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma_{\mathcal B}}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta) :=\sum_{\{j:\,\theta\in A_j\}}q_j(\theta).$$
Thus $q_j$ is the contribution of branch $j$, and contributions add at every
angle belonging to more than one image. The total density for this family is
left undefined at angles belonging to no branch image. No claim is made that
the branch images cover $(0,\pi)$ or that the family includes every
deflection of the model.

**(iii) Cross-section measure and truncated totals.** For one branch $j$ with image $A_j$, and a Borel angular window $Y\subseteq A_j$, define
$$\sigma_j(Y):=\int_Yq_j(\theta)\,2\pi\sin\theta\,d\lambda_1(\theta)=\int_{Y\times(0,2\pi)}b_j(\theta)|b_j'(\theta)|\,d\lambda_2.$$
When only one branch is under discussion, write $\sigma(Y)$ for this
branch-specific measure.
For the finite family $\mathcal B$ of clause (ii), define
$$\sigma_{\mathcal B}(Y):=\sum_{j=1}^N\sigma_j(Y\cap A_j)=\int_{Y\cap A}\frac{\mathrm d\sigma_{\mathcal B}}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta)\,2\pi\sin\theta\,d\lambda_1(\theta)$$
for every Borel $Y\subseteq(0,\pi)$. These are nonnegative Lebesgue integrals over measurable sets in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], with extended value $+\infty$ allowed. The measure-level identity of [[thm-cm-differential-cross-section-density]] identifies each branch integral with the area of that branch's incident preimage; finite additivity gives the family formula, including where angular images overlap. On a compact interior interval each branch integral equals the ordinary Riemann integral; on an open interval its value is the monotone limit over compact interior truncations, equivalently the nonnegative improper integral when finite. General Borel windows use the Lebesgue integral, not a two-piece interval improper integral.
The **ideal total cross-section** of a branch is $\sigma_j(A_j)$; for a family it is $\sigma_{\mathcal B}(A)$. If infinite, there is no finite ideal total. Every compact interior angular window in a branch image has finite branch cross-section; more generally a cutoff whose incident preimage is bounded has finite cross-section. An arbitrary positive angular cutoff need not suffice for an arbitrary branch.

**(iv) The uniform-incident reading.** Under the uniform-incident preparation
of [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] clause (iv) with cutoff $b_{\max}$ and flux
$\Phi$, the model predicts the expected rate of scattered labels into a
Borel angular window $Y$ from one branch to be the flux times its cutoff
cross-section for the portion of that branch with $b<b_{\max}$. Writing
$T_j(b,\varphi)=(\theta_j(b),\varphi)$ on the branch rectangle and
$D_{\max}=(0,b_{\max})\times(0,2\pi)$, the branch cutoff measure is
$$\sigma_{j,b_{\max}}(Y):=\nu\!\left(T_j^{-1}(Y\times(0,2\pi))\cap ((a_1^{(j)},a_2^{(j)})\times(0,2\pi))\cap D_{\max}\right),$$
and its expected rate is $\Phi\sigma_{j,b_{\max}}(Y)$. For a finite family
with pairwise disjoint incident intervals, define
$\sigma_{\mathcal B,b_{\max}}(Y):=\sum_{j=1}^N\sigma_{j,b_{\max}}(Y)$;
the expected rate is $\Phi\sigma_{\mathcal B,b_{\max}}(Y)$, including when
the angular images overlap. If the entire incident preimage of $Y$ lies
below the cutoff, this sum is $\Phi\sigma_{\mathcal B}(Y)$. This is a
prediction of the model under the adopted preparation. In particular:

- $\sigma_j(Y)$ and $\sigma_{\mathcal B}(Y)$ are **not** probabilities per
  incident label, **not** counts of detected events, and **not** apparatus
  properties;
- a comparison with data requires a separately specified experiment: an
  apparatus model, a detector with finite angular resolution and acceptance,
  a sampling model and uncertainties, and a statistical analysis, none of
  which is supplied by this page;
- an ideal branch cross-section may diverge at a forward angle, while
  the adopted finite incident cutoff gives
  $\sigma_{\mathcal B,b_{\max}}(Y)\le\pi b_{\max}^{2}$ for every
  window $Y$, because the branch incident intervals are disjoint. Thus
  these cutoff rates are finite even if the ideal window cross-section
  is infinite. Without an incident cutoff, the rate $\Phi\sigma_{\mathcal B}(Y)$
  is finite exactly when that ideal window cross-section is finite.
  A finite measured rate constrains the model jointly with its incident
  preparation and apparatus acceptance;
- finite samples fluctuate: an observed angular distribution can miss a
  branch's features with positive probability under ordinary sampling models,
  and agreement is evidence about the model-plus-apparatus assumptions, not a
  proof of the model.

**(v) Status and exclusions.** The branch hypothesis includes
$\theta'\ne0$: the definition excludes angles at which
$\theta'(b)=0$ (rainbow-type stationary deflections) and leaves them to
separate limiting measures. It also excludes, at the level of this page,
friction and tangential contact laws, attractive capture, screening,
radiation, relativistic and quantum modifications, and any identification of
the model parameters with measured electromagnetic quantities; those require
separate models or cross-framework items. The functions $\theta$, $b$ and the
data $E$, $J$, $u$, $b_{\max}$, $\Phi$ are model data
([[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] clause (vi)).

**Why the objects are defined.** The inverse $b$ is $C^1$ with
$b'(\theta)=1/\theta'(b(\theta))$ because a $C^1$ function on an interval with
nowhere vanishing derivative is strictly monotone and has a differentiable
inverse ([[def-cm-scattering-data]]); $\sin\theta>0$ on $(0,\pi)$; hence the
denominators do not vanish and the density is finite at every interior point
of the branch image. The pushforward identity that justifies the reading
"density carried by the branch" is
[[thm-cm-differential-cross-section-density]], a theorem of this page's
mathematical suppliers.

By [[lem-tangent-principal-branch-is-bijective]], tangent restricts to a
continuous strictly increasing bijection

$$\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\longrightarrow\mathbb R.$$

Its inverse is the **principal inverse tangent**

$$\arctan:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(-\pi/2,\pi/2).$$

Thus $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ for every real $y$, while
$\arctan(\tan x)=x$ precisely for $x$ in the displayed principal interval.
The inverse is continuous and strictly increasing by [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

Define
$$	an x:= rac{\sin x}{\cos x}\quad(x
e\pi/2+m\pi),\qquad\cot x:= rac{\cos x}{\sin x}\quad(x
e m\pi),$$
$$\sec x:= rac1{\cos x}\quad(x
e\pi/2+m\pi),\qquad\csc x:= rac1{\sin x}\quad(x
e m\pi),$$
where $m$ ranges over the integers. The exclusions are exactly the zero sets of [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]].

On their natural domains,
$$(\tan x)'=\sec^2x,\qquad(\cot x)'=-\csc^2x,\qquad(\sec x)'=\sec x\tan x,\qquad(\csc x)'=-\csc x\cot x.$$
Tangent and cotangent have least positive period $\pi$; secant and cosecant have least positive period $2\pi$.

For every real $x$, $\sin ^2x+\cos ^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. Wherever the displayed quotients are defined, $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, $\cot(-x)=-\cot x$, $\sec(-x)=\sec x$, $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$, $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$, and $1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: Clause 1: [L1] gives that $V$ is strictly decreasing from $+\infty$ to $0$ and that the unique solution $r_*$ of $V=E$ is simple with $V(r)<E$ for $r>r_*$; strict decrease also gives $V(r)>E$ for $0<r<r_*$. This is clause 1.

Clause 2, motion and asymptotics: by [L2] the relative coordinate is a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ with the attached data, so the trajectory hypotheses of [L1] hold; [L1] then gives the unique extension to all of $\mathbb R$ with no collision, the monotone branches with unique apsis, and the existence of $v_\pm$ with $|v_\pm|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}$ and asymptotic perpendicular distance $b=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}$ on both branches. The extension is the relative coordinate of a motion of the model with its autonomous force law extended to time window $\mathbb R$ by [L2], since $|\bar r(t)|\in(0,\infty)$ keeps the configuration admissible and the affine centre-of-mass extension is defined on all of $\mathbb R$. Because $u\not\equiv0$ on any outer region, no exact free tail is asserted; this is clause 2.

Clause 3: [L1] gives $\Delta=\pi/2-\arctan(\kappa/(2Eb))$ with $\alpha=\kappa/(2Eb)>0$, so $\arctan\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$ and $\Delta\in(0,\pi/2)$; [L3] then gives the scattering angle $\theta_{\mathrm s}=\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi)$ and the signed rotation $2\Delta-\pi$; substituting the arctangent expression gives $\theta_{\mathrm s}=2\arctan(\kappa/(2Eb))$. [L3] further gives that $\theta_{\mathrm{def}}$ is $C^1$ and strictly decreasing with image $(0,\pi)$ and the stated inverse, and $\theta_{\mathrm{def}}'(b)=2\cdot\frac{1}{1+(\kappa/(2Eb))^2}\cdot(-\frac{\kappa}{2Eb^2})<0$, so $\theta_{\mathrm{def}}'\ne0$ everywhere and the single branch covers $(0,\infty)$. For each $b>0$, [L1] supplies the apsis trajectory at $J(b)$ and [L2] reconstructs it into a two-label motion with any affine centre of mass. Thus these are actual model motions throughout the claimed family. Since every $b>0$ gives $0<\Delta<\pi/2$, the branch never wraps. This is clause 3.

Clause 4, density: the cross-section density of the branch is $b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|/\sin\theta$ by [L3], and substituting $b'(\theta)=-(\kappa/4E)\csc^2(\theta/2)$ and $b(\theta)=(\kappa/2E)\cot(\theta/2)$ and using $\sin\theta=2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)$ and $\csc^2=1+\cot^2$ gives $(\kappa/(4E))^2\csc^4(\theta/2)$, finite and positive for $0<\theta<\pi$; this is the displayed density.

Clause 4, band computation: put $F(\theta):=\pi b(\theta)^2$. By [L4] and the chain rule, $F'(\theta)=2\pi b(\theta)b'(\theta) =2\pi\cdot\frac{\kappa}{2E}\cot\frac{\theta}{2}\cdot\bigl(-\frac{\kappa}{4E}\csc^2\frac{\theta}{2}\bigr) =-\frac{\pi\kappa^2}{4E^2}\,\frac{\cos(\theta/2)}{\sin^3(\theta/2)}$, while the solid-angle integrand is $\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta)\,2\pi\sin\theta =\bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\bigr)^2\csc^4\frac{\theta}{2}\cdot 4\pi\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cos\frac{\theta}{2} =\frac{\pi\kappa^2}{4E^2}\frac{\cos(\theta/2)}{\sin^3(\theta/2)}=-F'(\theta)$, using $\sin\theta=2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)$. Hence by the fundamental theorem [L5], for $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi$ $$\sigma\bigl((\theta_1,\theta_2)\bigr)=\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta)\,2\pi\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta =-\bigl(F(\theta_2)-F(\theta_1)\bigr)=\pi\bigl(b(\theta_1)^2-b(\theta_2)^2\bigr),$$ finite because $b$ is continuous on $[\theta_1,\theta_2]$. Since the integrand is nonnegative, the truncated integral over $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ increases as $\theta_2\uparrow\pi$ and tends to $\pi b(\theta_1)^2$ because $b(\theta_2)^2\to0$; this gives the band value. The divergence of the truncated integral over $(0,\theta_0)$ is the corresponding clause of [L3]. For the single branch, its incident preimage restricted to $0<b<b_{\max}$ is a subset of the disc of incident area $\pi b_{\max}^2$. Clause (iv) of [[def-cm15-cross-section]] therefore gives $\sigma_{b_{\max}}(Y)\le\pi b_{\max}^2$ and the finite expected rate $\Phi\sigma_{b_{\max}}(Y)$ for every Borel angular window, including $Y=(0,\pi)$. These are model expectations; a detected-rate comparison needs the separately specified apparatus and uncertainty. This is clause 4.

Clause 5: the statement records only the mechanical model's parameter $\kappa$, its conditional prediction and the explicit exclusions; no identification, measurement or additional model is used in steps 1.1-5.1, each of which cites only model data and the cited mathematical and physical suppliers. This completes the proof.

boundaries.evidence: Every angular band in clause 4 has $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi$ by hypothesis and the branch is the nondegenerate $(0,\infty)$; step 5.1 integrates over such a band.
$E>0$, $J>0$ and $\kappa>0$ give $b>0$, and the forward limits are taken as limits in steps 3.1 and 5.1 rather than at $\theta=0$ or $b=0$.
A single turning point and a single branch: step 1.1 proves uniqueness of $r_*$ and step 3.1 proves the deflection map is a bijection.

citations.quote:
Adopt, as this page's **impact and open-mass extensions** of the force
branch of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the following three model extensions. Each is an adopted model, not a
consequence of the smooth-force postulates; each applies only where a
statement explicitly invokes it.

**(i) The isolated reciprocal impulse model.** A two-label force model with
masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), time window $I_0$,
configuration domain $Q$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]) and continuous
external-plus-pair force maps $F_1,F_2$ is **run in the isolated reciprocal
impulse model at $t_*\in I_0$** when there is an interval
$I\subseteq I_0$ with $t_*\in\operatorname{int}I$ and a position curve
$x=(x_1,x_2):I\to Q$ such that the following conditions hold. This curve is
called an **impulse motion**; only its restrictions away from $t_*$ are
motions of the associated first-order system of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]],
and no differentiability at $t_*$ is required:

1. $x_1,x_2$ are continuous on $I$ and twice continuously differentiable on
   each of $I\cap(-\infty,t_*)$ and $I\cap(t_*,\infty)$
   ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]],
   [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and
   $m_ix_i''(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ for every $t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}$;
2. the one-sided limits
   $v_i^{\pm}:=\lim_{t\to t_*\pm}x_i'(t)$ exist in $\mathbb R^3$
   ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]);
3. there is a vector $J\in\mathbb R^3$, the **impulse**, with
   $$m_1\bigl(v_1^+-v_1^-\bigr)=J,\qquad m_2\bigl(v_2^+-v_2^-\bigr)=-J .$$

The two equations of clause 3 are the **reciprocal finite-jump form** of the
isolated impulse: the two labels receive equal and opposite momentum changes.
The regular force maps remain continuous on their state domain; their
evaluations along the curve can have different one-sided limits because the
velocity can jump. The dimension of the impulse
is $[J]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

For the distributional rendering on $\operatorname{int}I$, assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Put
$p_i(t)=m_ix_i'(t)$ and $f_i(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ off $t_*$, assigning both
the value $0$ at $t_*$. Their one-sided limits are finite: those of $p_i$
are $m_iv_i^\pm$, and continuity of the state-domain force maps gives
$f_i(t_*^\pm)=F_i(t_*,x(t_*),v^\pm)$, with
$v^\pm=(v_1^\pm,v_2^\pm)$. Also $p_i'=f_i$ off the impulse. Thus each
component meets the piecewise-$C^1$ and one-sided derivative-limit
hypotheses of [[lem-cm-piecewise-c1-jump-derivative]]. Its identity,
summed componentwise, gives for every real vector test function
$\Phi\in C_c^\infty(\operatorname{int}I;\mathbb R^3)$ (each component is
smooth and compactly supported, [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]])
$$-\int_{\operatorname{int}I}\langle p_i,\Phi'\rangle\,d\lambda=\int_{\operatorname{int}I}\langle f_i,\Phi\rangle\,d\lambda+s_i\langle J,\Phi(t_*)\rangle,\qquad s_1=1,\quad s_2=-1,$$
where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure and the integral convention is that of
[[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]. This is the pairing form of the
adopted jumps. Unlike [[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]], whose
hypotheses require continuous time forces and assume the pairings to derive
the jumps, this rendering allows distinct one-sided regular-force values.

**(ii) The collinear restitution contact law.** A model run in the isolated
reciprocal impulse model at $t_*$ is **collinear** when there is a unit vector
$n\in\mathbb R^3$ (the **contact direction**) with $v_i^{\pm}\parallel n$ for
$i=1,2$ and $\langle v_2^--v_1^-,n\rangle<0$ (the labels approach along $n$).
For a collinear contact, adopt a **coefficient of restitution** $e\in[0,1]$ —
a dimensionless model datum of the pair and the contact — and the **restitution
law**
$$v_2^+-v_1^+=-e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr).$$
For $e=1$ the contact is called **elastic**, for $e=0$ **perfectly inelastic**
and otherwise **semi-elastic**; the law is a constitutive assumption, not a
consequence of the impulse equations of clause (i), and $e$ is not derived
from the masses or the approach speed. The law is stated only for a single
collinear contact; simultaneous contacts, repeated contacts and tangential
(friction) impulses are outside the model.

**(iii) The open-body material accounting.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a
nonempty open interval. Adopt for a body whose mass
$m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and velocity $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ are differentiable, and
whose external force and exchanged matter are described by maps
$F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and
$w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ (mass rates and *inertial*
velocities of the matter entering and leaving, measured in the same inertial
frame as $v$), the **material balance identities**
$$m'=r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad (mv)'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}\,w_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}\,w_{\mathrm{out}} .$$
They are the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,\mathrm dt$ of
matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,\mathrm dt$
with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$", and they
are adopted rather than derived from a closed-system law. Their product-rule
consequence $mv'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$
is proved in [[thm-cm-variable-mass-momentum-balance]]; in particular the
closed-system law $(mv)'=F$ is recovered only when
$r_{\mathrm{in}}w_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}$.
The quantities have types and SI dimensions
$[m]=\mu$, $[v]=[w_{\mathrm{in}}]=[w_{\mathrm{out}}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$,
$[F]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ and
$[r_{\mathrm{in}}]=[r_{\mathrm{out}}]=\mu\tau^{-1}$; they are model
data, not measured values.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]), let $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and let $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be maps. Suppose the two **material balance identities**

$$m'(t)=r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t),\qquad (mv)'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)$$

hold for every $t\in I$, where $mv$ denotes the pointwise scalar multiple. Then

$$m(t)v'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in I).$$

In particular, if $F\equiv0$, $r_{\mathrm{in}}\equiv0$ and $r_{\mathrm{out}}\equiv r$ for a constant $r\ge0$, then $mv'=-r(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$: the acceleration is governed by the momentum carried away per unit time relative to the body, not by $(mv)'=0$.

The two balance identities are the **adopted content of the material momentum accounting** — the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,dt$ of matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,dt$ with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$". They are not derived here from any closed-system law; the deduction below is their product-rule consequence.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about
forces and motion, in the spacetime, frames and worldlines of
[[post-cm01-spacetime]], [[post-cm01-frames]] and [[post-cm01-worldlines]].

**(i) Setting and configuration domain.** A model of the framework has
$N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed positive masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]], clause (v)) and a configuration domain $Q$ in one
fixed inertial frame, in the unconstrained branch of
[[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a): $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open,
possibly with the collision set $\Delta$ removed when the force law of the
model is singular at coincident positions. The constrained branch of that
definition, with its reaction forces, is **not** covered by this postulate; the
dynamics of constrained systems is a separate development with its own
assumptions. A **state** of the model is a pair $z=(x,v)\in Q\times\mathbb
R^{3N}$ of positions and coordinate velocities of the labels in the chosen
frame ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]).

**(ii) Time window.** A model carries a nondegenerate open interval
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, its **time window**, read in seconds
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(iii) Force map and standing regularity.** A **force map** on this data is a
map

$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v)=\bigl(F_{1}(t,x,v),\dots,F_{N}(t,x,v)\bigr),$$

with components of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons
([[def-cm01-units]]). The standing hypotheses of this branch, which every
force map of a model is required to satisfy, are:

1. **Continuity.** $F$ is continuous on its domain
   $D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
2. **State-local Lipschitz regularity, locally uniform in time.** $F$ is
   locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z=(x,v)$, locally uniformly in
   time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]: every
   compact cylinder $C\subseteq D$ carries a finite $L\ge0$ with
   $\lVert F(t,z)-F(t,z')\rVert_{2}\le L\lVert z-z'\rVert_{2}$ whenever
   $(t,z),(t,z')\in C$ share their time coordinate.

A map that fails clause 1 or clause 2 is **not** a force map of this branch,
whatever its other merits. When a later statement differentiates the force map
(for instance in a linearization or a smooth-dependence claim), it adds the
required differentiability hypothesis of the state variable explicitly; clause
2 alone licenses only the existence, uniqueness and continuation statements
proved on this page.

**(iv) Equation of motion.** Adopt: the motion of the labels of a model with
force map $F$ in an inertial frame is governed by

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N),$$

imposed along families of $C^{2}$ coordinate curves of the labels
$x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):J\to Q$, where $J\subseteq I_{0}$ is an interval with
nonempty interior and the derivatives are those of
[[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. The precise notion of a motion of the
model, its associated first-order system and its maximal motions is
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. The force map is **primitive data** of the model:
the equations above are the model's law, not an operational definition of $F$
from a measured acceleration, and $F$ is not an extra observable measured
independently of the motion. The mass $m_{i}$ in (iv) is the fixed inertial
mass of clause (v) of [[post-cm01-worldlines]]; no other mass occurs in this
clause.

**(v) Additive composition of force contributions.** When a model presents its
force map as composed of contributions, the composition is the pointwise sum:
for force maps $F^{(1)},\dots,F^{(k)}$ on a common domain satisfying (iii),

$$F(t,z)=\sum_{a=1}^{k}F^{(a)}(t,z),$$

and the sum again satisfies (iii), because a finite sum of continuous maps is
continuous and a finite sum of maps that are locally Lipschitz in the state
variable is locally Lipschitz with a locally uniform constant. This
**superposition of forces** is an adopted modelling rule, not a theorem about
nature: it says how the model's total force is composed from the contributions
it declares. Two decompositions with the same sum define the same force map
and the same model; the framework does not measure an individual contribution
in isolation, and no observation of motions alone determines a decomposition.
Nor does (v) assert that sums of motions are motions: if $F$ is not affine in
the state, the sum of two solutions of (iv) generally does not satisfy (iv),
and superposing solutions is a separate question from superposing forces.

**(vi) Description in another inertial frame.** Let $F_{*}=\bigl(o',u',
(e_{1}',e_{2}',e_{3}')\bigr)$ be a second inertial frame related to the frame
of (i) by the Galilean transformation

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x_i'=Rx_i+\upsilon t+a_{0}\quad(i=1,\dots,N)$$

with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a_{0},\upsilon\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $R\in SO(3)$
([[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]] clause 1;
[[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]); $\upsilon$ is the boost velocity
denoted by $v$ in that theorem. Define the block-diagonal map
$$R_{N}:=\operatorname{diag}(R,\dots,R):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$$
and the repeated tuples $\bar a_{0}:=(a_{0},\dots,a_{0})$ and
$\bar\upsilon:=(\upsilon,\dots,\upsilon)$ in $(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$. Thus
$R_N x=(Rx_{1},\dots,Rx_{N})$, and the same componentwise rule applies to
velocities and forces; since $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3}$,
$R_N^{\mathsf T}R_N=I_{3N}$. If $x:J\to Q$ is a family of motions of the
labels in the first frame, then the description of the same worldlines in the second
frame is
$$\eta(t'):=R_{N}x(t'-b)+\bar\upsilon(t'-b)+\bar a_{0}\qquad(t'\in J+b).$$
By clause 2 of the cited theorem, each $\eta_i$ is $C^{2}$ and
$\eta_i''(t')=R\ddot x_i(t'-b)$, so along the motion
$$m_i\eta_i''(t')=R F_i\bigl(t'-b,x(t'-b),\dot x(t'-b)\bigr).$$

Adopt: the same interaction, read in the second frame, is represented on the
transferred data by the force map below. Let $P$ be the inverse affine
transfer from new-frame data to old-frame data,
$$P(t',y,w):=\bigl(t'-b,\,R_N^{\mathsf T}(y-\bar\upsilon(t'-b)-\bar a_{0}),\,R_N^{\mathsf T}(w-\bar\upsilon)\bigr).$$
Its preimage of the original domain is
$$D_{*}:=P^{-1}(D)=\{(t',y,w):P(t',y,w)\in D\};$$
it is open because $P$ is a homeomorphism and $D$ is open. Define
$$F_{*}:D_{*}\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},\qquad F_{*}(t',y,w):=R_N F\Bigl(t'-b,\ R_N^{\mathsf T}\bigl(y-\bar\upsilon(t'-b)-\bar a_{0}\bigr),\ R_N^{\mathsf T}(w-\bar\upsilon)\Bigr).$$
The map $F_{*}$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in its state variable:
the transfer and its inverse are affine, and at fixed time they act linearly
on state differences; on compact time intervals their state Lipschitz
constants are uniform, so precomposition preserves the stated regularity of
$F$. The framework
formulates the equation of motion in every inertial frame; a rule that does
not transform by this law is a description tied to the frame in which it was
written, and the framework attaches no kinematic covariance to it. When
$Q=\mathbb R^{3N}$ — the case of the models of the companion page — the
transferred domain is again a product
$I_{0}'\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with $I_{0}'=I_{0}+b$, and
$F_{*}$ is a force map in the sense of (iii); for a proper open $Q$ the
transferred position set $R_NQ+\bar\upsilon(t'-b)+\bar a_0$ may depend on
$t'$, and the equation is then read on that transferred set.

**(vii) What this branch excludes.** Impulsive forcing (a finite momentum
transfer at an instant is not a force map); Coulomb sliding friction, whose
expression contains the factor $v/\lvert v\rvert$ and is undefined at $v=0$;
static friction, which requires an inequality or a set-valued reaction model;
stochastic forcing; and forces that exist only as distributions. Each of these
requires its own stated model and solution notion, and none is covered by
(iii)–(iv). A singular force law is admissible on a configuration domain with
the singular configurations removed — for instance an inverse-square law on
the collision-excluded $Q$ of clause (i) — and what the removal of those
configurations implies for existence in time is stated by the continuation
theorem of this page.

**(viii) Status.** Clause (iii) states the hypotheses under which the theorems
of this page are proved; clause (iv) is the adopted law of motion; clauses (v)
and (vi) are the adopted composition and frame rules. Nothing here is deduced
from experiment, from a symmetry principle or from the uniqueness theory of
differential equations, and nothing here asserts that any physical
interaction is exactly of this form: the theorems of this page are conditional
consequences of the adopted model. The empirical significance of a concrete
model lies in fully specified model parameters and reported observations
compared with its predictions, and this postulate supplies neither.

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $(t,z(t))\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $(t,z(t))\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

Fix a model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$
particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb
R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with its collision
set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an
interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). All sums below range over
$i=1,\dots,N$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $u\times v$, $\langle u,v\rangle$
and $\lVert u\rVert_{2}$ are the cross product, the Euclidean inner product and
the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(a) Curve families and motions.** A **curve family** of the model is a map
$x:J\to Q$, $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$, of class $C^{2}$ on $J$
([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]); its **coordinate velocities** are
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$ on $J$, written $w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{N}):J\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
A curve family is a **motion** of the model when
$$m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J),$$
the notion of clause (c) of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Every quantity of
this definition is defined for an arbitrary curve family; the balance theorems
of this page state which of their properties use the equations of motion.
Along a curve family the force map is evaluated at $(t,x(t),w(t))\in
I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; when the model invokes the
external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the maps $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $F_{ij}$ are evaluated at their declared
arguments on the motion's state graph, where the presentation is an identity
for $F_{i}$.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define
$$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$
Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$
the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$.
The dimensions are $[M]=\mu$, $[p_{i}]=[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and $[X]=[\rho_{i}]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]). Since $x_{i}$ is $C^{2}$, each $p_{i}$ is $C^{1}$ and
each of $P$, $X$, $\rho_{i}$ is differentiable, as a finite sum of
differentiable curves ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); write
$$V:=X'$$
for the **centre-of-mass velocity**. The algebraic identities
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}=0$, $P=MV$ and the splitting of the kinetic sum
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}$ are proved in the kinetic-splitting
theorem of this page; they are not part of this definition.

**(c) Angular momentum, torque, internal torque sum.** Let a **reference
curve** $o:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{1}$ be given: a point about which
moments are taken, allowed to move (a constant map $o\equiv o_{0}$ is the
fixed-origin case). Define the **angular momentum about $o$** and the **total
torque about $o$** by
$$J_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times p_{i}(t),\qquad T_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),$$
with dimensions $[J_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{2}\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and
$[T_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m$). When the
model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of
[[post-cm02-interactions]], define in addition the **external torque** and the
**internal torque sum**
$$T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr),\qquad I(t):=\sum_{i<j}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-x_{j}(t)\bigr)\times F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr).$$
The sum $I$ does not involve $o$; it is defined whenever the pair
presentation is declared. The identity $T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I$ uses the
antisymmetry $F_{ji}=-F_{ij}$ of clause (ii)1 of that postulate to reindex the
ordered pairs and is proved as step 1.1 of the angular-momentum balance of
this page.

**(d) Kinetic energy, power, work.** Define the **kinetic energy** and the
**power of the total force** along the curve family by
$$K(t):=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}(t)\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad \mathcal P(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl\langle F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),\,w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle,$$
of dimensions $[K]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules) and
$[\mathcal P]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-3}$ (read in watts), and for
$t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$ the **work of the total force** over $[t_{0},t_{1}]$ by
$$W([t_{0},t_{1}]):=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal P(t)\,dt,$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules); $\mathcal P$ is
continuous on $J$ because $F$, $x$ and $w$ are continuous, so the Riemann
integral exists ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], see the page
`the-riemann-integral`). The **potential energy** is not defined by this item:
it belongs to the potential branch of the model and is defined in the
potential-and-mechanical-energy item of this page.

**(e) Frame and reference-point dependence.** The quantities $p_{i}$, $P$,
$X$, $\rho_{i}$, $V$, $K$, $\mathcal P$ and $W$ are read in the one inertial
frame fixed above, and $J_{o}$, $T_{o}$, $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$, $I$ are read
about the reference curve $o$ in that frame. They are not invariant under a
change of frame or reference point: their transformation laws under a change
of inertial frame are stated and proved in the frame-transformation item of
this page, and every conservation statement involving them names the frame
and the reference point in which it is made.

**(f) Status.** This item is a definition: it introduces symbols, their
domains, regularity, dimensions and frame dependence from the model's data.
It adopts no force law beyond the force branch already fixed, asserts no
balance of any of these quantities and records no measured value.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
