$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $N\in\mathbb N$, $N\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $m_1,\dots,m_N>0$ and let $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable at every point of $I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). All sums over $i$ range over $1,\dots,N$: for a real family $a_1,\dots,a_N$, define $\sum_i a_i:=\sum_{k<N}b_k$, where $b:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ has $b_k=a_{k+1}$ for $k<N$ and $b_k=0$ for $k\ge N$, using the finite sums of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]; vector sums are defined coordinatewise, and sums of curves pointwise. Put $M:=\sum_i m_i>0$, $X:=M^{-1}\sum_i m_ix_i$ and $\rho_i:=x_i-X$. The symbols $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ denote the Euclidean inner product and norm on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

1. $X$ and every $\rho_i$ are differentiable on $I$, with $X'=M^{-1}\sum_im_ix_i'$ and $\rho_i'=x_i'-X'$, and the identities $\sum_im_i\rho_i=0$ and $\sum_im_i\rho_i'=0$ hold on $I$;
2. for every $t\in I$, $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\sum_{i}m_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2;$$
3. if $N=2$, then with $r:=x_1-x_2$ and $\mu:=m_1m_2/M$ one has $\sum_im_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$ and hence $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$$ for every $t\in I$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ carries the
Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
[[def-p-norms-on-rn]], whose induced metric is the published $d_2$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]],
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). A function into $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is called
**vector-valued**.

### Continuity

Let $(X, d_X)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$
carry the restricted metric $d_A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]), let
$f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $a \in A$. Then $f$ is **continuous at $a$**
when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ d_X(x,a) < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ \lVert f(x) - f(a)\rVert_2 < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon, \delta$ ranging over the positive reals, and **continuous on
$A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**This is not a new notion, and that is the point of writing it down.** Since
$\lVert f(x)-f(a)\rVert_2 = d_2\bigl(f(x),f(a)\bigr)$ and $d_A$ is the
restriction of $d_X$, the displayed condition is **verbatim** the condition of
[[def-metric-continuity]] for the map of metric spaces
$f : (A,d_A) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$. So every theorem about continuous maps
of metric spaces applies to vector-valued functions with no translation, and
this library has exactly one notion of continuity here. The same move was made
once before, between the $\mathbb{R}$-native and the metric notions, in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]]; this item is that move one dimension up in
the codomain.

The two cases used below are $X = \mathbb{R}$ with $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) and $X = \mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $d_2$, for
$n \ge 1$.

### Limits, for a real domain

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$, let $c$ be a limit
point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) and let $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. We say
$f(x)$ **tends to $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$**, and write
$\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$, when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ 0 < |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ \lVert f(x) - L\rVert_2 < \varepsilon\ \bigr].$$

This is the condition of [[def-function-limit]] with the absolute value in the
codomain replaced by $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$; as there, the puncture $0 < |x-c|$ is
what makes $c$ a point the function need not be defined at, and the hypothesis
that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is what stops the condition from being satisfied
vacuously.

**The notation denotes: at most one $L$ satisfies the condition.** Suppose $L$
and $L'$ both do and $L \ne L'$. Then $\varepsilon := \lVert L-L'\rVert_2 / 2 > 0$
by (N1) for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). Take $\delta$
and $\delta'$ for this $\varepsilon$ and put $\eta := \min\{\delta,\delta'\} > 0$.
Since $c$ is a limit point of $A$ there is $x \in A$ with $0 < |x-c| < \eta$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), and then

$$\lVert L - L'\rVert_2 \;\le\; \lVert L - f(x)\rVert_2 + \lVert f(x) - L'\rVert_2 \;<\; \varepsilon + \varepsilon \;=\; \lVert L-L'\rVert_2$$

by (N3) and (N2), which trichotomy forbids. So $L = L'$.

### Components

For $i < m$ define the $i$-th **coordinate projection**
$\pi_i : \mathbb{R}^{m} \to \mathbb{R}$ by $\pi_i(y) := y_i = y(i)$, and for
$f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ the $i$-th **component** $f_i := \pi_i \circ f$, a
real-valued function on $A$.

**Each $\pi_i$ is $1$-Lipschitz** ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]): for
$y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$,

$$\bigl|\pi_i(y) - \pi_i(z)\bigr| \;=\; |y_i - z_i| \;\le\; \lVert y - z\rVert_2 \;=\; d_2(y,z),$$

the middle inequality being $|w_i| \le \lVert w\rVert_2$ at $w := y-z$
([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]] clause 3, or
directly because $w_i^{2}$ is one term of the sum $\sum_{k<m}w_k^{2}$). Written
in coordinates, $f(x)$ is the vector whose $i$-th coordinate is $f_i(x)$, and
$f(x) = \sum_{i<m} f_i(x)\,e_i$ in the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]).

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about particles and their motion, in the spacetime of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] and the frames of [[post-cm01-frames]].

**(i) Particle labels and worldlines.** A model of the framework has **particle
labels** $i=1,\dots,N$ for some $N\ge1$. To each label and each *inertial
frame* of the model — an adapted chart $(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}))$ with
coordinates $(t,x)$ in the sense of [[post-cm01-frames]] — there is assigned a
**worldline** $\gamma_{i}:I\to A$ described in that frame, where
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval — that is, an interval
of the form $(a,b)$ with $-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ and at least two points —
the curve $\gamma_{i}$ is of class $C^{2}$ in the adapted coordinates of the frame,
and the **parameter condition**

$$\tau\bigl(\gamma_{i}(t)-o\bigr)=t\qquad(t\in I)$$

holds: the curve parameter is the elapsed time from the origin of the frame, so
in the frame's coordinates $\gamma_{i}(t)=(t,x_{i}(t))$ with
$x_{i}:I\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{2}$. The parameter condition replaces
the causal conditions of relativistic kinematics: no timelike condition on the
velocity and no upper bound on its Euclidean norm is imposed, and the
parameter is not free up to reparametrization.

**(ii) Description in another frame.** The same motion described in a second
inertial frame is the curve obtained by the time reparametrization of the two
frames: if $(t',x')$ are the coordinates of the second frame and
$t'=t+b$ is the time component of the transformation between the two frames
([[post-cm01-frames]], [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]]),
then the description of the motion in the second frame is the curve
$\gamma_{i,b}(t'):=\gamma_{i}(t'-b)$, defined on $I+b$, and it again satisfies
the parameter condition $\tau(\gamma_{i,b}(t')-o')=t'$ with respect to the
second frame's origin $o'$. This is a consistency requirement of the model's
frame language; the accompanying spatial transformation of the coordinate
curve is the affine law of [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]],
and its kinematic consequences are proved in [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]].

**(iii) Regularity is frame-independent.** The class of the worldline is
independent of the frame used to describe it: by the transformation law of
[[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]], the coordinates of the
same event in two inertial frames differ by
$t'=t+b$, $x'=Rx+vt+a$ with constant $b,a,v$ and $R\in SO(3)$, so a coordinate
curve is twice continuously differentiable in one inertial frame exactly when
its reparametrized description is twice continuously differentiable in the
other. The assumptions of this postulate are therefore read in any one inertial
frame without loss.

**(iv) Velocity and acceleration.** In a fixed inertial frame the quantities
$w_{i}:=dx_{i}/dt$ and $a_{i}:=d^{2}x_{i}/dt^{2}$ are the **coordinate
velocity** and **coordinate acceleration** of the label, of dimensions
$\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ by [[def-cm01-units]]; they are defined
precisely, and their transformation under a change of inertial frame is
recorded, in [[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]].

**(v) Fixed inertial mass.** Each particle label $i$ carries a **mass**
$m_{i}>0$, a primitive parameter of the model with dimension $\mu$
([[def-cm01-units]]). The mass is fixed: it is the same positive number at all
times and in all inertial frames of this model; the index $i$ identifies a label within that model and asserts no cross-model identification or equality of mass parameters. It
is not a function of the time coordinate, of the position or of the velocity,
and no variable-mass model is a model of this clause. The mass enters the
dynamics only through its later appearance in the equation of motion; this
postulate attaches no dynamics to it. Distinct labels may carry distinct
masses, and the masses are model data, not measured values.

**(vi) Point-particle idealization.** The model retains of each label only its
position and its fixed mass, together with the label index: size, shape, spin,
deformation, temperature and internal degrees of freedom are omitted, and the
quantity $x_{i}(t)$ is the single point representing the label at time $t$. An
application of the model must state when this idealization is adequate for the
system at hand; for a body whose rotation, deformation or internal structure
matters for the question asked, the point-particle model is not adequate and a
richer model must be specified. The framework makes no claim that every
physical body is a point particle.

**(vii) Calibration caveat.** An apparatus calibration may *estimate* a mass
parameter of a concrete body under a stated measurement model, with its
assumptions, sampling and uncertainty; such an estimate neither defines the
mass parameter of a label nor verifies the equation of motion in which it
occurs, and it is not deduced from this postulate. No measured value of any
mass is asserted by this item.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

Let $N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ be given as
in [[post-cm01-worldlines]], and fix one inertial frame of the model with
spatial coordinates $x_{i}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ for each label $i$. Identify the
space of all position tuples with $\mathbb R^{3N}=(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ and
write its points as $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$; each component $x_{i}$ has
dimension $\ell$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(a) Unconstrained branch.** The **unconstrained configuration domain** is an
open set $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, chosen as part of the model. A tuple
$x\in Q$ is an **admissible configuration**: an assignment of one position to
each label at one time. A **singular-force exclusion** is the removal of the
**collision set**

$$\Delta:=\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:\ \text{there are }i\ne j\text{ with }x_{i}=x_{j}\Bigr\}$$

from the domain, which is done when the model's force law is not defined at
coincident positions: $\Delta$ is closed (it is the union of the finitely many
closed sets $\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}$, each the zero set of the continuous map
$x\mapsto x_{i}-x_{j}$), so $Q:=\mathbb R^{3N}\setminus\Delta$ is open and is a
legitimate configuration domain. Whether the exclusion is part of the model is
a modelling decision recorded with the force law; the framework itself only
requires $Q$ to be open and stated.

**(b) Holonomic constraint branch.** Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ be an open
**ambient set**, let $k\in\mathbb N$ with $1\le k\le3N-1$, and let

$$G=(G_{1},\dots,G_{k}):O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k}$$

be a smooth map, each component carrying a declared dimension and unit fixed
by the model (a component can always be rescaled by a nonzero constant without
changing its zero set, and the rescaling is part of the declaration). Assume:

1. **Nonempty level set:** $G^{-1}(0)\ne\varnothing$;
2. **Rank condition:** the differential $DG(x):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k}$
   is surjective, equivalently has rank $k$, at every $x\in G^{-1}(0)$.

Then $0$ is a regular value of $G$ in the sense of
[[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]], and the **constrained
configuration space** is $Q:=G^{-1}(0)$. By
[[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] — applied to the smooth
map $G$ from the open subset $O$ of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ to $\mathbb R^{k}$, whose
regular value $0$ has nonempty fibre — $Q$ is an embedded submanifold of
$\mathbb R^{3N}$ of dimension $3N-k$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]).
The **degrees of freedom** of this branch of the model is the number
$$\dim Q=3N-k.$$ In the sense of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]], $Q$ together with the inclusion $X:Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}$ is then a particle configuration, and the mass metric of that definition is available with the masses $m_{i}$; the configuration is constrained to $Q$ for all times in this branch.

**(c) Time-dependent holonomic constraints.** If the constraint map depends on
time,

$$G:\mathbb R\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k},\qquad (t,x)\longmapsto G(t,x),$$

with $G$ smooth and $D_{x}G(t_{0},x)$ of rank $k$ at every $x$ of the nonempty
set $G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$, then for each fixed $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$ the
**instantaneous configuration space** $Q_{t_{0}}:=G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$ is an
embedded submanifold of dimension $3N-k$ by the same theorem applied to
$G(t_{0},\cdot)$. The family $\{Q_{t_{0}}\}$ varies with $t_{0}$; a curve
$t\mapsto q(t)$ with $G(t,q(t))=0$ is not thereby a curve in one fixed
manifold, and the kinematic treatment of such constraints (velocities, the
reaction forces that maintain them and the distinction between rheonomic and
scleronomic constraints) belongs to the framework's constraint development and
is not part of this definition.

**(d) Mass operator.** In the ambient coordinates define the **mass operator**
$\mathsf M:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ by block multiplication,

$$\mathsf M(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):=(m_{1}x_{1},\dots,m_{N}x_{N});$$

its matrix in the standard basis is block diagonal with blocks $m_{i}I_{3}$,
the **mass matrix** of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]].
Its dimension is $\mu$: it multiplies positions of dimension $\ell$ by masses
of dimension $\mu$. On the constrained branch, for the inclusion
$X:Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}$ and tangent vectors $h,z\in T_qQ$,
the mass metric of that item is
$$\mathcal G_q(h,z):=\langle dX_q(h),\mathsf M\,dX_q(z)\rangle_{3N}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}m_i\,h_i\cdot z_i,$$
where $h_i,z_i\in\mathbb R^3$ are the blocks of $dX_q(h),dX_q(z)$ under
the canonical Euclidean tangent identification specified in that supplier.
It restricts the mass-weighted ambient bilinear form to $T_qQ$, rather than
the unweighted Euclidean inner product.

**(e) Velocity constraints are a different object.** A **velocity-map
constraint** on the open ambient set $O$ is a pair of smooth maps
$$A:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'\times3N},\qquad b:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'},\qquad 1\le k'\le3N,$$
with $A(t,x)$ of constant rank $k'$ everywhere in the declared domain,
imposing $A(t,x(t))\dot x(t)+b(t,x(t))=0$ on a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to O$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval, the parameter $t$ is frame time, and $\dot x(t):=x'(t)$ is the componentwise derivative in the convention of [[def-cm01-units]]. Equivalently $A(t,x)$ is a linear map
$\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k'}$. Each row's output unit is declared, and
its corresponding component of $b$ has that same unit. The allowed velocities
at $(t,x)$ form the affine set $\{v:A(t,x)v+b(t,x)=0\}$; its differences form
$\ker A(t,x)$.

The law is **locally holonomic-equivalent at $(t_0,x_0)$** if on some open
neighbourhood $V\subseteq\mathbb R\times O$ of that point there are a $C^2$
map $g:V\to\mathbb R^{k'}$ with $D_xg$ of rank $k'$ and a $C^2$ matrix map
$C:V\to\mathbb R^{k'\times k'}$ with $\det C\ne0$ such that
$$A=C\,D_xg,\qquad b=C\,\partial_tg\qquad\text{on }V.$$
Thus the velocity law is locally the derivative of the regular positional
constraints $g(t,x)=\text{constant}$. It is **locally nonholonomic at the
specified point** when no such neighbourhood and pair $(g,C)$ exists; a
nonholonomic model in this local sense declares a point (or a region of
points) with this failure. For a homogeneous time-independent law this
rules out such a regular-level-set representation throughout a neighbourhood.
It need not rule out an individual embedded submanifold $S\subseteq O$ with
$T_xS=\ker A(x)$ for every $x\in S$, using the ambient tangent identification
of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]]; for an affine
time-dependent law the criterion also includes the drift $b$.
Absence of a single global pair alone does not establish local
nonintegrability. The rank of $A$ counts instantaneous velocity restrictions,
not the dimension of a positional configuration manifold; accessibility
requires its own definition. Rank changes require a separate model.

Adopt, as this page's **impact and open-mass extensions** of the force
branch of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the following three model extensions. Each is an adopted model, not a
consequence of the smooth-force postulates; each applies only where a
statement explicitly invokes it.

**(i) The isolated reciprocal impulse model.** A two-label force model with
masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), time window $I_0$,
configuration domain $Q$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]) and continuous
external-plus-pair force maps $F_1,F_2$ is **run in the isolated reciprocal
impulse model at $t_*\in I_0$** when there is an interval
$I\subseteq I_0$ with $t_*\in\operatorname{int}I$ and a position curve
$x=(x_1,x_2):I\to Q$ such that the following conditions hold. This curve is
called an **impulse motion**; only its restrictions away from $t_*$ are
motions of the associated first-order system of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]],
and no differentiability at $t_*$ is required:

1. $x_1,x_2$ are continuous on $I$ and twice continuously differentiable on
   each of $I\cap(-\infty,t_*)$ and $I\cap(t_*,\infty)$
   ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]],
   [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and
   $m_ix_i''(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ for every $t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}$;
2. the one-sided limits
   $v_i^{\pm}:=\lim_{t\to t_*\pm}x_i'(t)$ exist in $\mathbb R^3$
   ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]);
3. there is a vector $J\in\mathbb R^3$, the **impulse**, with
   $$m_1\bigl(v_1^+-v_1^-\bigr)=J,\qquad m_2\bigl(v_2^+-v_2^-\bigr)=-J .$$

The two equations of clause 3 are the **reciprocal finite-jump form** of the
isolated impulse: the two labels receive equal and opposite momentum changes.
The regular force maps remain continuous on their state domain; their
evaluations along the curve can have different one-sided limits because the
velocity can jump. The dimension of the impulse
is $[J]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

For the distributional rendering on $\operatorname{int}I$, assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Put
$p_i(t)=m_ix_i'(t)$ and $f_i(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ off $t_*$, assigning both
the value $0$ at $t_*$. Their one-sided limits are finite: those of $p_i$
are $m_iv_i^\pm$, and continuity of the state-domain force maps gives
$f_i(t_*^\pm)=F_i(t_*,x(t_*),v^\pm)$, with
$v^\pm=(v_1^\pm,v_2^\pm)$. Also $p_i'=f_i$ off the impulse. Thus each
component meets the piecewise-$C^1$ and one-sided derivative-limit
hypotheses of [[lem-cm-piecewise-c1-jump-derivative]]. Its identity,
summed componentwise, gives for every real vector test function
$\Phi\in C_c^\infty(\operatorname{int}I;\mathbb R^3)$ (each component is
smooth and compactly supported, [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]])
$$-\int_{\operatorname{int}I}\langle p_i,\Phi'\rangle\,d\lambda=\int_{\operatorname{int}I}\langle f_i,\Phi\rangle\,d\lambda+s_i\langle J,\Phi(t_*)\rangle,\qquad s_1=1,\quad s_2=-1,$$
where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure and the integral convention is that of
[[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]. This is the pairing form of the
adopted jumps. Unlike [[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]], whose
hypotheses require continuous time forces and assume the pairings to derive
the jumps, this rendering allows distinct one-sided regular-force values.

**(ii) The collinear restitution contact law.** A model run in the isolated
reciprocal impulse model at $t_*$ is **collinear** when there is a unit vector
$n\in\mathbb R^3$ (the **contact direction**) with $v_i^{\pm}\parallel n$ for
$i=1,2$ and $\langle v_2^--v_1^-,n\rangle<0$ (the labels approach along $n$).
For a collinear contact, adopt a **coefficient of restitution** $e\in[0,1]$ —
a dimensionless model datum of the pair and the contact — and the **restitution
law**
$$v_2^+-v_1^+=-e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr).$$
For $e=1$ the contact is called **elastic**, for $e=0$ **perfectly inelastic**
and otherwise **semi-elastic**; the law is a constitutive assumption, not a
consequence of the impulse equations of clause (i), and $e$ is not derived
from the masses or the approach speed. The law is stated only for a single
collinear contact; simultaneous contacts, repeated contacts and tangential
(friction) impulses are outside the model.

**(iii) The open-body material accounting.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a
nonempty open interval. Adopt for a body whose mass
$m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and velocity $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ are differentiable, and
whose external force and exchanged matter are described by maps
$F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and
$w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ (mass rates and *inertial*
velocities of the matter entering and leaving, measured in the same inertial
frame as $v$), the **material balance identities**
$$m'=r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad (mv)'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}\,w_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}\,w_{\mathrm{out}} .$$
They are the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,\mathrm dt$ of
matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,\mathrm dt$
with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$", and they
are adopted rather than derived from a closed-system law. Their product-rule
consequence $mv'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$
is proved in [[thm-cm-variable-mass-momentum-balance]]; in particular the
closed-system law $(mv)'=F$ is recovered only when
$r_{\mathrm{in}}w_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}$.
The quantities have types and SI dimensions
$[m]=\mu$, $[v]=[w_{\mathrm{in}}]=[w_{\mathrm{out}}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$,
$[F]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ and
$[r_{\mathrm{in}}]=[r_{\mathrm{out}}]=\mu\tau^{-1}$; they are model
data, not measured values.

derivations.claim: Clause 1: by [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (i) and [L1], $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=J$ and $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=-J$; adding gives $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)+m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=0$, which is exactly $P(t_*^+)=P(t_*^-)$. This is clause 1.

Clause 2: suppose the candidate motion $x$ of clause 1 also satisfies the smooth-force equation on all of $I$ with continuous force maps along it. By [L3] the curves $x_i''=F_i/m_i$ are continuous, hence $x_i$ is $C^2$ and $p_i=m_ix_i'$ is $C^1$ on $I$; a $C^1$ function on an interval has equal one-sided limits at every interior point, so $p_i(t_*^+)=p_i(t_*^-)$ for each label. Clause 1 gives $p_1(t_*^+)-p_1(t_*^-)=J$, hence $J=0$. Thus no candidate with a nonzero impulse is a smooth-force motion, as asserted.

Clause 5: fix any real $J_n\le\mu d_n$ and put $v_1^+:=v_1^-+\frac{J_n}{m_1}n$, $v_2^+:=v_2^--\frac{J_n}{m_2}n$; then $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=J_nn$ and $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=-J_nn$, so the reciprocal impulse equations of clause 1 hold with impulse $J=J_nn$, and adding the two equations shows that the total momentum is preserved. The relative velocity becomes $d^+=d^--\frac{J_n}{\mu}n$; hence $d^+\cdot n=d_n-\frac{J_n}{\mu}\ge0$ precisely for $J_n\le\mu d_n$, which is the stated admissibility (the contact separates or grazes). By the kinetic identity [L4], $\Delta K(J_n)=\frac{\mu}{2}\bigl(\lVert d^+\rVert_2^2-\lVert d^-\rVert_2^2\bigr) =\frac{\mu}{2}\bigl(-2\frac{J_n}{\mu}d_n+\frac{J_n^2}{\mu^2}\bigr) =-J_nd_n+\frac{J_n^2}{2\mu}$, a quadratic in $J_n$ with minimum $-\frac{\mu}{2}d_n^2$ at $J_n=\mu d_n$; the restitution law selects $J_n=\mu(1+e)d_n$, which lies in the admissible range because $1+e\ge1$ and $d_n<0$, and reproduces clause 3.

Clause 3: put $d^-=v_2^--v_1^-$ and $d^+=v_2^+-v_1^+$. The jump equations [L1] give $d^+=d^--J/\mu$, while restitution gives $d^+=-ed^-$. Hence $J=\mu(1+e)d^-$, parallel to $n$ since $d^-\parallel n$. By step 1.1, the two mass-weighted means are the same $V$. Solving $m_1v_1^++m_2v_2^+=MV$ and $v_2^+-v_1^+=d^+$ gives uniquely $v_1^+=V-(m_2/M)d^+=V+(m_2/M)ed^-$ and $v_2^+=V+(m_1/M)d^+=V-(m_1/M)ed^-$.

Clause 4: the kinetic split [L4] applied on both sides, with the same $V$ by step 1.1, gives $\Delta K=(\mu/2)(\lVert d^+\rVert_2^2-\lVert d^-\rVert_2^2)$. Substituting $d^+=-ed^-$ from step 2.1 and expanding the inner product gives $\Delta K=-(1-e^2)\mu\lVert d^-\rVert_2^2/2\le0$. Since $\mu>0$ and $0\le e\le1$, equality holds exactly when $e=1$ or $d^-=0$; the approach condition excludes $d^-=0$ for a contact. The computed deficit is not identified with any measured heat, sound or deformation observable.

Clause 6: differentiability of $m$ and $v$ on $I$ is part of [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (iii), so [L2] applies and gives the derived law from the material balance identities. The three special cases are its substitutions: (a) $r_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ leaves $mv'=F$, while $(mv)'=m'v+mv'=F$ because $m'=0$; (b) $r_{\mathrm{in}}=0$, $r_{\mathrm{out}}=-m'$ gives $mv'=F-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)=F+r_{\mathrm{out}}(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})$; and $(mv)'=m'v+mv'=F+r_{\mathrm{out}}(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})+m'v=F-r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}+r_{\mathrm{out}}v-r_{\mathrm{out}}v=F-r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}$, which equals $F$ exactly when $w_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ or $r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$; (c) $r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$, $w_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ gives $mv'=F-r_{\mathrm{in}}v$, while $(mv)'=m'v+mv'=r_{\mathrm{in}}v+F-r_{\mathrm{in}}v=F$. This is clause 6.

boundaries.evidence: The interval $I$ is nonempty with $t_*\in I$ and the label set $\{1,2\}$ is nonempty; step 1.2 uses the motion on $I$.
The perfectly inelastic value $e=0$ is included; step 2.1 handles every $e\in[0,1]$ and step 3.1 records that the energy change vanishes exactly at $e=1$ or $v_2^-=v_1^-$.
One impulse vector $J$ and one contact direction $n$; step 1.1 pairs the two momentum changes through the single $J$.
The collinear contact is the degenerate one-dimensional geometry solved in steps 2.1-1.3, and the grazing endpoint $J_n=\mu d_n$ lies in the admissible range of step 1.3.
The one-sided limits at $t_*$ and the endpoint $e=1$ of $[0,1]$ are hypotheses used in steps 1.1 and 2.1, not limiting conclusions of the proof.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), inherited from the statement of [[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]], whose distributional jump lemma uses it; declared in the Statement and carried by the citation of step 1.1.
Clause 4's equality case is an equivalence: step 3.1 proves $\Delta K\le0$ and the exact vanishing condition $e=1$ or $v_2^-=v_1^-$.
The converse of the vanishing case is the same equivalence, established in step 3.1 through the factor $(1-e^2)\mu\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2/2$.

risk_review.notes: Assigned Step-5 adjudication repair reviewed locally; The original motion premise inherited the global C2 contradiction of the postulate. Specified an impulse motion and derived momentum, restitution velocities and energy directly from finite jumps and the kinetic split, since the cited pairing theorem requires continuous time forces not guaranteed here. Corrected the false assertion that a nonzero impulse makes the regular force map discontinuous; a zero regular force map is compatible with singular forcing.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport theorem. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, let $\chi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]), and let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$. Define the swept region

$$\Sigma:=\bigl\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\bigr\}.$$

Write $\mathcal D_\chi:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}$ for the open domain of the spatial velocity $u$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]). Let $U\subseteq\mathcal D_\chi$ be open and contain the swept region $\Sigma$. Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); call it a **density field**. A **material subregion** is a nonempty bounded open $B'\subseteq B$ with $\overline{B'}\subseteq B$ ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]); for such $B'$ the same $\chi$ is a motion of $B'$.

**(i) Localization.** Assume for every material subregion $B'$ and every $t\in J_0$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)\,dx=0, \tag{CM}$$

It is sufficient to assume this identity only for those pairs $(t,B')$ for which $\chi_t(B')$ is an open Euclidean ball with closure inside $\chi_t(B)$. Under either version of the conservation hypothesis,

$$\partial_t\rho(t,x)+\operatorname{div}\bigl(\rho u\bigr)(t,x)=0$$

for every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$, with the material derivative and divergence of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]].

**(ii) Converse.** Conversely, if $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ on an open neighbourhood of $\Sigma$ in $U$, then (CM) holds for every material subregion $B'$ and every $t\in J_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport and divergence theorems. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, let $\chi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$ and material derivative $D_t$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]], [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]), and let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$. Define the swept region $\Sigma=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\}$.

Write $\mathcal D_\chi:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}$ for the open domain of the spatial velocity $u$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]), and take $U\subseteq\mathcal D_\chi$ open and containing $\Sigma$. Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ be a $C^1$ density field, let $\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^1$ field (the stress field of [[def-cm-traction-and-stress]]), and let $b:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Suppose:

**(K)** $\rho$ satisfies $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ at every $(t,x)$ with $t\in J_0$ and $x\in\chi_t(B)$;

**(L)** for every material subregion $B'$ (nonempty bounded open with $\overline{B'}\subseteq B$) and every $t\in J_0$ for which $\chi_t(B')$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]) , the balance is

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)u(t,x)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)b(t,x)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(B')}\sigma(t,y)\,\nu(y)\,dS(y),$$

where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal and the surface integral is that of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]].

Define the **row divergence** of $\sigma$ componentwise by

$$g(t,x):=\Bigl(\sum_{j}\partial_j\sigma_{1j},\ \sum_{j}\partial_j\sigma_{2j},\ \sum_{j}\partial_j\sigma_{3j}\Bigr)(t,x).$$

Then for every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$,

$$\rho(t,x)\,D_tu(t,x)=\rho(t,x)\,b(t,x)+g(t,x).$$

Throughout, $\mathbb R^3$ carries its standard ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$, its Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $a\in O$ and let $v:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that the total derivative $Dv(a):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is a linear map ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) whose matrix in the standard bases is $\bigl(\partial_jv_i(a)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le3}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). The **divergence** of $v$ at $a$ is

$$\operatorname{div}v(a):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Dv(a)\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_iv_i(a),$$

the trace of the total derivative ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]), read in the standard basis of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]).

For a $C^1$ scalar field $f:O\to\mathbb R$ and $a\in O$, the **gradient** $\nabla f(a)\in\mathbb R^3$ is the vector of partial derivatives of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; it is the unique vector with $Df(a)h=\langle\nabla f(a),h\rangle_2$ for every $h\in\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). We write $\langle\nabla f(a),v(a)\rangle_2=:\nabla f(a)\cdot v(a)$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $f:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For $(t,x)\in I\times O$ write $D_x f(t,x):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ for the total derivative of $y\mapsto f(t,y)$ at fixed $t$, and $\nabla_xf(t,x)$ for its gradient. The derivative $Df(t,x)$ of the full map on $I\times O$ acts on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$; it is distinct from $D_x f$. Define the partial time derivative $\partial_tf(t,x):=\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=t}f(s,x)$ and the **material derivative** of $f$ along $u$

$$D_tf(t,x):=\partial_tf(t,x)+D_xf(t,x)\bigl(u(t,x)\bigr)=\partial_tf(t,x)+\nabla_x f(t,x)\cdot u(t,x).$$

Spatial derivatives $Du$, $Dw$, $\nabla f$ and $\operatorname{div}u$ of time-dependent fields always mean $D_xu$, $D_xw$, $\nabla_x f$ and spatial divergence at fixed time; a stationary field $u(x)$ is included by setting $u(t,x)=u(x)$. The same definitions apply on any open spacetime domain, by restriction to a product neighborhood of each point.

For a $C^1$ vector field $w:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ the material derivative $D_tw$ is defined componentwise, and $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)$ means the divergence of $x\mapsto w(t,x)$ at $x$ at each fixed $t$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a spatial set and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a time interval. No openness of $\Omega$ or regularity of a traction map is assumed by this definition; consumers impose any needed additional hypotheses. Let $S^2:=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:\|n\|_2=1\}$ be the unit sphere of [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]].

A **traction field** is a map

$$t:S^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,$$

read with the following convention: $t(n)$ is the force per unit area exerted **by the material on the side towards which $n$ points upon the material on the other side**, at the point of a surface whose unit normal is $n$. The dependence of $t$ on position and time is suppressed in this notation; a traction **field on a set** $\Omega\times I$ is a map $t:\Omega\times I\times S^2\to\mathbb R^3$, and all statements below apply to each fixed $(y,s)$.

For $v\in\mathbb R^3$ use one-based component labels $v_i:=v(i-1)$, and for $\sigma\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ use $\sigma_{ij}:=\sigma(i-1,j-1)$, where $1\le i,j\le3$; $e_i$ is the vector with value $1$ at $i-1$ and $0$ at the other two indices. Define the matrix-vector action $\sigma v\in\mathbb R^3$ by $(\sigma v)(k):=\sum_{j<3}\sigma(k,j)v(j)$ for $0\le k<3$, equivalently $(\sigma v)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\sigma_{ij}v_j$. It is the rectangular product of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] after identifying $v$ with the column matrix $C_v(j,0):=v(j)$ and the result with its sole column.

A matrix $\sigma\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]) **represents** the traction field $t$ when

$$t(n)=\sigma n\qquad\text{for every }n\in S^2,$$

the product being the matrix-vector action defined above. A matrix representing a traction field is called a **stress matrix** for it.

The **reversed normal convention** is the identity $t(-n)=-t(n)$; it is a property some traction fields have and is not part of the definition. A traction field is **normal** when $t(n)$ is a real multiple of $n$ for every $n$, and **purely tangential** when $\langle t(n),n\rangle_2=0$ for every $n$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the change-of-variables theorem below. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]), let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]) and let $\psi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ in the sense of [[def-cm-continuum-motion]], with associated spatial velocity

$$w\bigl(t,\psi(t,X)\bigr)=\partial_t\psi(t,X)$$

and Jacobian $J(t,X)=\det D_X\psi_t(X)$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]], [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]).

Let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, put

$$\Sigma:=\bigl\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\psi_t(\overline B)\bigr\},$$

and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ containing $\Sigma$. Then

$$F(t):=\int_{\psi_t(B)}f(t,x)\,dx$$

is defined and differentiable on $J_0$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]), and for every $t\in J_0$

$$F'(t)=\int_{\psi_t(B)}\bigl(\partial_tf+\operatorname{div}(fw)\bigr)(t,x)\,dx,$$

with the divergence and spatial derivative of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]] and the Lebesgue integral of [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]. The same formula holds componentwise for $f$ replaced by a $C^1$ vector field.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport and divergence theorems. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, and let $\chi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$. Write

$$\mathcal D_\chi:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}$$

for the open domain on which $u$ is defined ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]). Let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with compact closure in $I$, and let $U\subseteq\mathcal D_\chi$ be open and contain the swept region of $B$ over $\overline{J_0}$.

Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ and $\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be $C^1$ and let $b:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Define $g_i:=\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$ and suppose, on $U$:

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\rho\,D_tu=\rho b+g . \tag{KM}$$

Let $\psi:I\times O'\to\mathbb R^3$ be a second motion of a material region $B'\subseteq B$ (with the same reference chart domain $O'=O$ used for $B$; write $w$ for its spatial velocity), and suppose that for every $t\in J_0$ the control region $C_t:=\psi_t(B')$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]) with outward unit normal $\nu$ and boundary surface integral as in [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]].

Assume also that the control sweep $\Sigma_C:=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\psi_t(\overline{B'})\}$ is contained in $U$. Thus the fields and the local equations (KM) are defined on a neighbourhood of every closed control region. No condition that the control motion coincide with the material motion is imposed.

Then for every $t\in J_0$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C_t}\rho\,dx=-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,dS, \tag{CV1}$$

and componentwise

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C_t}\rho u_i\,dx=\int_{C_t}\rho b_i\,dx+\Bigl(\int_{\partial C_t}\sigma\nu\,dS\Bigr)_i-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho u_i\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,dS\qquad(i=1,2,3). \tag{CV2}$$

Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region (nonempty, bounded, open, [[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]) and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]).

A **motion of $B$ on $I$** consists of an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $\overline B\subseteq O$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) together with a map

$$\chi:I\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3$$

such that:

1. $\chi$ is of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]);
2. for every $t\in I$ the map $\chi_t:=\chi(t,\cdot):O\to\mathbb R^3$ is of class $C^1$, is injective, and has $D_X\chi_t(X)$ invertible for every $X\in O$;
3. writing

$$J(t,X):=\det\bigl(D_X\chi_t(X)\bigr)$$

with the determinant of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]], one has $J(t,X)>0$ for every $(t,X)\in I\times B$.

We call $X\in B$ the **material label** (reference position), $x=\chi(t,X)$ the **position** at time $t$ of the label $X$, and

$$\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$$

the **current (material) region** at time $t$. Condition 2 makes each $\chi_t:O\to\chi_t(O)$ a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto the open set $\chi_t(O)$ ([[cor-injective-regular-ck-map-is-a-ck-diffeomorphism-onto-its-image]]).

The **spatial velocity field** of the motion is

$$u:\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,\qquad u\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr):=\partial_t\chi(t,X),$$

and the **spatial acceleration field** is the material derivative of $u$ in the sense of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]],

$$a(t,x):=D_tu(t,x)=\partial_tu(t,x)+Du(t,x)u(t,x).$$

For a compact subinterval $K\subseteq I$ the **swept region** of $B$ over $K$ is

$$\Sigma_K:=\bigl\{(t,x):t\in K,\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\bigr\},$$

and for a scalar field $f$ on a neighbourhood of $\Sigma_K$ the spatial field $f(t,x)$ of a material quantity $F(t,X)$ is defined by $f(t,\chi(t,X))=F(t,X)$.

Throughout this surface-integration page assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the earlier Lebesgue and polar measure machinery. Let $n\ge2$. A bounded $C^1$ domain is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid change of coordinates, the graph $z=h(y)$ of a $C^1$ function, with $\Omega$ locally exactly the subgraph $z<h(y)$. Connectedness is not required. The outward normal in these coordinates is $\nu=(-Dh,1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$, transported by the orthogonal coordinate map. Its overlap agreement is justified with surface charts below.

The convention $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$ means F is continuously differentiable in $\Omega$, and F and its first derivatives extend continuously to its closure. For $C^2$ require the same for derivatives through order two. No ambient extension across the boundary is required. Derivatives use [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]; products are the real Euclidean inner products of [[def-inner-product-space]]. Write $\operatorname{div}F=\sum_i\partial_iF_i$, $Du=(\partial_iu)_i$ and $\Delta u=\sum_i\partial_i^2u$.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport and divergence theorems. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, and let $\chi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$. Write

$$\mathcal D_\chi:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}$$

for the open domain on which $u$ is defined ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]). Let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with compact closure in $I$, and let $U\subseteq\mathcal D_\chi$ be open and contain the swept region of $B$ over $\overline{J_0}$.

Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ and $\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be $C^1$ and let $b:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Define $g_i:=\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$ and suppose, on $U$:

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\rho\,D_tu=\rho b+g . \tag{KM}$$

Let $\psi:I\times O'\to\mathbb R^3$ be a second motion of a material region $B'\subseteq B$ (with the same reference chart domain $O'=O$ used for $B$; write $w$ for its spatial velocity), and suppose that for every $t\in J_0$ the control region $C_t:=\psi_t(B')$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]) with outward unit normal $\nu$ and boundary surface integral as in [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]].

Assume also that the control sweep $\Sigma_C:=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\psi_t(\overline{B'})\}$ is contained in $U$. Thus the fields and the local equations (KM) are defined on a neighbourhood of every closed control region. No condition that the control motion coincide with the material motion is imposed.

Then for every $t\in J_0$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C_t}\rho\,dx=-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,dS, \tag{CV1}$$

and componentwise

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C_t}\rho u_i\,dx=\int_{C_t}\rho b_i\,dx+\Bigl(\int_{\partial C_t}\sigma\nu\,dS\Bigr)_i-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho u_i\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,dS\qquad(i=1,2,3). \tag{CV2}$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]), let $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and let $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be maps. Suppose the two **material balance identities**

$$m'(t)=r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t),\qquad (mv)'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)$$

hold for every $t\in I$, where $mv$ denotes the pointwise scalar multiple. Then

$$m(t)v'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in I).$$

In particular, if $F\equiv0$, $r_{\mathrm{in}}\equiv0$ and $r_{\mathrm{out}}\equiv r$ for a constant $r\ge0$, then $mv'=-r(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$: the acceleration is governed by the momentum carried away per unit time relative to the body, not by $(mv)'=0$.

The two balance identities are the **adopted content of the material momentum accounting** — the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,dt$ of matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,dt$ with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$". They are not derived here from any closed-system law; the deduction below is their product-rule consequence.

Fix a model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$
particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb
R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with its collision
set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an
interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). All sums below range over
$i=1,\dots,N$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $u\times v$, $\langle u,v\rangle$
and $\lVert u\rVert_{2}$ are the cross product, the Euclidean inner product and
the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(a) Curve families and motions.** A **curve family** of the model is a map
$x:J\to Q$, $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$, of class $C^{2}$ on $J$
([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]); its **coordinate velocities** are
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$ on $J$, written $w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{N}):J\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
A curve family is a **motion** of the model when
$$m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J),$$
the notion of clause (c) of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Every quantity of
this definition is defined for an arbitrary curve family; the balance theorems
of this page state which of their properties use the equations of motion.
Along a curve family the force map is evaluated at $(t,x(t),w(t))\in
I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; when the model invokes the
external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the maps $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $F_{ij}$ are evaluated at their declared
arguments on the motion's state graph, where the presentation is an identity
for $F_{i}$.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define
$$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$
Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$
the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$.
The dimensions are $[M]=\mu$, $[p_{i}]=[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and $[X]=[\rho_{i}]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]). Since $x_{i}$ is $C^{2}$, each $p_{i}$ is $C^{1}$ and
each of $P$, $X$, $\rho_{i}$ is differentiable, as a finite sum of
differentiable curves ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); write
$$V:=X'$$
for the **centre-of-mass velocity**. The algebraic identities
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}=0$, $P=MV$ and the splitting of the kinetic sum
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}$ are proved in the kinetic-splitting
theorem of this page; they are not part of this definition.

**(c) Angular momentum, torque, internal torque sum.** Let a **reference
curve** $o:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{1}$ be given: a point about which
moments are taken, allowed to move (a constant map $o\equiv o_{0}$ is the
fixed-origin case). Define the **angular momentum about $o$** and the **total
torque about $o$** by
$$J_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times p_{i}(t),\qquad T_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),$$
with dimensions $[J_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{2}\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and
$[T_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m$). When the
model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of
[[post-cm02-interactions]], define in addition the **external torque** and the
**internal torque sum**
$$T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr),\qquad I(t):=\sum_{i<j}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-x_{j}(t)\bigr)\times F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr).$$
The sum $I$ does not involve $o$; it is defined whenever the pair
presentation is declared. The identity $T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I$ uses the
antisymmetry $F_{ji}=-F_{ij}$ of clause (ii)1 of that postulate to reindex the
ordered pairs and is proved as step 1.1 of the angular-momentum balance of
this page.

**(d) Kinetic energy, power, work.** Define the **kinetic energy** and the
**power of the total force** along the curve family by
$$K(t):=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}(t)\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad \mathcal P(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl\langle F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),\,w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle,$$
of dimensions $[K]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules) and
$[\mathcal P]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-3}$ (read in watts), and for
$t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$ the **work of the total force** over $[t_{0},t_{1}]$ by
$$W([t_{0},t_{1}]):=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal P(t)\,dt,$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules); $\mathcal P$ is
continuous on $J$ because $F$, $x$ and $w$ are continuous, so the Riemann
integral exists ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], see the page
`the-riemann-integral`). The **potential energy** is not defined by this item:
it belongs to the potential branch of the model and is defined in the
potential-and-mechanical-energy item of this page.

**(e) Frame and reference-point dependence.** The quantities $p_{i}$, $P$,
$X$, $\rho_{i}$, $V$, $K$, $\mathcal P$ and $W$ are read in the one inertial
frame fixed above, and $J_{o}$, $T_{o}$, $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$, $I$ are read
about the reference curve $o$ in that frame. They are not invariant under a
change of frame or reference point: their transformation laws under a change
of inertial frame are stated and proved in the frame-transformation item of
this page, and every conservation statement involving them names the frame
and the reference point in which it is made.

**(f) Status.** This item is a definition: it introduces symbols, their
domains, regularity, dimensions and frame dependence from the model's data.
It adopts no force law beyond the force branch already fixed, asserts no
balance of any of these quantities and records no measured value.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.
