**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about particles and their motion, in the spacetime of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] and the frames of [[post-cm01-frames]].

**(i) Particle labels and worldlines.** A model of the framework has **particle
labels** $i=1,\dots,N$ for some $N\ge1$. To each label and each *inertial
frame* of the model — an adapted chart $(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}))$ with
coordinates $(t,x)$ in the sense of [[post-cm01-frames]] — there is assigned a
**worldline** $\gamma_{i}:I\to A$ described in that frame, where
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval — that is, an interval
of the form $(a,b)$ with $-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ and at least two points —
the curve $\gamma_{i}$ is of class $C^{2}$ in the adapted coordinates of the frame,
and the **parameter condition**

$$\tau\bigl(\gamma_{i}(t)-o\bigr)=t\qquad(t\in I)$$

holds: the curve parameter is the elapsed time from the origin of the frame, so
in the frame's coordinates $\gamma_{i}(t)=(t,x_{i}(t))$ with
$x_{i}:I\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{2}$. The parameter condition replaces
the causal conditions of relativistic kinematics: no timelike condition on the
velocity and no upper bound on its Euclidean norm is imposed, and the
parameter is not free up to reparametrization.

**(ii) Description in another frame.** The same motion described in a second
inertial frame is the curve obtained by the time reparametrization of the two
frames: if $(t',x')$ are the coordinates of the second frame and
$t'=t+b$ is the time component of the transformation between the two frames
([[post-cm01-frames]], [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]]),
then the description of the motion in the second frame is the curve
$\gamma_{i,b}(t'):=\gamma_{i}(t'-b)$, defined on $I+b$, and it again satisfies
the parameter condition $\tau(\gamma_{i,b}(t')-o')=t'$ with respect to the
second frame's origin $o'$. This is a consistency requirement of the model's
frame language; the accompanying spatial transformation of the coordinate
curve is the affine law of [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]],
and its kinematic consequences are proved in [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]].

**(iii) Regularity is frame-independent.** The class of the worldline is
independent of the frame used to describe it: by the transformation law of
[[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]], the coordinates of the
same event in two inertial frames differ by
$t'=t+b$, $x'=Rx+vt+a$ with constant $b,a,v$ and $R\in SO(3)$, so a coordinate
curve is twice continuously differentiable in one inertial frame exactly when
its reparametrized description is twice continuously differentiable in the
other. The assumptions of this postulate are therefore read in any one inertial
frame without loss.

**(iv) Velocity and acceleration.** In a fixed inertial frame the quantities
$w_{i}:=dx_{i}/dt$ and $a_{i}:=d^{2}x_{i}/dt^{2}$ are the **coordinate
velocity** and **coordinate acceleration** of the label, of dimensions
$\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ by [[def-cm01-units]]; they are defined
precisely, and their transformation under a change of inertial frame is
recorded, in [[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]].

**(v) Fixed inertial mass.** Each particle label $i$ carries a **mass**
$m_{i}>0$, a primitive parameter of the model with dimension $\mu$
([[def-cm01-units]]). The mass is fixed: it is the same positive number at all
times and in all inertial frames of this model; the index $i$ identifies a label within that model and asserts no cross-model identification or equality of mass parameters. It
is not a function of the time coordinate, of the position or of the velocity,
and no variable-mass model is a model of this clause. The mass enters the
dynamics only through its later appearance in the equation of motion; this
postulate attaches no dynamics to it. Distinct labels may carry distinct
masses, and the masses are model data, not measured values.

**(vi) Point-particle idealization.** The model retains of each label only its
position and its fixed mass, together with the label index: size, shape, spin,
deformation, temperature and internal degrees of freedom are omitted, and the
quantity $x_{i}(t)$ is the single point representing the label at time $t$. An
application of the model must state when this idealization is adequate for the
system at hand; for a body whose rotation, deformation or internal structure
matters for the question asked, the point-particle model is not adequate and a
richer model must be specified. The framework makes no claim that every
physical body is a point particle.

**(vii) Calibration caveat.** An apparatus calibration may *estimate* a mass
parameter of a concrete body under a stated measurement model, with its
assumptions, sampling and uncertainty; such an estimate neither defines the
mass parameter of a label nor verifies the equation of motion in which it
occurs, and it is not deduced from this postulate. No measured value of any
mass is asserted by this item.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

A **material region** is a nonempty, bounded, open subset $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. This region predicate is choice-free and does not assume a density or measure.

For the following **Lebesgue density and mass construction**, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]): [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]] supplies the measure $\lambda_3$ on its Lebesgue sigma-algebra ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure]]). Since $B$ is open, it is Lebesgue measurable by the Borel-measurability theorem ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Put $\mathcal L_B:=\{E\cap B:E\in\mathcal L(\mathbb R^3)\}$ and $\lambda_B(C):=\lambda_3(C)$ for $C\in\mathcal L_B$. The trace family $\mathcal L_B$ is a sigma-algebra on $B$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]); countable additivity of $\lambda_B$ follows by applying that of $\lambda_3$ to disjoint trace-measurable sets, so $(B,\mathcal L_B,\lambda_B)$ is a measure space ([[def-measure]]). In the displays below, $\int_B\rho\,d\lambda_3$ means the Lebesgue integral of $\rho$ on this measure space ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). A **density** on $B$ is a measurable function

$$\rho:B\longrightarrow[0,\infty)$$

measurable as a map from $(B,\mathcal L_B)$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ ([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) and integrable on $(B,\mathcal L_B,\lambda_B)$; the **mass** of the pair $(B,\rho)$ is

$$\operatorname{mass}(B,\rho):=\int_B\rho\,d\lambda_3\ \in[0,\infty).$$

For this scalar function, **bounded** means that some $M<\infty$ satisfies $0\le\rho(X)\le M$ for every $X\in B$. **Continuous** means that for every $X\in B$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $Y\in B$ and $\|X-Y\|_2<\delta$ imply $|\rho(X)-\rho(Y)|<\varepsilon$. For $k\ge1$, **of class $C^k$ on $B$** means that every iterated coordinate partial derivative of order at most $k$ exists on $B$ and is continuous there; no extension to $\partial B$ is required unless a consuming statement says so. A **measured material region** is a triple $(B,\rho,m)$ with $m=\operatorname{mass}(B,\rho)$ recorded.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a spatial set and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a time interval. No openness of $\Omega$ or regularity of a traction map is assumed by this definition; consumers impose any needed additional hypotheses. Let $S^2:=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:\|n\|_2=1\}$ be the unit sphere of [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]].

A **traction field** is a map

$$t:S^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,$$

read with the following convention: $t(n)$ is the force per unit area exerted **by the material on the side towards which $n$ points upon the material on the other side**, at the point of a surface whose unit normal is $n$. The dependence of $t$ on position and time is suppressed in this notation; a traction **field on a set** $\Omega\times I$ is a map $t:\Omega\times I\times S^2\to\mathbb R^3$, and all statements below apply to each fixed $(y,s)$.

For $v\in\mathbb R^3$ use one-based component labels $v_i:=v(i-1)$, and for $\sigma\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ use $\sigma_{ij}:=\sigma(i-1,j-1)$, where $1\le i,j\le3$; $e_i$ is the vector with value $1$ at $i-1$ and $0$ at the other two indices. Define the matrix-vector action $\sigma v\in\mathbb R^3$ by $(\sigma v)(k):=\sum_{j<3}\sigma(k,j)v(j)$ for $0\le k<3$, equivalently $(\sigma v)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\sigma_{ij}v_j$. It is the rectangular product of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] after identifying $v$ with the column matrix $C_v(j,0):=v(j)$ and the result with its sole column.

A matrix $\sigma\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]) **represents** the traction field $t$ when

$$t(n)=\sigma n\qquad\text{for every }n\in S^2,$$

the product being the matrix-vector action defined above. A matrix representing a traction field is called a **stress matrix** for it.

The **reversed normal convention** is the identity $t(-n)=-t(n)$; it is a property some traction fields have and is not part of the definition. A traction field is **normal** when $t(n)$ is a real multiple of $n$ for every $n$, and **purely tangential** when $\langle t(n),n\rangle_2=0$ for every $n$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

derivations.claim: Fix $t\in J_0$, which is interior to $I$ even if it is an endpoint of $J_0$. Each sufficiently small current ball $A$ with closure in $\chi_t(B)$ has an admissible inverse-image material subregion under the $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\chi_t$. Transport [L2] applies on a small open time neighbourhood of $t$. The adopted mass balance at $t$ gives $\int_A(\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u))=0$. A continuous integrand with zero integral on all such balls vanishes pointwise: a nonzero value would retain its strict sign on a sufficiently small ball, contradicting the zero integral. Thus the local mass equation holds. Componentwise transport and row-wise divergence applied to the momentum balance give $\int_A(\rho D_tu-\rho b-g)_i=0$, since the mass-equation terms cancel by the product rule. The same sign argument proves the local momentum equation. This is the instantaneous localization argument of [L1], including the compact $J_0$'s endpoints.

Fix $t\in J_0$. The control-sweep hypothesis and continuity of the control motion put its closed regions in the field domain on a small open time neighbourhood of $t$. The local equations on $C_t$ follow from step 1.1 in the material-interior case, and are adopted in the alternative case. Transport gives $m'=\int_{C_t}(\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho w))=\int_{C_t}\operatorname{div}(\rho(w-u))$; divergence gives (CV1). Componentwise transport, the product rule and the local equations give $P_i'=\int_{C_t}(\rho b_i+g_i+\operatorname{div}(\rho u_i(w-u)))$; divergence of the stress row and of the last vector field gives (CV2). These calculations of [L2] use the local equations only at $t$, and therefore include the endpoints without assuming balances outside $J_0$.

Clause 2: if $\psi=\chi$ then $w=u$ on $\partial C_t$, so $(u-w)\cdot\nu=0$ and both flux integrals in (CV1) and (CV2) vanish; the identities become the material balances of the model. If $\psi$ is constant then $w=0$ and $u-w=u$, giving the displayed fixed-region equations with $m_C$, $P_C$; when in addition the fields are steady and $C$ is fixed, the left sides are the rates of the steady-flow treatment and the equations reduce to the balance between the external force and the momentum flux difference.

Clause 3, mass balance: decomposing $\partial C_t$ into the inlet, outlet and zero-flux pieces, the boundary term of (CV1) becomes $-\int_{\partial C_t}ho(u-w)\cdot
u =-\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{in}}}ho(u-w)\cdot
u-\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{out}}}ho(u-w)\cdot
u =r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}$ by the definitions, so (CV1) reads $m'=r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}$; the rates are nonnegative because the integrands are nonnegative on the two pieces.

Clause 3, momentum balance: similarly the flux term of (CV2) decomposes as $-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho u_i(u-w)\cdot\nu =r_{\mathrm{in}}(w_{\mathrm{in}})_i-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}})_i$ by the definitions of the flux averages, and the remaining terms are $F_{\mathrm{ext}}$ componentwise, giving $P'=F_{\mathrm{ext}}+r_{\mathrm{in}}w_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}$.

Clause 3, derived law: the two identities of steps 3.2 and 3.3 have exactly the form to which [L3] applies with $F=F_{\mathrm{ext}}$; hence $mv'=F_{\mathrm{ext}}+r_{\mathrm{in}}(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$ for the lumped body, and the two special cases are its substitutions ($r_{\mathrm{in}}=0$, $r_{\mathrm{out}}=-m'$ for the thrust form; $w=u$ for the material case).

Clause 4 is the scope: steps 1.1-3.3 use only the adopted balances, the cited mathematical theorems and the stated regularity, and introduce no constitutive relation, boundary condition or measured input. This completes the proof.

citations.quote:
For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Sine is differentiable, hence continuous, and strictly increasing on
$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$; its endpoint values are $-1$ and $1$
([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]],
[[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]],
[[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]). The intermediate value
theorem therefore makes its restricted image exactly $[-1,1]$
([[thm-intermediate-value]]). Likewise, cosine is continuous and strictly
decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, with endpoint values $1$ and $-1$, so its restricted
image is $[-1,1]$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-intermediate-value]]).
Their principal inverses are denoted

$$\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2],\qquad\arccos:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi],$$

and are characterised by

$$\sin(\arcsin y)=y,\qquad\cos(\arccos y)=y\qquad(-1\le y\le1).$$

The chosen target intervals are part of the notation: without them, inverse
sine and inverse cosine would be multivalued relations rather than functions.
Their continuity follows from [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Borel/Lebesgue measure foundation below.

**Data.** Let $\mu>0$, let $U:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $R>0$ satisfy $U(r)=0$
for every $r\ge R$ (a **finite-range potential**), and let $E>0$ and $J>0$ be
reals. Write

$$V(r):=U(r)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2}\qquad(r>0).$$

**Incident flux measure.** Let $\nu$ be the Borel measure on the open rectangle
$(0,\infty)\times(0,2\pi)$ given by the density $b$ against Lebesgue measure
$\lambda_2$,

$$\nu(A):=\int_A b\,d\lambda_2(b,\varphi)\qquad(A\subseteq(0,\infty)\times(0,2\pi)\ \text{Borel}),$$

the integral being that of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]; the
nonnegative Borel function $(b,\varphi)\mapsto b$ defines a measure by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]
([[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]]). In the model this
measure records a uniform incident beam: an annulus of impact parameters
$[b_1,b_2)$ contributes $\pi(b_2^2-b_1^2)$ over the full azimuth range, or
$\tfrac12(b_2^2-b_1^2)$ per unit azimuth.

**Solid-angle element.** Let $\Omega$ be the Borel measure on
$(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$ with density $\sin$ against $\lambda_2$,

$$\Omega(B):=\int_B\sin\theta\,d\lambda_2(\theta,\varphi)\qquad(B\subseteq(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\ \text{Borel}),$$

where $\sin$ is the function of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]].
It is continuous, being differentiable by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]].
Also $\sin0=\sin\pi=0$ by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]];
strict increase on $[0,\pi/2]$ and strict decrease on $[\pi/2,\pi]$
([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]]) give $\sin\theta>0$ for
$0<\theta<\pi$. Thus $(\theta,\varphi)\mapsto\sin\theta$ is a nonnegative
Borel function (continuous preimages of Borel sets are Borel,
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), and
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]
establishes that $\Omega$ is a measure. This
is the standard solid-angle element written $\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi$
(the surface measure of the unit sphere in spherical coordinates, restricted
to the open chart).

**Deflection branch.** A **deflection branch** is an interval
$(a_1,a_2)\subseteq(0,\infty)$ with at least two points together with a
function $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ that is of class $C^1$ and satisfies
$\theta'(b)\ne0$ for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$. Such a $\theta$ is strictly
monotone (the continuous nonvanishing derivative has constant sign, and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]] gives strict monotonicity) and its image is an interval with endpoints $\theta_1<\theta_2$
([[def-interval]]); its inverse $b:(\theta_1,\theta_2)\to(a_1,a_2)$ is
differentiable with $b'(\theta)=1/\theta'(b(\theta))$, by the
derivative-of-an-inverse theorem [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]] applied to
the continuous injective $\theta$ (every point of $(a_1,a_2)$ is a limit point
of it, [[def-limit-point-r]], [[def-derivative]]).

**Cross-section density.** The **cross-section density of the branch** is the
function

$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(\theta):=\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'\bigl(b(\theta)\bigr)\bigr|} \qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2).$$

**Mathematical status.** The measures, branches and density are abstract data
independent of the finite-range trajectory data $(\mu,U,R,E,J)$. A branch is not asserted to arise from any
trajectory; the scattering theorems of this page identify the deflection
angle computed from the central-force equation with the values of such a
function under their hypotheses, and they compute the pushforward of $\nu$ under the induced map. No counting of
detected particles, and no empirical claim, is part of this definition.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(\theta_1,\theta_2)\subseteq(0,\pi)$ be a deflection
branch of [[def-cm-scattering-data]], with inverse $b(\theta)$, and set
$D=(a_1,a_2)\times(0,2\pi)$, $H=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\times(0,2\pi)$ and
$T(b,\varphi)=(\theta(b),\varphi)$. Restrict the incident measure $\nu$ to
$D$. Its pushforward, defined by $T_*\nu(B)=\nu(T^{-1}(B))$ for Borel
$B\subseteq H$, satisfies
$$T_*\nu(B)=\int_B b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|\,d\lambda_2(\theta,\varphi).$$
For every nonnegative Borel $g:H\to[0,+\infty]$, and for every real Borel
$g$ with either side's integral of $|g|$ finite, consequently
$$\int_D g(\theta(b),\varphi)b\,d\lambda_2(b,\varphi)=\int_H g(\theta,\varphi)b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|\,d\lambda_2(\theta,\varphi).$$
The nonnegative equality allows $+\infty$; in the real case both sides are
finite and absolute integrability on one side is equivalent to that on the
other. In particular it applies to continuous periodic test functions that
are nonnegative or absolutely integrable, and to compactly supported
continuous test functions. No equality of undefined signed improper
integrals is asserted. Nonnegative double-integral notation denotes the
corresponding Lebesgue integrals, with iterated integrals justified by Tonelli.

Thus the outgoing angular measure has density $b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|$
against $d\theta\,d\varphi$ and density
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(\theta)=\frac{b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|}{\sin\theta}=\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,|\theta'(b(\theta))|}$$
against the solid-angle measure. For finitely many branches on disjoint
incident intervals the measures add, including on overlapping image
intervals; in particular contributions with pairwise disjoint images add.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: Reflection and conservation: by [L1], $|v^+|=|v^-|=v_\infty$ and the angular momentum about the centre is conserved across the contact; hence the two free pieces of the motion are straight lines and the motion has a constant angular momentum $j$ with $|j|=\mu b v_\infty$. This verifies directly for the incoming line the same geometric identity $b=J/(\mu v_\infty)$ used in [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] clause (ii); the contact trajectory itself is outside that definition's smooth central-model class.

Deflection: let $\alpha$ be the acute angle between the inward normal $-n$ at first contact and the incoming direction $\hat u$, so that $\sin\alpha=b/a$ by [L2]. The reflection turns the velocity by the angle computed in [L2], namely $\pi-2\alpha$; since $b\in(0,a)$ we have $\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$ and $\theta=\pi-2\alpha\in(0,\pi)$.

Branch and inverse: the map $b\mapsto\theta(b)=\pi-2\arcsin(b/a)$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,a)$ by [L3] and its image is $(0,\pi)$; solving $\sin((\pi-\theta)/2)=b/a$ gives $b(\theta)=a\cos(\theta/2)$ on $(0,\pi)$, which is $C^1$ with $b'(\theta)=-\frac{a}{2}\sin(\theta/2)\ne0$. Thus the model realises a single deflection branch with image $(0,\pi)$, and no branch sum is needed for it.

Contact pushforward: step 2.1 verifies the abstract branch hypotheses of [L4], and substituting $n=(b e_\varphi-\sqrt{a^2-b^2}\,\hat u)/a$ into the reflection rule gives $v^+/v_\infty=(2b^2/a^2-1)\hat u+[2b\sqrt{a^2-b^2}/a^2]e_\varphi$. The transverse coefficient is positive for $0<b<a$, verifying that the outgoing azimuth is $\varphi$ and the direction map is $T$. Therefore, for every Borel $B\subseteq Y$, $\sigma(B)=\int_B b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|\,d\lambda_2$. Since $\sin\theta>0$, the locally defined differential contact cross-section is $\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta)=\frac{b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|}{\sin\theta} =\frac{a\cos(\theta/2)\cdot\frac{a}{2}\sin(\theta/2)}{\sin\theta}$. Using $\sin\theta=2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)$ this equals $\frac{a^2}{4}$ for every $\theta\in(0,\pi)$: the contact pushforward is $(a^2/4)\Omega$, so the outgoing angular distribution of uniformly incident contacts is uniform, and the density is finite, positive and independent of $\theta$.

Truncated total: by [L4] and the fundamental theorem, for the full image interval $$\sigma\bigl((0,\pi)\bigr)=\int_0^{\pi}\frac{a^2}{4}\,2\pi\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{a^2}{4}\cdot2\pi\cdot\bigl[-\cos\theta\bigr]_0^{\pi} =\frac{a^2}{4}\cdot 4\pi=\pi a^2,$$ and for $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi$ the band value is $\frac{a^2}{4}\cdot2\pi(\cos\theta_1-\cos\theta_2)$, finite; in particular the branch has a finite ideal total $\pi a^2$.

Model boundary: the motion just computed is piecewise linear with a contact rule, not a central-force trajectory of class $C^2$ with a finite-range potential; the quadrature theorem [[pthm-cm15-central-scattering]] does not apply to it, and the finite total $\pi a^2$ is a property of this contact model, not a counterexample to the forward divergence of the ideal Coulomb branch. The declared data are model data: no measurement is reported, and the agreement of the algebraic form with the cited impenetrable-sphere computation is a consistency check of the model, not evidence about nature.

boundaries.evidence: The range $0<b<a$ of step 1.2 is nonempty and the branch image $(0,\pi)$ of step 2.1 is nondegenerate.
The head-on limit $b\downarrow0$ and the grazing limit $b\uparrow a$ are endpoints of the branch, not evaluated states: step 2.1 states the open branch and step 4.1 integrates its whole image.
One sphere, one contact and one reflection; step 1.2 computes the single deflection angle.
The grazing value $b=a$ where $\sin\alpha=1$ is excluded from the open branch; step 4.1 treats the image endpoints only as limits of integration.
The truncated total over the full image is the finite $\pi a^2$ computed in step 4.1, where the endpoint values $\cos0$ and $\cos\pi$ are evaluated.

boundaries.reason: Step 1.2 fixes alpha=arcsin(b/a) for the given b in (0,a); step 2.1 gives b(theta)=a cos(theta/2). The contact data and the inverse branch are explicit rather than selected from arbitrary nonempty sets.

Example derives the reflection angle, inverse branch and cross-section from the adopted elastic contact rule. Step 2.1 solves b=a sin(alpha) explicitly; this coordinate identity does not assert that a constant cross-section implies the reflection rule.

risk_review.notes: Read six Verification steps, explicit contact geometry and abstract measure suppliers. Fixed-wall rule preserves speed/tangent/angular momentum; first-contact formula yields positive outgoing azimuth coefficient for b in (0,a). Inverse a cos(theta/2) has nonzero derivative on (0,pi), density a²/4 and total pi a². Endpoint/seam sets have zero incident area, no artificial atom; misses b>a excluded. Separate model never invokes finite-mass restitution or smooth-force quadrature outside hypotheses.

citations.quote:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the cross-section measures.

Adopt a central scattering model of [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] clause (i)
with masses $m_1,m_2>0$, reduced mass $\mu$, and the **repulsive Coulomb
potential**
$$u(r)=\frac{\kappa}{r}\qquad(r>0),\qquad \kappa>0,$$
where $\kappa$ is a model datum of the mechanical model
([[def-cm01-units]]: $[\kappa]=\mu\ell^3\tau^{-2}$), so that
$$V(r)=\frac{\kappa}{r}+\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2}\qquad(r>0).$$
Let the data satisfy $E>0$, $J>0$ and put
$$b:=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}>0,\qquad \alpha:=\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}>0.$$
Then:

1. **(Turning data.)** $V$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, with
   $V(r)\to+\infty$ as $r\downarrow0$ and $V(r)\to0$ as $r\to\infty$; the
   equation $V(r)=E$ has exactly one solution $r_*>0$, it is simple
   ($V'(r_*)<0$), one has $V(r)<E$ for every $r>r_*$ and $V(r)>E$ for every
   $0<r<r_*$, and $V=U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$ is of class $C^2$ with no other
   crossing of the level $E$.
2. **(Global non-colliding scattering motion.)** Let $I\subseteq I_0$ be a time interval with nonempty interior and $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$
   be the relative coordinate of a motion of the model with attached angular
   momentum $j=\mu\,r\times r'=Je_3$ and energy $E$, with $|r(t)|\ge r_*$ for
   every $t\in I$ and $|r(t_*)|=r_*$ for some $t_*\in I$. Then $r$
   extends uniquely to a central-force trajectory $\bar r:\mathbb R\to
   \mathbb R^3$ whose extension is the relative coordinate of a motion of
   the two-label model with its autonomous force law extended to time window $\mathbb R$; $\rho:=|\bar r|$ satisfies
   $\rho\ge r_*>0$ (no collision), $\rho(t)>r_*$ for $t\ne t_*$, and $\rho$
   is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and strictly increasing on
   $[t_*,\infty)$; the asymptotic velocities $v_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}
   \bar r'(t)$ exist with
   $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}=:v_\infty$, and the asymptotic perpendicular
   distance of each branch to its limiting direction equals
   $b=J/(\mu v_\infty)=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}$, so that $J=\mu b\,v_\infty$. Unlike
   the finite-range case, there is no radius beyond which the motion is
   exactly free: the limits above are asymptotic.
3. **(Deflection and its single branch.)** With polar data $(\rho,\theta)$ in
   a triad with $e_3=j/J$, the half-angle of the motion is
   $$\Delta=\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}\in\Bigl(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\Bigr),$$
   its scattering angle is
   $$\theta_{\mathrm s}=\pi-2\Delta=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}\in(0,\pi),$$
   and its signed velocity rotation is $2\Delta-\pi=-2\arctan(\kappa/(2Eb))$.
   For the family at fixed $\mu,\kappa,E$ and varying $J(b)=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b$, realised by the apsis initial data of [[thm-cm-coulomb-scattering]] clause 4, the **deflection map**
   $$\theta_{\mathrm{def}}:(0,\infty)\to(0,\pi),\qquad \theta_{\mathrm{def}}(b):=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb},$$
   is $C^1$ and strictly decreasing, hence a $C^1$ bijection with inverse
   $b(\theta)=\dfrac{\kappa}{2E}\cot\dfrac{\theta}{2}$; it is a single
   deflection branch of the model on $(0,\infty)$ with
   $\theta_{\mathrm{def}}'(b)\ne0$ everywhere and no wrapping
   ($0<\Delta<\pi/2$ for every $b>0$).
4. **(Cross-section, angular cutoffs and divergence.)** The differential
   cross-section of that branch is
   $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta)=\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\Bigr)^2\csc^4\frac{\theta}{2}\qquad(0<\theta<\pi),$$
   finite and positive; for $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi$ the truncated total
   cross-section over the angular band is the finite number
   $$\sigma\bigl((\theta_1,\theta_2)\bigr) =\pi\bigl(b(\theta_1)^2-b(\theta_2)^2\bigr),$$
   and by monotonicity the band $\theta\ge\theta_1$ has
   $\sigma\bigl((\theta_1,\pi)\bigr)=\pi b(\theta_1)^2 =\pi\bigl(\frac{\kappa}{2E}\bigr)^2\cot^2\frac{\theta_1}{2}$; whereas the
   truncated integral over $(0,\theta_0)$ diverges for every
   $\theta_0\in(0,\pi)$, so the **model has no finite ideal total cross-section**. Every positive angular cutoff therefore yields a finite
   truncated ideal cross-section. Under the declared uniform-incident
   preparation with $b_{\max}>0$ and flux $\Phi>0$, the cutoff
   cross-section satisfies $\sigma_{b_{\max}}(Y)\le\pi b_{\max}^2$
   for every Borel angular window $Y\subseteq(0,\pi)$, and the expected
   scattered rate is $\Phi\sigma_{b_{\max}}(Y)<\infty$
   ([[def-cm15-cross-section]] clause (iv)). Thus ideal cross-section
   divergence does not imply an infinite rate under the finite incident
   cutoff; comparison with detected rates additionally requires a declared
   apparatus acceptance and its uncertainties.
5. **(Status of the parameter and exclusions.)** The coupling $\kappa$ is a
   parameter of the mechanical model. This item does not identify it with
   $q_1q_2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$ or with any electromagnetic quantity, states
   no measured value, and asserts no screening law for a medium of
   scatterers. Attractive Coulomb scattering (for which capture is possible
   for suitable data), inelastic, radiative, relativistic and quantum
   modifications are outside the adopted model and this statement.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the cross-section measures. Fix $\mu>0$, $\kappa>0$ and $E>0$. For every $b>0$ put $J(b)=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b$ and use the Coulomb trajectory family of [[thm-cm-coulomb-scattering]] clause 4. Its impact distance is $b$ and its
**deflection map**
$$\theta_{\rm def}:(0,\infty)\to(0,\pi),\qquad \theta_{\rm def}(b):=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$
Then:

1. $\theta_{\rm def}$ is $C^1$ and strictly decreasing, with
   $\theta_{\rm def}(b)\to\pi$ as $b\downarrow0$ and
   $\theta_{\rm def}(b)\to0$ as $b\to\infty$; it is a $C^1$ bijection
   $(0,\infty)\to(0,\pi)$ with inverse
   $$b(\theta)=\frac{\kappa}{2E}\cot\frac{\theta}{2}\qquad(0<\theta<\pi).$$
2. For every interval $(\theta_1,\theta_2)\subseteq(0,\pi)$ the pair
   $(\theta,b)$ is a deflection branch with cross-section density
   $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta) =b(\theta)\Bigl|\frac{\mathrm db}{\mathrm d\theta}(\theta)\Bigr|\frac{1}{\sin\theta} =\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\Bigr)^2\csc^4\frac{\theta}{2},$$
   finite and positive on $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$; and the pushforward of the
   incident flux measure under the branch is described by
   [[thm-cm-differential-cross-section-density]].
3. For every $\theta_0\in(0,\pi)$ the truncated total cross-section
   $$\int_0^{\theta_0}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\Bigr)^2 \csc^4\frac{\theta}{2}\,\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi\,\mathrm d\theta=+\infty,$$
   while for $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi$ the integral over
   $(\theta_1,\theta_2)\times(0,2\pi)$ is finite; in this sense the total
   cross-section of the ideal Coulomb model diverges at forward angles and
   every compact angular acceptance away from $0$ has finite cross-section.

By [[lem-tangent-principal-branch-is-bijective]], tangent restricts to a
continuous strictly increasing bijection

$$\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\longrightarrow\mathbb R.$$

Its inverse is the **principal inverse tangent**

$$\arctan:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(-\pi/2,\pi/2).$$

Thus $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ for every real $y$, while
$\arctan(\tan x)=x$ precisely for $x$ in the displayed principal interval.
The inverse is continuous and strictly increasing by [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

Define
$$	an x:= rac{\sin x}{\cos x}\quad(x
e\pi/2+m\pi),\qquad\cot x:= rac{\cos x}{\sin x}\quad(x
e m\pi),$$
$$\sec x:= rac1{\cos x}\quad(x
e\pi/2+m\pi),\qquad\csc x:= rac1{\sin x}\quad(x
e m\pi),$$
where $m$ ranges over the integers. The exclusions are exactly the zero sets of [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]].

For every real $x$, $\sin ^2x+\cos ^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. Wherever the displayed quotients are defined, $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, $\cot(-x)=-\cot x$, $\sec(-x)=\sec x$, $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$, $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$, and $1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $\alpha \in
\mathbb{R}$. Suppose the limits of $f$ and of $g$ at $c$ exist, and write
$L := \lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ and $M := \lim_{x \to c} g(x)$
([[def-function-limit]]). Then:

1. the limit of $f + g$ at $c$ exists, and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} (f + g)(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} f(x) + \lim_{x \to c} g(x) \;=\; L + M ;$$
2. the limit of $\alpha f$ at $c$ exists, and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} (\alpha f)(x) \;=\; \alpha \lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; \alpha L ;$$
3. the limit of $fg$ at $c$ exists, and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} (fg)(x) \;=\; \Bigl(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\Bigr)\Bigl(\lim_{x \to c} g(x)\Bigr) \;=\; LM ;$$
4. if $M \ne 0$, then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the point
   $c$ is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient $f/g$ is defined on $A_0$ by
   $(f/g)(x) = f(x) / g(x)$, the limit of $(f/g)|_{A_0}$ at $c$ exists, and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} (f/g)|_{A_0}(x) \;=\; \frac{\lim_{x \to c} f(x)}{\lim_{x \to c} g(x)} \;=\; \frac{L}{M} .$$

Each equation asserts two things at once: that the limit on the left exists, and
that it has the stated value. Both are proved. The symbols denote by
[[lem-function-limit-unique]].

**Everything below is proved directly from $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$.** No
sequence is constructed and no choice principle is used, so all four claims are
theorems of ZF. Passing through
[[thm-sequential-criterion-for-function-limits]] instead would import the
countable choice spent in that theorem's converse direction, for no gain; see
[[rem-heine-criterion-choice-cost]].

**Why the quotient is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is simply not defined
where $g$ vanishes, and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ arbitrarily far from
$c$; restricting to $A_0$ is therefore forced. That this restriction still has
$c$ as a limit point, so that the limit there means anything at all, is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]]. The sequential analogue
[[thm-algebra-of-limits]] needs the corresponding hypothesis in the form "the
denominator sequence is nonzero at every index".

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

derivations.claim: Speed and impact parameter: $2E/\mu=2\times10^{-18}/(2\times10^{-26})=10^{8}\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, so $v_\infty=\sqrt{10^{8}}=10^4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; then $b=J/(\mu v_\infty)=4\times10^{-34}/(2\times10^{-26}\cdot10^{4})=2\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$.

Special values: at $x=\pi/4$, the double-angle identity gives $0=\cos(\pi/2)=\cos^2x-\sin^2x$; positivity and the Pythagorean identity yield $\sin x=\cos x=1/\sqrt2$, hence $\cot x=1$, $\csc^4x=4$ and $\arctan1=\pi/4$. At $x=\pi/6$, the addition formulas give $0=\cos(3x)=4\cos^3x-3\cos x$. Since $\cos x>0$, $\cos x=\sqrt3/2$ and $\sin x=1/2$, so $\cot x=\sqrt3$. Applying the difference formulas to $\pi/12=\pi/4-\pi/6$ now gives $\cot(\pi/12)=(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)/(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)=2+\sqrt3$. Finally continuity and positivity give $\sin(\pi/2)=1$; thus $\cot(\theta/2)\to0$ as $\theta\uparrow\pi$.

Angle: $\alpha=\kappa/(2Eb)=4\times10^{-30}/(2\times10^{-18}\cdot2\times10^{-12})=1$, so $\arctan\alpha=\pi/4$ and $\Delta=\pi/2-\pi/4=\pi/4$, giving $\theta=2\arctan1=\pi/2\in(0,\pi)$, consistent with $b(\theta)|_{\theta=\pi/2}=\kappa_2\cot(\pi/4)=2\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}=b$.

Band values: using $b(\theta)=\kappa_2\cot(\theta/2)$ and the endpoint limit $\lim_{\theta\uparrow\pi}b(\theta)=0$, for the band $(\pi/2,\pi)$ the value is $\sigma=\pi\bigl(b(\pi/2)^2-0^2\bigr)=\pi(2\times10^{-12})^2=4\pi\times10^{-24}\approx1.257\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{m^2}$; for $(\pi/3,\pi)$, $b(\pi/3)=2\times10^{-12}\sqrt3$, so $\sigma=12\pi\times10^{-24}\approx3.770\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{m^2}$; for $(\pi/6,\pi)$, $b(\pi/6)=2\times10^{-12}(2+\sqrt3)$, so $\sigma=\pi\cdot4\times10^{-24}(2+\sqrt3)^2\approx1.750\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{m^2}$. These are exact expressions in $\pi$ and $\sqrt3$ evaluated to four significant digits; all are finite.

Density at $\pi/2$: $\kappa_4=\kappa/(4E)=10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$ and $\csc^4(\pi/4)=(\sqrt2)^4=4$, so $\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\pi/2)=\kappa_4^2\cdot4=4\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, with dimension $\ell^2$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

Small-angle growth: the derivative definition and [L3] give $\sin x/x=(\sin x-\sin0)/(x-0)\to\sin'(0)=1$ as $x\downarrow0$, and continuity gives $\cos x\to1$. Since $\sin x>0$ on $(0,\pi/2)$, quotient limits yield $x\cot x=\cos x/(\sin x/x)\to1$. With $x=\theta_1/2$, this proves $\cot(\theta_1/2)\sim2/\theta_1$, so $\pi b(\theta_1)^2=\pi\kappa_2^2\cot^2(\theta_1/2)\sim4\pi\kappa_2^2/\theta_1^2=16\pi\times10^{-24}/\theta_1^2$ in $\mathrm{m^2}$. At $\theta_1=10^{-2}$ rad, $b(\theta_1)=2\times10^{-12}\cot(5\times10^{-3})\approx4.000\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$ and $\sigma\approx5.026\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{m^2}$. The positive asymptotic coefficient implies unbounded band values as $\theta_1\downarrow0$, agreeing with [[pthm-cm15-rutherford-model]] clause 4.

Reading: every number above was obtained by substituting the declared model data into the model formulas; no measurement, uncertainty, detector acceptance or sampling model is supplied, so the computation is a check of the model's arithmetic and not a comparison with nature. In particular the divergence of the truncated total at forward angles is a feature of the declared idealisation, and any empirical statement would require a separate experiment item with measured inputs and uncertainties.

boundaries.evidence: The bands $(\pi/2,\pi)$, $(\pi/3,\pi)$ and $(\pi/6,\pi)$ of steps 2.2 and 3.2 are nondegenerate; each has positive length.
The forward endpoint $\theta_1\downarrow0$ is treated as a limit in step 3.2; the limits $\theta\to0$ and $\theta\to\pi$ of $b(\theta)$ are limits, not attained values.
One declared data set and one branch formula; steps 1.1-3.2 substitute the same declared numbers throughout.
The band endpoints used, such as $\theta_1=\pi/2$, are interior to $(0,\pi)$, and step 2.1 evaluates the nondegenerate angle $\pi/2$.
The divergent forward cutoff and the finite band values are the content of steps 2.2 and 3.2, with no ideal total assigned at the forward end.

boundaries.reason: Step 1.1 evaluates v_infinity and b from the fixed numbers; step 2.2 evaluates two declared angular bands. No choice of a trajectory, detector or member of an indexed collection occurs.
