citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]),
inherited from the statement of
[[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]], whose distributional jump
lemma uses it; the algebraic clauses used here do not otherwise use choice.
Adopt the impact and open-mass extensions of [[post-cm15-impulse]], with
$m_1,m_2>0$, an interval $I$ with nonempty interior, $t_*\in\operatorname{int} I$, an impulse motion
$x=(x_1,x_2):I\to Q$ run in the isolated reciprocal impulse model at $t_*$
with impulse $J$ and one-sided velocities $v_i^\pm$, and write
$$M:=m_1+m_2,\qquad \mu:=\frac{m_1m_2}{M},\qquad P(t):=m_1x_1'(t)+m_2x_2'(t)\qquad(t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}).$$
Only the one-sided limits of $P$ at $t_*$ are used; no derivative of the
position curves at the contact time is assumed.
Then:

1. **(Momentum continuity.)** The total momentum is continuous across the
   impact,
   $$P(t_*^+)=P(t_*^-),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \sum_{i=1}^2 m_i\bigl(v_i^+-v_i^-\bigr)=0,$$
   and the impulse delivered to label $1$ is removed from label $2$:
   $J=m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=-m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)$.
2. **(Smooth-force exclusion.)** Suppose this same candidate motion $x$ from
   clause 1 also satisfies the smooth force branch of
   [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]] on $I$,
   with the force maps continuous there. Then the momentum curves
   $p_i=m_ix_i'$ are of class $C^1$ on $I$; in particular
   $$p_i(t_*^+)=p_i(t_*^-)\qquad(i=1,2).$$
   Clause 1 identifies the jump of $p_1$ with the same impulse $J$, so
   $J=0$: no candidate motion carrying a nonzero isolated impulse can also
   be a motion of that smooth-force class. The finite-jump model of
   [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (i) is therefore a genuine extension of the
   smooth-force branch, not one of its cases.
3. **(Collinear restitution solution.)** Suppose in addition that the
   contact is collinear with contact direction $n$ and coefficient of
   restitution $e\in[0,1]$ ([[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (ii)). Then
   $$J=\mu(1+e)\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr),$$
   $J$ is parallel to $n$, the centre-of-mass velocity
   $V:=M^{-1}(m_1v_1^-+m_2v_2^-)$ is unchanged across the impact, and the
   post-impact velocities are
   $$v_1^+=V+\frac{m_2}{M}\,e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr),\qquad v_2^+=V-\frac{m_1}{M}\,e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr).$$
4. **(Kinetic energy of the impact.)** The kinetic-energy change across the
   impact is
   $$\Delta K:=\frac{m_1\lVert v_1^+\rVert_2^2+m_2\lVert v_2^+\rVert_2^2}{2} -\frac{m_1\lVert v_1^-\rVert_2^2+m_2\lVert v_2^-\rVert_2^2}{2} =-\frac{1-e^2}{2}\,\mu\,\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2\le0,$$
   with equality if and only if $e=1$ or $v_2^-=v_1^-$. For $0\le e<1$ the
   contact model is dissipative: the total kinetic energy of the two labels
   is not conserved across the impact, and the deficit
   $\frac{1-e^2}{2}\mu\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2$ is a quantity of the
   adopted contact law. This item identifies it with no measured heat,
   temperature, sound or deformation observable.
5. **(Momentum balance alone does not determine the impact.)** In the
   collinear case with $d^-:=v_2^--v_1^-$ and $d_n:=\langle d^-,n\rangle<0$,
   the impulse equations of clause 1 alone leave the scalar impulse magnitude
   free: for every real $J_n$ with $J_n\le \mu d_n$ (so that the contact is
   separating or grazing) the velocities
   $$v_1^+=v_1^-+\frac{J_n}{m_1}n,\qquad v_2^+=v_2^--\frac{J_n}{m_2}n$$
   satisfy the reciprocal impulse equations with impulse $J=J_nn$ and
   preserve the total momentum, and their kinetic-energy change is
   $$\Delta K(J_n)=-J_n\,d_n+\frac{J_n^2}{2\mu},$$
   whose minimum over the admissible range is
   $\Delta K(\mu d_n)=-\frac{\mu}{2}d_n^2$ at the perfectly inelastic value
   $J_n=\mu d_n$ (that is, $e=0$). The value of
   $J_n$ is fixed only by the contact law of [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause
   (ii), which selects $J_n=\mu(1+e)d_n$; in particular momentum balance
   alone does not determine the post-impact velocities.
6. **(Open-body and rocket laws.)** Under [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause
   (iii), with differentiable $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$,
   $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$,
   and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfying the
   material balance identities, one has on $I$
   $$m\,v'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v\bigr).$$
   In particular: (a) if $r_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ then
   $m\,v'=F$ and $(mv)'=F$; (b) if $r_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ and
   $r_{\mathrm{out}}=-m'>0$ (mass loss) then
   $$m\,v'=F+r_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(v-w_{\mathrm{out}}\bigr)=F-m'\bigl(v-w_{\mathrm{out}}\bigr),$$
   so the **thrust** is $T:=r_{\mathrm{out}}(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})=-m'(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})$,
   and the closed-system law $(mv)'=F$ fails unless
   $w_{\mathrm{out}}=0$; (c) if $r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}}=0$
   then $m\,v'=F-r_{\mathrm{in}}v$: capture contributes the acceleration
   $-(r_{\mathrm{in}}/m)v$, opposing $v$, while $(mv)'=F$ still holds.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]), inherited from the jump lemma below.
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $t_*\in I$, let $m_1,m_2>0$, and let $x_1,x_2:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous on $I$ and twice continuously differentiable on each of the two open intervals $I\cap(-\infty,t_*)$ and $I\cap(t_*,\infty)$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Assume the one-sided limits
$$v_i^-:=\lim_{t\uparrow t_*}x_i'(t),\qquad v_i^+:=\lim_{t\downarrow t_*}x_i'(t)\qquad(i=1,2)$$
exist in $\mathbb R^3$. Define $p_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $p_i(t):=m_ix_i'(t)$ for $t\ne t_*$ and fix the representative value $p_i(t_*):=0$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]). Let $F_1,F_2:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous and let $J\in\mathbb R^3$. The **isolated reciprocal impulse model** at $t_*$ consists of the two requirements:

1. regular dynamics off the impulse: $m_ix_i''(t)=F_i(t)$ for every $t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}$ and $i=1,2$;
2. impulse pairing: for every $\Phi\in C_c^\infty(I;\mathbb R^3)$ — meaning every map whose three components lie in $C_c^\infty(I)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) — $$-\int_I\langle p_1(t),\Phi'(t)\rangle\,d\lambda(t)=\int_I\langle F_1(t),\Phi(t)\rangle\,d\lambda(t)+\langle J,\Phi(t_*)\rangle,$$ $$-\int_I\langle p_2(t),\Phi'(t)\rangle\,d\lambda(t)=\int_I\langle F_2(t),\Phi(t)\rangle\,d\lambda(t)-\langle J,\Phi(t_*)\rangle,$$ with integrals against Lebesgue measure $\lambda$ and the Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), using the fixed representative $p_i(t_*)=0$ above.

Under this model, with $M:=m_1+m_2$ and $\mu:=m_1m_2/M$:

**a.** $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=J$ and $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=-J$; consequently the total momentum is continuous across the impulse, $p_1(t_*^+)+p_2(t_*^+)=p_1(t_*^-)+p_2(t_*^-)$.

**b.** Let $e\in[0,1]$ satisfy the **restitution law** $v_2^+-v_1^+=-e(v_2^--v_1^-)$. Then the post-impulse velocities are uniquely determined: with $V:=\frac{m_1v_1^-+m_2v_2^-}{M}=\frac{m_1v_1^++m_2v_2^+}{M}$, $$v_1^+=V+\frac{m_2}{M}e\,(v_2^--v_1^-),\qquad v_2^+=V-\frac{m_1}{M}e\,(v_2^--v_1^-).$$

**c.** The kinetic-energy change across the impulse is $$\Delta K:=\frac{m_1\lVert v_1^+\rVert_2^2+m_2\lVert v_2^+\rVert_2^2}{2}-\frac{m_1\lVert v_1^-\rVert_2^2+m_2\lVert v_2^-\rVert_2^2}{2}=-\frac{1-e^2}{2}\,\mu\,\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2\le0;$$ in particular $\Delta K=0$ for $e=1$ and $\Delta K=-\frac12\mu\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2$ for $e=0$.

Let $N\in\mathbb N$, $N\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $m_1,\dots,m_N>0$ and let $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable at every point of $I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). All sums over $i$ range over $1,\dots,N$: for a real family $a_1,\dots,a_N$, define $\sum_i a_i:=\sum_{k<N}b_k$, where $b:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ has $b_k=a_{k+1}$ for $k<N$ and $b_k=0$ for $k\ge N$, using the finite sums of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]; vector sums are defined coordinatewise, and sums of curves pointwise. Put $M:=\sum_i m_i>0$, $X:=M^{-1}\sum_i m_ix_i$ and $\rho_i:=x_i-X$. The symbols $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ denote the Euclidean inner product and norm on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

1. $X$ and every $\rho_i$ are differentiable on $I$, with $X'=M^{-1}\sum_im_ix_i'$ and $\rho_i'=x_i'-X'$, and the identities $\sum_im_i\rho_i=0$ and $\sum_im_i\rho_i'=0$ hold on $I$;
2. for every $t\in I$, $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\sum_{i}m_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2;$$
3. if $N=2$, then with $r:=x_1-x_2$ and $\mu:=m_1m_2/M$ one has $\sum_im_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$ and hence $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$$ for every $t\in I$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: Common data: $M=8$, $\mu=\frac32$, $V=0$ and $d^-=-4n$, so $\lVert d^-\rVert_2^2=16$ and $\frac{\mu}{2}\lVert d^-\rVert_2^2=12\ \mathrm{J}$; the initial kinetic energy is $\frac12\cdot2\cdot9+\frac12\cdot6\cdot1=9+3=12\ \mathrm{J}$; the incoming relative speed is $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Elastic case $e=1$: [L1] gives $v_1^+=V+\frac{m_2}{M}d^-=\frac68(-4)n=-3n$ and $v_2^+=V-\frac{m_1}{M}d^-=-\frac28(-4)n=+1n$, so each velocity is reversed and the total momentum is $2(-3)+6(1)=0=P^-$; $\Delta K=-\frac{1-1}{2}\mu\lVert d^-\rVert_2^2=0$, and directly $K^+=\frac12\cdot2\cdot9+\frac12\cdot6\cdot1=12\ \mathrm{J}=K^-$.

Semi-elastic case $e=\frac12$: $v_1^+=\frac68\cdot\frac12\cdot(-4)n=-\frac32n$, $v_2^+=-\frac28\cdot\frac12\cdot(-4)n=+\frac12n$; the impulse is $J=m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=2(-\frac32-3)n=-9n\ \mathrm{N\,s}$, and indeed $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=6(\frac12+1)n=9n=-J$; the total momentum is $2(-\frac32)+6(\frac12)=0=P^-$; $\Delta K=-\frac{1-\frac14}{2}\cdot\frac32\cdot16=-\frac{3}{4}\cdot12=-9\ \mathrm{J}$, and directly $K^+=\frac12\cdot2\cdot\frac94+\frac12\cdot6\cdot\frac14=\frac94+\frac34=3\ \mathrm{J}=12-9$.

Sticking case $e=0$: $v_1^+=v_2^+=V=0$; the total momentum is $0=P^-$; $\Delta K=-\frac12\cdot\frac32\cdot16=-12\ \mathrm{J}$, so $K^+=0$; the impulse is $J=2(0-3)n=-6n\ \mathrm{N\,s}$, consistent with $m_2(0+1)n=6n=-J$.

Reading: all three outcomes satisfy the reciprocal impulse equations with different impulses and different energy changes; the momentum data alone ($P=0$) are compatible with all of them, illustrating clause 5 of [[pthm-cm15-impact-balance]]: the coefficient $e$ is model data and must be supplied by the contact law. Every number above is a declared model datum substituted into the model formulas; no measurement, uncertainty or empirical inference is involved.

citations.quote:
Adopt, as this page's **impact and open-mass extensions** of the force
branch of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the following three model extensions. Each is an adopted model, not a
consequence of the smooth-force postulates; each applies only where a
statement explicitly invokes it.

**(i) The isolated reciprocal impulse model.** A two-label force model with
masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), time window $I_0$,
configuration domain $Q$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]) and continuous
external-plus-pair force maps $F_1,F_2$ is **run in the isolated reciprocal
impulse model at $t_*\in I_0$** when there is an interval
$I\subseteq I_0$ with $t_*\in\operatorname{int}I$ and a position curve
$x=(x_1,x_2):I\to Q$ such that the following conditions hold. This curve is
called an **impulse motion**; only its restrictions away from $t_*$ are
motions of the associated first-order system of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]],
and no differentiability at $t_*$ is required:

1. $x_1,x_2$ are continuous on $I$ and twice continuously differentiable on
   each of $I\cap(-\infty,t_*)$ and $I\cap(t_*,\infty)$
   ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]],
   [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and
   $m_ix_i''(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ for every $t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}$;
2. the one-sided limits
   $v_i^{\pm}:=\lim_{t\to t_*\pm}x_i'(t)$ exist in $\mathbb R^3$
   ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]);
3. there is a vector $J\in\mathbb R^3$, the **impulse**, with
   $$m_1\bigl(v_1^+-v_1^-\bigr)=J,\qquad m_2\bigl(v_2^+-v_2^-\bigr)=-J .$$

The two equations of clause 3 are the **reciprocal finite-jump form** of the
isolated impulse: the two labels receive equal and opposite momentum changes.
The regular force maps remain continuous on their state domain; their
evaluations along the curve can have different one-sided limits because the
velocity can jump. The dimension of the impulse
is $[J]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

For the distributional rendering on $\operatorname{int}I$, assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Put
$p_i(t)=m_ix_i'(t)$ and $f_i(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ off $t_*$, assigning both
the value $0$ at $t_*$. Their one-sided limits are finite: those of $p_i$
are $m_iv_i^\pm$, and continuity of the state-domain force maps gives
$f_i(t_*^\pm)=F_i(t_*,x(t_*),v^\pm)$, with
$v^\pm=(v_1^\pm,v_2^\pm)$. Also $p_i'=f_i$ off the impulse. Thus each
component meets the piecewise-$C^1$ and one-sided derivative-limit
hypotheses of [[lem-cm-piecewise-c1-jump-derivative]]. Its identity,
summed componentwise, gives for every real vector test function
$\Phi\in C_c^\infty(\operatorname{int}I;\mathbb R^3)$ (each component is
smooth and compactly supported, [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]])
$$-\int_{\operatorname{int}I}\langle p_i,\Phi'\rangle\,d\lambda=\int_{\operatorname{int}I}\langle f_i,\Phi\rangle\,d\lambda+s_i\langle J,\Phi(t_*)\rangle,\qquad s_1=1,\quad s_2=-1,$$
where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure and the integral convention is that of
[[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]. This is the pairing form of the
adopted jumps. Unlike [[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]], whose
hypotheses require continuous time forces and assume the pairings to derive
the jumps, this rendering allows distinct one-sided regular-force values.

**(ii) The collinear restitution contact law.** A model run in the isolated
reciprocal impulse model at $t_*$ is **collinear** when there is a unit vector
$n\in\mathbb R^3$ (the **contact direction**) with $v_i^{\pm}\parallel n$ for
$i=1,2$ and $\langle v_2^--v_1^-,n\rangle<0$ (the labels approach along $n$).
For a collinear contact, adopt a **coefficient of restitution** $e\in[0,1]$ —
a dimensionless model datum of the pair and the contact — and the **restitution
law**
$$v_2^+-v_1^+=-e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr).$$
For $e=1$ the contact is called **elastic**, for $e=0$ **perfectly inelastic**
and otherwise **semi-elastic**; the law is a constitutive assumption, not a
consequence of the impulse equations of clause (i), and $e$ is not derived
from the masses or the approach speed. The law is stated only for a single
collinear contact; simultaneous contacts, repeated contacts and tangential
(friction) impulses are outside the model.

**(iii) The open-body material accounting.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a
nonempty open interval. Adopt for a body whose mass
$m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and velocity $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ are differentiable, and
whose external force and exchanged matter are described by maps
$F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and
$w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ (mass rates and *inertial*
velocities of the matter entering and leaving, measured in the same inertial
frame as $v$), the **material balance identities**
$$m'=r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad (mv)'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}\,w_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}\,w_{\mathrm{out}} .$$
They are the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,\mathrm dt$ of
matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,\mathrm dt$
with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$", and they
are adopted rather than derived from a closed-system law. Their product-rule
consequence $mv'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$
is proved in [[thm-cm-variable-mass-momentum-balance]]; in particular the
closed-system law $(mv)'=F$ is recovered only when
$r_{\mathrm{in}}w_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}$.
The quantities have types and SI dimensions
$[m]=\mu$, $[v]=[w_{\mathrm{in}}]=[w_{\mathrm{out}}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$,
$[F]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ and
$[r_{\mathrm{in}}]=[r_{\mathrm{out}}]=\mu\tau^{-1}$; they are model
data, not measured values.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]), let $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and let $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be maps. Suppose the two **material balance identities**

$$m'(t)=r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t),\qquad (mv)'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)$$

hold for every $t\in I$, where $mv$ denotes the pointwise scalar multiple. Then

$$m(t)v'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in I).$$

In particular, if $F\equiv0$, $r_{\mathrm{in}}\equiv0$ and $r_{\mathrm{out}}\equiv r$ for a constant $r\ge0$, then $mv'=-r(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$: the acceleration is governed by the momentum carried away per unit time relative to the body, not by $(mv)'=0$.

The two balance identities are the **adopted content of the material momentum accounting** — the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,dt$ of matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,dt$ with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$". They are not derived here from any closed-system law; the deduction below is their product-rule consequence.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]),
inherited from the statement of
[[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]], whose distributional jump
lemma uses it; the algebraic clauses used here do not otherwise use choice.
Adopt the impact and open-mass extensions of [[post-cm15-impulse]], with
$m_1,m_2>0$, an interval $I$ with nonempty interior, $t_*\in\operatorname{int} I$, an impulse motion
$x=(x_1,x_2):I\to Q$ run in the isolated reciprocal impulse model at $t_*$
with impulse $J$ and one-sided velocities $v_i^\pm$, and write
$$M:=m_1+m_2,\qquad \mu:=\frac{m_1m_2}{M},\qquad P(t):=m_1x_1'(t)+m_2x_2'(t)\qquad(t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}).$$
Only the one-sided limits of $P$ at $t_*$ are used; no derivative of the
position curves at the contact time is assumed.
Then:

1. **(Momentum continuity.)** The total momentum is continuous across the
   impact,
   $$P(t_*^+)=P(t_*^-),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \sum_{i=1}^2 m_i\bigl(v_i^+-v_i^-\bigr)=0,$$
   and the impulse delivered to label $1$ is removed from label $2$:
   $J=m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=-m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)$.
2. **(Smooth-force exclusion.)** Suppose this same candidate motion $x$ from
   clause 1 also satisfies the smooth force branch of
   [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]] on $I$,
   with the force maps continuous there. Then the momentum curves
   $p_i=m_ix_i'$ are of class $C^1$ on $I$; in particular
   $$p_i(t_*^+)=p_i(t_*^-)\qquad(i=1,2).$$
   Clause 1 identifies the jump of $p_1$ with the same impulse $J$, so
   $J=0$: no candidate motion carrying a nonzero isolated impulse can also
   be a motion of that smooth-force class. The finite-jump model of
   [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (i) is therefore a genuine extension of the
   smooth-force branch, not one of its cases.
3. **(Collinear restitution solution.)** Suppose in addition that the
   contact is collinear with contact direction $n$ and coefficient of
   restitution $e\in[0,1]$ ([[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (ii)). Then
   $$J=\mu(1+e)\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr),$$
   $J$ is parallel to $n$, the centre-of-mass velocity
   $V:=M^{-1}(m_1v_1^-+m_2v_2^-)$ is unchanged across the impact, and the
   post-impact velocities are
   $$v_1^+=V+\frac{m_2}{M}\,e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr),\qquad v_2^+=V-\frac{m_1}{M}\,e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr).$$
4. **(Kinetic energy of the impact.)** The kinetic-energy change across the
   impact is
   $$\Delta K:=\frac{m_1\lVert v_1^+\rVert_2^2+m_2\lVert v_2^+\rVert_2^2}{2} -\frac{m_1\lVert v_1^-\rVert_2^2+m_2\lVert v_2^-\rVert_2^2}{2} =-\frac{1-e^2}{2}\,\mu\,\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2\le0,$$
   with equality if and only if $e=1$ or $v_2^-=v_1^-$. For $0\le e<1$ the
   contact model is dissipative: the total kinetic energy of the two labels
   is not conserved across the impact, and the deficit
   $\frac{1-e^2}{2}\mu\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2$ is a quantity of the
   adopted contact law. This item identifies it with no measured heat,
   temperature, sound or deformation observable.
5. **(Momentum balance alone does not determine the impact.)** In the
   collinear case with $d^-:=v_2^--v_1^-$ and $d_n:=\langle d^-,n\rangle<0$,
   the impulse equations of clause 1 alone leave the scalar impulse magnitude
   free: for every real $J_n$ with $J_n\le \mu d_n$ (so that the contact is
   separating or grazing) the velocities
   $$v_1^+=v_1^-+\frac{J_n}{m_1}n,\qquad v_2^+=v_2^--\frac{J_n}{m_2}n$$
   satisfy the reciprocal impulse equations with impulse $J=J_nn$ and
   preserve the total momentum, and their kinetic-energy change is
   $$\Delta K(J_n)=-J_n\,d_n+\frac{J_n^2}{2\mu},$$
   whose minimum over the admissible range is
   $\Delta K(\mu d_n)=-\frac{\mu}{2}d_n^2$ at the perfectly inelastic value
   $J_n=\mu d_n$ (that is, $e=0$). The value of
   $J_n$ is fixed only by the contact law of [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause
   (ii), which selects $J_n=\mu(1+e)d_n$; in particular momentum balance
   alone does not determine the post-impact velocities.
6. **(Open-body and rocket laws.)** Under [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause
   (iii), with differentiable $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$,
   $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$,
   and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfying the
   material balance identities, one has on $I$
   $$m\,v'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v\bigr).$$
   In particular: (a) if $r_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ then
   $m\,v'=F$ and $(mv)'=F$; (b) if $r_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ and
   $r_{\mathrm{out}}=-m'>0$ (mass loss) then
   $$m\,v'=F+r_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(v-w_{\mathrm{out}}\bigr)=F-m'\bigl(v-w_{\mathrm{out}}\bigr),$$
   so the **thrust** is $T:=r_{\mathrm{out}}(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})=-m'(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})$,
   and the closed-system law $(mv)'=F$ fails unless
   $w_{\mathrm{out}}=0$; (c) if $r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}}=0$
   then $m\,v'=F-r_{\mathrm{in}}v$: capture contributes the acceleration
   $-(r_{\mathrm{in}}/m)v$, opposing $v$, while $(mv)'=F$ still holds.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: Mass identity: $m'=-r_0=r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}$ on $I$, in $\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$. Since $-1/2<q<5/2$, $m(t)=(3-q)\ \mathrm{kg}>0$, so the first balance identity and the positive-mass condition hold.

Velocity candidate: define $v(t):=u_e\ln(m_0/m(t))n$. By [L2] and $m'=-r_0$, $\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\ln(m_0/m(t))=r_0/m(t)$, so $v'(t)=u_er_0n/m(t)$, with acceleration units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, and $v(0)=u_e\ln1\cdot n=0$. The logarithm acts on the positive dimensionless ratio $m_0/m(t)$.

Strong form: $mv'=r_0u_en$, while $F+r_{\mathrm{in}}(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)=-r_0((v-u_en)-v)=r_0u_en$. Thus the derived law holds with thrust $r_0u_e=2\ \mathrm N$ along $n$.

Material identities: the product rule gives $(mv)'=m'v+mv'=-r_0v+r_0u_en=-r_0w_{\mathrm{out}}=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}w_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}$. Along with step 1.1 this verifies both balance identities of [L1], with every term in this momentum-rate identity having force units.

Failure of the naive law: $(mv)'=F\equiv0$ would make $mv$ constant and, since $m(0)v(0)=0$ and $m>0$, would force $v\equiv0$ by [L2]. But the computed $v(t)$ is nonzero for $0<t<2\ \mathrm s$; at $t=2\ \mathrm s$, $(mv)'=(2-2\ln3)n\ \mathrm N\approx-0.197n\ \mathrm N\ne F$. Hence the naive law fails for this open body, as [[pthm-cm15-impact-balance]] clause 6(b) records.

Tsiolkovsky value: at $t=1\ \mathrm s$, $q=1$, $m=2\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $v=2\ln(3/2)n\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx0.8109n\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The momentum is approximately $1.6219n\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, whereas the naive law gives zero. These values come from the exact logarithm before rounding; all are declared model computations, with no measurement or empirical inference.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport and divergence theorems.
**Adopt the finite-regularity open-flow model** with the following model data in one
fixed inertial frame (the adapted affine chart of [[post-cm01-frames]]) and
with SI conventions ([[def-cm01-units]]): a nonempty open interval $I$; a
material region $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ (bounded open with $C^1$ boundary);
a motion $\chi$ of $B$ on $I$ of class $C^2$ whose time slices are
diffeomorphisms with positive Jacobian onto their images. Let $U\subseteq
\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ be an open common field domain containing the
swept region over a compact subinterval $J_0$ with
$\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$. On $U$ take a scalar mass-density field
$\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ of class $C^1$ with
$[\rho]=\mu\ell^{-3}$ ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]], where
mass on a spatial region $C$ is $\int_C\rho\,dx$); its spatial velocity
field $u:U\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^1$ with $[u]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and
$u(t,\chi(t,X))=\partial_t\chi(t,X)$
([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]); a Cauchy stress matrix field
$\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ of class $C^1$ with
$[\sigma]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$, representing the traction by
$\mathbf t(\nu)=\sigma\nu$ on a surface with unit normal $\nu$
([[def-cm-traction-and-stress]]); and a continuous specific body-force vector
$b:U\to\mathbb R^3$, meaning force per unit mass and distinct from the
material acceleration, with $[b]=\ell\tau^{-2}$.
For the material derivative used below, make the time-dependent convention
explicit:
$$D_tu(t,x):=\partial_tu(t,x)+(D_xu(t,x))u(t,x),\qquad (D_tu)_i=\partial_tu_i+\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\,\partial_{x_j}u_i,$$
where $\partial_t$ differentiates at fixed $x$ and $D_xu$ is the spatial
Jacobian at fixed $t$ ([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]],
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]). Define the row divergence by
$g_i:=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$, so $g$ is a vector force
density with units $\mu\ell^{-2}\tau^{-2}$. Adopt as the model's
**material balances**: for every material subregion $B'\subseteq B$ (a
nonempty bounded open subset with $\overline{B'}\subseteq B$ whose images
$\chi_t(B')$ are bounded $C^1$ domains,
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]) and every
$t\in J_0$,

$$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho\,\mathrm dx=0,\qquad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho u\,\mathrm dx=\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho b\,\mathrm dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(B')}\sigma\nu\,\mathrm dS,$$

with $\nu$ the outward unit normal and the surface integral that of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. These two balance
laws are **adopted model assumptions** of this item, in the sense of the
open-body accounting of [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (iii); they are not
derived from the particle postulates. Then, for every second motion $\psi$ of
a material region $B'\subseteq B$ on $I$ (the **control motion**) with
control regions $C_t:=\psi_t(B')$ that are bounded $C^1$ domains for
   $t\in J_0$, spatial velocity $w$ with $[w]=\ell\tau^{-1}$, and outward
   unit normal $\nu$.
Require its closed sweep $\Sigma_C:=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\psi_t(\overline{B'})\}$ to lie in the common open field domain. Require also either that this sweep lie locally inside the current material region $\chi_t(B)$, where localization supplies the local mass and momentum equations, or that those same local equations $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ and $\rho D_tu=\rho b+g$ be explicitly adopted on a neighbourhood of the control sweep. The control motion need not coincide with $\chi$. Then:

1. **(Control-volume identities.)** For every $t\in J_0$,
   $$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_{C_t}\rho\,\mathrm dx =-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS, \tag{CV1}$$
   and componentwise
   $$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_{C_t}\rho u_i\,\mathrm dx =\int_{C_t}\rho b_i\,\mathrm dx+\Bigl(\int_{\partial C_t}\sigma\nu\,\mathrm dS\Bigr)_i -\int_{\partial C_t}\rho u_i\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS\qquad(i=1,2,3). \tag{CV2}$$
2. **(Material and fixed special cases.)** If $\psi=\chi$ (the control region
   is material, $w=u$ on the boundary), the flux terms vanish and (CV1),
   (CV2) reduce to the adopted material balances; if $\psi$ is the constant
   motion ($w=0$, $C_t=C$ fixed), then
   $$m_C'=-\int_{\partial C}\rho\,u\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS,\qquad P_C'=\int_C\rho b\,\mathrm dx+\int_{\partial C}\sigma\nu\,\mathrm dS-\int_{\partial C}\rho u\,(u\cdot\nu)\,\mathrm dS$$
   with $m_C:=\int_C\rho$, $P_C:=\int_C\rho u$; the last term is the momentum
   flux through the fixed boundary, and the relation is the fixed-region
   steady-flow balance of the engineering treatment when the fields are
   steady and the region fixed.
3. **(Inlet/outlet decomposition and the open-body law.)** Suppose that for
   every $t\in J_0$ the boundary decomposes into finitely many $C^1$ pieces,
   among which $\Sigma_{\mathrm{in},t}$ (where $(u-w)\cdot\nu<0$),
   $\Sigma_{\mathrm{out},t}$ (where $(u-w)\cdot\nu>0$) and the zero-flux rest,
   and put
   $$r_{\mathrm{in}}:=-\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{in},t}}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS\ge0,\qquad r_{\mathrm{out}}:=\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{out},t}}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS\ge0,$$
   $$w_{\mathrm{in}}:=\frac{1}{r_{\mathrm{in}}}\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{in},t}}\rho u\,\bigl(-(u-w)\cdot\nu\bigr)\mathrm dS,\qquad w_{\mathrm{out}}:=\frac{1}{r_{\mathrm{out}}}\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{out},t}}\rho u\,\bigl((u-w)\cdot\nu\bigr)\mathrm dS$$
   (the flux averages are used only where the corresponding rate is
   positive; define $r_{\mathrm{in}}w_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ when
   $r_{\mathrm{in}}=0$, and likewise for the outlet term), and write
   $$m:=\int_{C_t}\rho\,\mathrm dx>0,\qquad P:=\int_{C_t}\rho u\,\mathrm dx,\qquad F_{\mathrm{ext}}:=\int_{C_t}\rho b\,\mathrm dx+\int_{\partial C_t}\sigma\nu\,\mathrm dS .$$
   The units are $[m]=\mu$, $[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$,
   $[F_{\mathrm{ext}}]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$,
   $[r_{\mathrm{in}}]=[r_{\mathrm{out}}]=\mu\tau^{-1}$ and
   $[w_{\mathrm{in}}]=[w_{\mathrm{out}}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$. The control-volume
   theorem supplies the derivatives of $m$ and $P$; since $\rho>0$ and each
   $C_t$ is a nonempty open region, $m>0$, so $v:=P/m$ is differentiable on
   $J_0$. This verifies the differentiability hypotheses of
   [[thm-cm-variable-mass-momentum-balance]].
   Then the control-volume identities read
   $$m'=r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad P'=F_{\mathrm{ext}}+r_{\mathrm{in}}\,w_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}\,w_{\mathrm{out}},$$
   and the lumped body with mass $m$ and velocity $v:=P/m$ satisfies
   $$m\,v'=F_{\mathrm{ext}}+r_{\mathrm{in}}\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v\bigr),$$
   the derived law of [[thm-cm-variable-mass-momentum-balance]]. In
   particular, a body that only loses mass ($r_{\mathrm{in}}=0$,
   $r_{\mathrm{out}}=-m'$) has thrust
   $r_{\mathrm{out}}(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})=-m'(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})$, and a body
   whose boundary moves with the material ($w=u$; no flux) has
   $m'=0$ and $P'=F_{\mathrm{ext}}$.
4. **(Status.)** The balances displayed before clause 1 are adopted component
   models of the open flow, exactly as clause (iii) of
   [[post-cm15-impulse]] adopts the lumped accounting; this item proves only
   the two stated deductions (localization followed by the control-volume
   identities, and the inlet/outlet reading). It asserts no constitutive law
   for $\rho$ or $\sigma$, no boundary condition, no incompressibility, no
   regularity beyond that stated, and no empirical claim; the fields,
   the control motion and the region are model data.
