[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]) and every
$t\in J_0$,

$$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho\,\mathrm dx=0,\qquad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho u\,\mathrm dx=\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho b\,\mathrm dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(B')}\sigma\nu\,\mathrm dS,$$

with $\nu$ the outward unit normal and the surface integral that of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. These two balance
laws are **adopted model assumptions** of this item, in the sense of the
open-body accounting of [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (iii); they are not
derived from the particle postulates. Then, for every second motion $\psi$ of
a material region $B'\subseteq B$ on $I$ (the **control motion**) with
control regions $C_t:=\psi_t(B')$ that are bounded $C^1$ domains for
   $t\in J_0$, spatial velocity $w$ with $[w]=\ell\tau^{-1}$, and outward
   unit normal $\nu$.
Require its closed sweep $\Sigma_C:=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\psi_t(\overline{B'})\}$ to lie in the common open field domain. Require also either that this sweep lie locally inside the current material region $\chi_t(B)$, where localization supplies the local mass and momentum equations, or that those same local equations $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ and $\rho D_tu=\rho b+g$ be explicitly adopted on a neighbourhood of the control sweep. The control motion need not coincide with $\chi$. Then:

1. **(Control-volume identities.)** For every $t\in J_0$,
   $$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_{C_t}\rho\,\mathrm dx =-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS, \tag{CV1}$$
   and componentwise
   $$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_{C_t}\rho u_i\,\mathrm dx =\int_{C_t}\rho b_i\,\mathrm dx+\Bigl(\int_{\partial C_t}\sigma\nu\,\mathrm dS\Bigr)_i -\int_{\partial C_t}\rho u_i\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS\qquad(i=1,2,3). \tag{CV2}$$
2. **(Material and fixed special cases.)** If $\psi=\chi$ (the control region
   is material, $w=u$ on the boundary), the flux terms vanish and (CV1),
   (CV2) reduce to the adopted material balances; if $\psi$ is the constant
   motion ($w=0$, $C_t=C$ fixed), then
   $$m_C'=-\int_{\partial C}\rho\,u\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS,\qquad P_C'=\int_C\rho b\,\mathrm dx+\int_{\partial C}\sigma\nu\,\mathrm dS-\int_{\partial C}\rho u\,(u\cdot\nu)\,\mathrm dS$$
   with $m_C:=\int_C\rho$, $P_C:=\int_C\rho u$; the last term is the momentum
   flux through the fixed boundary, and the relation is the fixed-region
   steady-flow balance of the engineering treatment when the fields are
   steady and the region fixed.
3. **(Inlet/outlet decomposition and the open-body law.)** Suppose that for
   every $t\in J_0$ the boundary decomposes into finitely many $C^1$ pieces,
   among which $\Sigma_{\mathrm{in},t}$ (where $(u-w)\cdot\nu<0$),
   $\Sigma_{\mathrm{out},t}$ (where $(u-w)\cdot\nu>0$) and the zero-flux rest,
   and put
   $$r_{\mathrm{in}}:=-\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{in},t}}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS\ge0,\qquad r_{\mathrm{out}}:=\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{out},t}}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS\ge0,$$
   $$w_{\mathrm{in}}:=\frac{1}{r_{\mathrm{in}}}\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{in},t}}\rho u\,\bigl(-(u-w)\cdot\nu\bigr)\mathrm dS,\qquad w_{\mathrm{out}}:=\frac{1}{r_{\mathrm{out}}}\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{out},t}}\rho u\,\bigl((u-w)\cdot\nu\bigr)\mathrm dS$$
   (the flux averages are used only where the corresponding rate is
   positive; define $r_{\mathrm{in}}w_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ when
   $r_{\mathrm{in}}=0$, and likewise for the outlet term), and write
   $$m:=\int_{C_t}\rho\,\mathrm dx>0,\qquad P:=\int_{C_t}\rho u\,\mathrm dx,\qquad F_{\mathrm{ext}}:=\int_{C_t}\rho b\,\mathrm dx+\int_{\partial C_t}\sigma\nu\,\mathrm dS .$$
   The units are $[m]=\mu$, $[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$,
   $[F_{\mathrm{ext}}]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$,
   $[r_{\mathrm{in}}]=[r_{\mathrm{out}}]=\mu\tau^{-1}$ and
   $[w_{\mathrm{in}}]=[w_{\mathrm{out}}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$. The control-volume
   theorem supplies the derivatives of $m$ and $P$; since $\rho>0$ and each
   $C_t$ is a nonempty open region, $m>0$, so $v:=P/m$ is differentiable on
   $J_0$. This verifies the differentiability hypotheses of
   [[thm-cm-variable-mass-momentum-balance]].
   Then the control-volume identities read
   $$m'=r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad P'=F_{\mathrm{ext}}+r_{\mathrm{in}}\,w_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}\,w_{\mathrm{out}},$$
   and the lumped body with mass $m$ and velocity $v:=P/m$ satisfies
   $$m\,v'=F_{\mathrm{ext}}+r_{\mathrm{in}}\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v\bigr),$$
   the derived law of [[thm-cm-variable-mass-momentum-balance]]. In
   particular, a body that only loses mass ($r_{\mathrm{in}}=0$,
   $r_{\mathrm{out}}=-m'$) has thrust
   $r_{\mathrm{out}}(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})=-m'(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})$, and a body
   whose boundary moves with the material ($w=u$; no flux) has
   $m'=0$ and $P'=F_{\mathrm{ext}}$.
4. **(Status.)** The balances displayed before clause 1 are adopted component
   models of the open flow, exactly as clause (iii) of
   [[post-cm15-impulse]] adopts the lumped accounting; this item proves only
   the two stated deductions (localization followed by the control-volume
   identities, and the inlet/outlet reading). It asserts no constitutive law
   for $\rho$ or $\sigma$, no boundary condition, no incompressibility, no
   regularity beyond that stated, and no empirical claim; the fields,
   the control motion and the region are model data.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport and divergence theorems. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, and let $\chi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$. Write

$$\mathcal D_\chi:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}$$

for the open domain on which $u$ is defined ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]). Let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with compact closure in $I$, and let $U\subseteq\mathcal D_\chi$ be open and contain the swept region of $B$ over $\overline{J_0}$.

Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ and $\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be $C^1$ and let $b:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Define $g_i:=\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$ and suppose, on $U$:

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\rho\,D_tu=\rho b+g . \tag{KM}$$

Let $\psi:I\times O'\to\mathbb R^3$ be a second motion of a material region $B'\subseteq B$ (with the same reference chart domain $O'=O$ used for $B$; write $w$ for its spatial velocity), and suppose that for every $t\in J_0$ the control region $C_t:=\psi_t(B')$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]) with outward unit normal $\nu$ and boundary surface integral as in [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]].

Assume also that the control sweep $\Sigma_C:=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\psi_t(\overline{B'})\}$ is contained in $U$. Thus the fields and the local equations (KM) are defined on a neighbourhood of every closed control region. No condition that the control motion coincide with the material motion is imposed.

Then for every $t\in J_0$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C_t}\rho\,dx=-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,dS, \tag{CV1}$$

and componentwise

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C_t}\rho u_i\,dx=\int_{C_t}\rho b_i\,dx+\Bigl(\int_{\partial C_t}\sigma\nu\,dS\Bigr)_i-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho u_i\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,dS\qquad(i=1,2,3). \tag{CV2}$$

Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region (nonempty, bounded, open, [[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]) and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]).

A **motion of $B$ on $I$** consists of an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $\overline B\subseteq O$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) together with a map

$$\chi:I\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3$$

such that:

1. $\chi$ is of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]);
2. for every $t\in I$ the map $\chi_t:=\chi(t,\cdot):O\to\mathbb R^3$ is of class $C^1$, is injective, and has $D_X\chi_t(X)$ invertible for every $X\in O$;
3. writing

$$J(t,X):=\det\bigl(D_X\chi_t(X)\bigr)$$

with the determinant of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]], one has $J(t,X)>0$ for every $(t,X)\in I\times B$.

We call $X\in B$ the **material label** (reference position), $x=\chi(t,X)$ the **position** at time $t$ of the label $X$, and

$$\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$$

the **current (material) region** at time $t$. Condition 2 makes each $\chi_t:O\to\chi_t(O)$ a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto the open set $\chi_t(O)$ ([[cor-injective-regular-ck-map-is-a-ck-diffeomorphism-onto-its-image]]).

The **spatial velocity field** of the motion is

$$u:\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,\qquad u\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr):=\partial_t\chi(t,X),$$

and the **spatial acceleration field** is the material derivative of $u$ in the sense of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]],

$$a(t,x):=D_tu(t,x)=\partial_tu(t,x)+Du(t,x)u(t,x).$$

For a compact subinterval $K\subseteq I$ the **swept region** of $B$ over $K$ is

$$\Sigma_K:=\bigl\{(t,x):t\in K,\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\bigr\},$$

and for a scalar field $f$ on a neighbourhood of $\Sigma_K$ the spatial field $f(t,x)$ of a material quantity $F(t,X)$ is defined by $f(t,\chi(t,X))=F(t,X)$.

Throughout, $\mathbb R^3$ carries its standard ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$, its Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $a\in O$ and let $v:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that the total derivative $Dv(a):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is a linear map ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) whose matrix in the standard bases is $\bigl(\partial_jv_i(a)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le3}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). The **divergence** of $v$ at $a$ is

$$\operatorname{div}v(a):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Dv(a)\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_iv_i(a),$$

the trace of the total derivative ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]), read in the standard basis of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]).

For a $C^1$ scalar field $f:O\to\mathbb R$ and $a\in O$, the **gradient** $\nabla f(a)\in\mathbb R^3$ is the vector of partial derivatives of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; it is the unique vector with $Df(a)h=\langle\nabla f(a),h\rangle_2$ for every $h\in\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). We write $\langle\nabla f(a),v(a)\rangle_2=:\nabla f(a)\cdot v(a)$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $f:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For $(t,x)\in I\times O$ write $D_x f(t,x):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ for the total derivative of $y\mapsto f(t,y)$ at fixed $t$, and $\nabla_xf(t,x)$ for its gradient. The derivative $Df(t,x)$ of the full map on $I\times O$ acts on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$; it is distinct from $D_x f$. Define the partial time derivative $\partial_tf(t,x):=\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=t}f(s,x)$ and the **material derivative** of $f$ along $u$

$$D_tf(t,x):=\partial_tf(t,x)+D_xf(t,x)\bigl(u(t,x)\bigr)=\partial_tf(t,x)+\nabla_x f(t,x)\cdot u(t,x).$$

Spatial derivatives $Du$, $Dw$, $\nabla f$ and $\operatorname{div}u$ of time-dependent fields always mean $D_xu$, $D_xw$, $\nabla_x f$ and spatial divergence at fixed time; a stationary field $u(x)$ is included by setting $u(t,x)=u(x)$. The same definitions apply on any open spacetime domain, by restriction to a product neighborhood of each point.

For a $C^1$ vector field $w:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ the material derivative $D_tw$ is defined componentwise, and $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)$ means the divergence of $x\mapsto w(t,x)$ at $x$ at each fixed $t$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]), let $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and let $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be maps. Suppose the two **material balance identities**

$$m'(t)=r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t),\qquad (mv)'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)$$

hold for every $t\in I$, where $mv$ denotes the pointwise scalar multiple. Then

$$m(t)v'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in I).$$

In particular, if $F\equiv0$, $r_{\mathrm{in}}\equiv0$ and $r_{\mathrm{out}}\equiv r$ for a constant $r\ge0$, then $mv'=-r(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$: the acceleration is governed by the momentum carried away per unit time relative to the body, not by $(mv)'=0$.

The two balance identities are the **adopted content of the material momentum accounting** — the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,dt$ of matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,dt$ with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$". They are not derived here from any closed-system law; the deduction below is their product-rule consequence.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

For each admissible material subregion, applying [[thm-cm-control-volume-balance]] with control motion $\psi=\chi$ makes $w=u$ and gives the adopted material balances; thus the premises of [[pthm-cm15-control-volume-balance]] hold. The fixed and material balls stay in the stipulated neighbourhoods of their closed sweeps, so its control-volume identities apply to them. For (ii), the fixed elbow control region stays in its declared common field domain, its boundary has nonpositive flux on the inlet patch, nonnegative flux on the outlet patch and zero flux on the remainder. The local equations are adopted there, so (CV1) and (CV2) of [L1] apply. Splitting their integrals over these patches remains valid when a profile vanishes: those subsets contribute zero.

citations.quote:
Adopt, as this page's **impact and open-mass extensions** of the force
branch of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the following three model extensions. Each is an adopted model, not a
consequence of the smooth-force postulates; each applies only where a
statement explicitly invokes it.

**(i) The isolated reciprocal impulse model.** A two-label force model with
masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), time window $I_0$,
configuration domain $Q$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]) and continuous
external-plus-pair force maps $F_1,F_2$ is **run in the isolated reciprocal
impulse model at $t_*\in I_0$** when there is an interval
$I\subseteq I_0$ with $t_*\in\operatorname{int}I$ and a position curve
$x=(x_1,x_2):I\to Q$ such that the following conditions hold. This curve is
called an **impulse motion**; only its restrictions away from $t_*$ are
motions of the associated first-order system of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]],
and no differentiability at $t_*$ is required:

1. $x_1,x_2$ are continuous on $I$ and twice continuously differentiable on
   each of $I\cap(-\infty,t_*)$ and $I\cap(t_*,\infty)$
   ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]],
   [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and
   $m_ix_i''(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ for every $t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}$;
2. the one-sided limits
   $v_i^{\pm}:=\lim_{t\to t_*\pm}x_i'(t)$ exist in $\mathbb R^3$
   ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]);
3. there is a vector $J\in\mathbb R^3$, the **impulse**, with
   $$m_1\bigl(v_1^+-v_1^-\bigr)=J,\qquad m_2\bigl(v_2^+-v_2^-\bigr)=-J .$$

The two equations of clause 3 are the **reciprocal finite-jump form** of the
isolated impulse: the two labels receive equal and opposite momentum changes.
The regular force maps remain continuous on their state domain; their
evaluations along the curve can have different one-sided limits because the
velocity can jump. The dimension of the impulse
is $[J]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

For the distributional rendering on $\operatorname{int}I$, assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Put
$p_i(t)=m_ix_i'(t)$ and $f_i(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ off $t_*$, assigning both
the value $0$ at $t_*$. Their one-sided limits are finite: those of $p_i$
are $m_iv_i^\pm$, and continuity of the state-domain force maps gives
$f_i(t_*^\pm)=F_i(t_*,x(t_*),v^\pm)$, with
$v^\pm=(v_1^\pm,v_2^\pm)$. Also $p_i'=f_i$ off the impulse. Thus each
component meets the piecewise-$C^1$ and one-sided derivative-limit
hypotheses of [[lem-cm-piecewise-c1-jump-derivative]]. Its identity,
summed componentwise, gives for every real vector test function
$\Phi\in C_c^\infty(\operatorname{int}I;\mathbb R^3)$ (each component is
smooth and compactly supported, [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]])
$$-\int_{\operatorname{int}I}\langle p_i,\Phi'\rangle\,d\lambda=\int_{\operatorname{int}I}\langle f_i,\Phi\rangle\,d\lambda+s_i\langle J,\Phi(t_*)\rangle,\qquad s_1=1,\quad s_2=-1,$$
where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure and the integral convention is that of
[[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]. This is the pairing form of the
adopted jumps. Unlike [[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]], whose
hypotheses require continuous time forces and assume the pairings to derive
the jumps, this rendering allows distinct one-sided regular-force values.

**(ii) The collinear restitution contact law.** A model run in the isolated
reciprocal impulse model at $t_*$ is **collinear** when there is a unit vector
$n\in\mathbb R^3$ (the **contact direction**) with $v_i^{\pm}\parallel n$ for
$i=1,2$ and $\langle v_2^--v_1^-,n\rangle<0$ (the labels approach along $n$).
For a collinear contact, adopt a **coefficient of restitution** $e\in[0,1]$ —
a dimensionless model datum of the pair and the contact — and the **restitution
law**
$$v_2^+-v_1^+=-e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr).$$
For $e=1$ the contact is called **elastic**, for $e=0$ **perfectly inelastic**
and otherwise **semi-elastic**; the law is a constitutive assumption, not a
consequence of the impulse equations of clause (i), and $e$ is not derived
from the masses or the approach speed. The law is stated only for a single
collinear contact; simultaneous contacts, repeated contacts and tangential
(friction) impulses are outside the model.

**(iii) The open-body material accounting.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a
nonempty open interval. Adopt for a body whose mass
$m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and velocity $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ are differentiable, and
whose external force and exchanged matter are described by maps
$F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and
$w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ (mass rates and *inertial*
velocities of the matter entering and leaving, measured in the same inertial
frame as $v$), the **material balance identities**
$$m'=r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad (mv)'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}\,w_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}\,w_{\mathrm{out}} .$$
They are the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,\mathrm dt$ of
matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,\mathrm dt$
with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$", and they
are adopted rather than derived from a closed-system law. Their product-rule
consequence $mv'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$
is proved in [[thm-cm-variable-mass-momentum-balance]]; in particular the
closed-system law $(mv)'=F$ is recovered only when
$r_{\mathrm{in}}w_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}$.
The quantities have types and SI dimensions
$[m]=\mu$, $[v]=[w_{\mathrm{in}}]=[w_{\mathrm{out}}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$,
$[F]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ and
$[r_{\mathrm{in}}]=[r_{\mathrm{out}}]=\mu\tau^{-1}$; they are model
data, not measured values.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.
