citations.quote:
Adopt, as this page's **impact and open-mass extensions** of the force
branch of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the following three model extensions. Each is an adopted model, not a
consequence of the smooth-force postulates; each applies only where a
statement explicitly invokes it.

**(i) The isolated reciprocal impulse model.** A two-label force model with
masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), time window $I_0$,
configuration domain $Q$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]) and continuous
external-plus-pair force maps $F_1,F_2$ is **run in the isolated reciprocal
impulse model at $t_*\in I_0$** when there is an interval
$I\subseteq I_0$ with $t_*\in\operatorname{int}I$ and a position curve
$x=(x_1,x_2):I\to Q$ such that the following conditions hold. This curve is
called an **impulse motion**; only its restrictions away from $t_*$ are
motions of the associated first-order system of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]],
and no differentiability at $t_*$ is required:

1. $x_1,x_2$ are continuous on $I$ and twice continuously differentiable on
   each of $I\cap(-\infty,t_*)$ and $I\cap(t_*,\infty)$
   ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]],
   [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and
   $m_ix_i''(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ for every $t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}$;
2. the one-sided limits
   $v_i^{\pm}:=\lim_{t\to t_*\pm}x_i'(t)$ exist in $\mathbb R^3$
   ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]);
3. there is a vector $J\in\mathbb R^3$, the **impulse**, with
   $$m_1\bigl(v_1^+-v_1^-\bigr)=J,\qquad m_2\bigl(v_2^+-v_2^-\bigr)=-J .$$

The two equations of clause 3 are the **reciprocal finite-jump form** of the
isolated impulse: the two labels receive equal and opposite momentum changes.
The regular force maps remain continuous on their state domain; their
evaluations along the curve can have different one-sided limits because the
velocity can jump. The dimension of the impulse
is $[J]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

For the distributional rendering on $\operatorname{int}I$, assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Put
$p_i(t)=m_ix_i'(t)$ and $f_i(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ off $t_*$, assigning both
the value $0$ at $t_*$. Their one-sided limits are finite: those of $p_i$
are $m_iv_i^\pm$, and continuity of the state-domain force maps gives
$f_i(t_*^\pm)=F_i(t_*,x(t_*),v^\pm)$, with
$v^\pm=(v_1^\pm,v_2^\pm)$. Also $p_i'=f_i$ off the impulse. Thus each
component meets the piecewise-$C^1$ and one-sided derivative-limit
hypotheses of [[lem-cm-piecewise-c1-jump-derivative]]. Its identity,
summed componentwise, gives for every real vector test function
$\Phi\in C_c^\infty(\operatorname{int}I;\mathbb R^3)$ (each component is
smooth and compactly supported, [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]])
$$-\int_{\operatorname{int}I}\langle p_i,\Phi'\rangle\,d\lambda=\int_{\operatorname{int}I}\langle f_i,\Phi\rangle\,d\lambda+s_i\langle J,\Phi(t_*)\rangle,\qquad s_1=1,\quad s_2=-1,$$
where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure and the integral convention is that of
[[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]. This is the pairing form of the
adopted jumps. Unlike [[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]], whose
hypotheses require continuous time forces and assume the pairings to derive
the jumps, this rendering allows distinct one-sided regular-force values.

**(ii) The collinear restitution contact law.** A model run in the isolated
reciprocal impulse model at $t_*$ is **collinear** when there is a unit vector
$n\in\mathbb R^3$ (the **contact direction**) with $v_i^{\pm}\parallel n$ for
$i=1,2$ and $\langle v_2^--v_1^-,n\rangle<0$ (the labels approach along $n$).
For a collinear contact, adopt a **coefficient of restitution** $e\in[0,1]$ —
a dimensionless model datum of the pair and the contact — and the **restitution
law**
$$v_2^+-v_1^+=-e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr).$$
For $e=1$ the contact is called **elastic**, for $e=0$ **perfectly inelastic**
and otherwise **semi-elastic**; the law is a constitutive assumption, not a
consequence of the impulse equations of clause (i), and $e$ is not derived
from the masses or the approach speed. The law is stated only for a single
collinear contact; simultaneous contacts, repeated contacts and tangential
(friction) impulses are outside the model.

**(iii) The open-body material accounting.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a
nonempty open interval. Adopt for a body whose mass
$m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and velocity $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ are differentiable, and
whose external force and exchanged matter are described by maps
$F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and
$w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ (mass rates and *inertial*
velocities of the matter entering and leaving, measured in the same inertial
frame as $v$), the **material balance identities**
$$m'=r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad (mv)'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}\,w_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}\,w_{\mathrm{out}} .$$
They are the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,\mathrm dt$ of
matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,\mathrm dt$
with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$", and they
are adopted rather than derived from a closed-system law. Their product-rule
consequence $mv'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$
is proved in [[thm-cm-variable-mass-momentum-balance]]; in particular the
closed-system law $(mv)'=F$ is recovered only when
$r_{\mathrm{in}}w_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}$.
The quantities have types and SI dimensions
$[m]=\mu$, $[v]=[w_{\mathrm{in}}]=[w_{\mathrm{out}}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$,
$[F]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ and
$[r_{\mathrm{in}}]=[r_{\mathrm{out}}]=\mu\tau^{-1}$; they are model
data, not measured values.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]),
inherited from the statement of
[[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]], whose distributional jump
lemma uses it; the algebraic clauses used here do not otherwise use choice.
Adopt the impact and open-mass extensions of [[post-cm15-impulse]], with
$m_1,m_2>0$, an interval $I$ with nonempty interior, $t_*\in\operatorname{int} I$, an impulse motion
$x=(x_1,x_2):I\to Q$ run in the isolated reciprocal impulse model at $t_*$
with impulse $J$ and one-sided velocities $v_i^\pm$, and write
$$M:=m_1+m_2,\qquad \mu:=\frac{m_1m_2}{M},\qquad P(t):=m_1x_1'(t)+m_2x_2'(t)\qquad(t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}).$$
Only the one-sided limits of $P$ at $t_*$ are used; no derivative of the
position curves at the contact time is assumed.
Then:

1. **(Momentum continuity.)** The total momentum is continuous across the
   impact,
   $$P(t_*^+)=P(t_*^-),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \sum_{i=1}^2 m_i\bigl(v_i^+-v_i^-\bigr)=0,$$
   and the impulse delivered to label $1$ is removed from label $2$:
   $J=m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=-m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)$.
2. **(Smooth-force exclusion.)** Suppose this same candidate motion $x$ from
   clause 1 also satisfies the smooth force branch of
   [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]] on $I$,
   with the force maps continuous there. Then the momentum curves
   $p_i=m_ix_i'$ are of class $C^1$ on $I$; in particular
   $$p_i(t_*^+)=p_i(t_*^-)\qquad(i=1,2).$$
   Clause 1 identifies the jump of $p_1$ with the same impulse $J$, so
   $J=0$: no candidate motion carrying a nonzero isolated impulse can also
   be a motion of that smooth-force class. The finite-jump model of
   [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (i) is therefore a genuine extension of the
   smooth-force branch, not one of its cases.
3. **(Collinear restitution solution.)** Suppose in addition that the
   contact is collinear with contact direction $n$ and coefficient of
   restitution $e\in[0,1]$ ([[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (ii)). Then
   $$J=\mu(1+e)\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr),$$
   $J$ is parallel to $n$, the centre-of-mass velocity
   $V:=M^{-1}(m_1v_1^-+m_2v_2^-)$ is unchanged across the impact, and the
   post-impact velocities are
   $$v_1^+=V+\frac{m_2}{M}\,e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr),\qquad v_2^+=V-\frac{m_1}{M}\,e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr).$$
4. **(Kinetic energy of the impact.)** The kinetic-energy change across the
   impact is
   $$\Delta K:=\frac{m_1\lVert v_1^+\rVert_2^2+m_2\lVert v_2^+\rVert_2^2}{2} -\frac{m_1\lVert v_1^-\rVert_2^2+m_2\lVert v_2^-\rVert_2^2}{2} =-\frac{1-e^2}{2}\,\mu\,\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2\le0,$$
   with equality if and only if $e=1$ or $v_2^-=v_1^-$. For $0\le e<1$ the
   contact model is dissipative: the total kinetic energy of the two labels
   is not conserved across the impact, and the deficit
   $\frac{1-e^2}{2}\mu\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2$ is a quantity of the
   adopted contact law. This item identifies it with no measured heat,
   temperature, sound or deformation observable.
5. **(Momentum balance alone does not determine the impact.)** In the
   collinear case with $d^-:=v_2^--v_1^-$ and $d_n:=\langle d^-,n\rangle<0$,
   the impulse equations of clause 1 alone leave the scalar impulse magnitude
   free: for every real $J_n$ with $J_n\le \mu d_n$ (so that the contact is
   separating or grazing) the velocities
   $$v_1^+=v_1^-+\frac{J_n}{m_1}n,\qquad v_2^+=v_2^--\frac{J_n}{m_2}n$$
   satisfy the reciprocal impulse equations with impulse $J=J_nn$ and
   preserve the total momentum, and their kinetic-energy change is
   $$\Delta K(J_n)=-J_n\,d_n+\frac{J_n^2}{2\mu},$$
   whose minimum over the admissible range is
   $\Delta K(\mu d_n)=-\frac{\mu}{2}d_n^2$ at the perfectly inelastic value
   $J_n=\mu d_n$ (that is, $e=0$). The value of
   $J_n$ is fixed only by the contact law of [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause
   (ii), which selects $J_n=\mu(1+e)d_n$; in particular momentum balance
   alone does not determine the post-impact velocities.
6. **(Open-body and rocket laws.)** Under [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause
   (iii), with differentiable $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$,
   $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$,
   and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfying the
   material balance identities, one has on $I$
   $$m\,v'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v\bigr).$$
   In particular: (a) if $r_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ then
   $m\,v'=F$ and $(mv)'=F$; (b) if $r_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ and
   $r_{\mathrm{out}}=-m'>0$ (mass loss) then
   $$m\,v'=F+r_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(v-w_{\mathrm{out}}\bigr)=F-m'\bigl(v-w_{\mathrm{out}}\bigr),$$
   so the **thrust** is $T:=r_{\mathrm{out}}(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})=-m'(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})$,
   and the closed-system law $(mv)'=F$ fails unless
   $w_{\mathrm{out}}=0$; (c) if $r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}}=0$
   then $m\,v'=F-r_{\mathrm{in}}v$: capture contributes the acceleration
   $-(r_{\mathrm{in}}/m)v$, opposing $v$, while $(mv)'=F$ still holds.

Let $N\in\mathbb N$, $N\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $m_1,\dots,m_N>0$ and let $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable at every point of $I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). All sums over $i$ range over $1,\dots,N$: for a real family $a_1,\dots,a_N$, define $\sum_i a_i:=\sum_{k<N}b_k$, where $b:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ has $b_k=a_{k+1}$ for $k<N$ and $b_k=0$ for $k\ge N$, using the finite sums of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]; vector sums are defined coordinatewise, and sums of curves pointwise. Put $M:=\sum_i m_i>0$, $X:=M^{-1}\sum_i m_ix_i$ and $\rho_i:=x_i-X$. The symbols $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ denote the Euclidean inner product and norm on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

1. $X$ and every $\rho_i$ are differentiable on $I$, with $X'=M^{-1}\sum_im_ix_i'$ and $\rho_i'=x_i'-X'$, and the identities $\sum_im_i\rho_i=0$ and $\sum_im_i\rho_i'=0$ hold on $I$;
2. for every $t\in I$, $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\sum_{i}m_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2;$$
3. if $N=2$, then with $r:=x_1-x_2$ and $\mu:=m_1m_2/M$ one has $\sum_im_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$ and hence $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$$ for every $t\in I$.

Fix a model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$
particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb
R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with its collision
set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an
interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). All sums below range over
$i=1,\dots,N$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $u\times v$, $\langle u,v\rangle$
and $\lVert u\rVert_{2}$ are the cross product, the Euclidean inner product and
the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(a) Curve families and motions.** A **curve family** of the model is a map
$x:J\to Q$, $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$, of class $C^{2}$ on $J$
([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]); its **coordinate velocities** are
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$ on $J$, written $w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{N}):J\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
A curve family is a **motion** of the model when
$$m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J),$$
the notion of clause (c) of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Every quantity of
this definition is defined for an arbitrary curve family; the balance theorems
of this page state which of their properties use the equations of motion.
Along a curve family the force map is evaluated at $(t,x(t),w(t))\in
I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; when the model invokes the
external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the maps $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $F_{ij}$ are evaluated at their declared
arguments on the motion's state graph, where the presentation is an identity
for $F_{i}$.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define
$$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$
Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$
the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$.
The dimensions are $[M]=\mu$, $[p_{i}]=[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and $[X]=[\rho_{i}]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]). Since $x_{i}$ is $C^{2}$, each $p_{i}$ is $C^{1}$ and
each of $P$, $X$, $\rho_{i}$ is differentiable, as a finite sum of
differentiable curves ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); write
$$V:=X'$$
for the **centre-of-mass velocity**. The algebraic identities
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}=0$, $P=MV$ and the splitting of the kinetic sum
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}$ are proved in the kinetic-splitting
theorem of this page; they are not part of this definition.

**(c) Angular momentum, torque, internal torque sum.** Let a **reference
curve** $o:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{1}$ be given: a point about which
moments are taken, allowed to move (a constant map $o\equiv o_{0}$ is the
fixed-origin case). Define the **angular momentum about $o$** and the **total
torque about $o$** by
$$J_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times p_{i}(t),\qquad T_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),$$
with dimensions $[J_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{2}\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and
$[T_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m$). When the
model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of
[[post-cm02-interactions]], define in addition the **external torque** and the
**internal torque sum**
$$T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr),\qquad I(t):=\sum_{i<j}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-x_{j}(t)\bigr)\times F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr).$$
The sum $I$ does not involve $o$; it is defined whenever the pair
presentation is declared. The identity $T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I$ uses the
antisymmetry $F_{ji}=-F_{ij}$ of clause (ii)1 of that postulate to reindex the
ordered pairs and is proved as step 1.1 of the angular-momentum balance of
this page.

**(d) Kinetic energy, power, work.** Define the **kinetic energy** and the
**power of the total force** along the curve family by
$$K(t):=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}(t)\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad \mathcal P(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl\langle F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),\,w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle,$$
of dimensions $[K]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules) and
$[\mathcal P]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-3}$ (read in watts), and for
$t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$ the **work of the total force** over $[t_{0},t_{1}]$ by
$$W([t_{0},t_{1}]):=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal P(t)\,dt,$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules); $\mathcal P$ is
continuous on $J$ because $F$, $x$ and $w$ are continuous, so the Riemann
integral exists ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], see the page
`the-riemann-integral`). The **potential energy** is not defined by this item:
it belongs to the potential branch of the model and is defined in the
potential-and-mechanical-energy item of this page.

**(e) Frame and reference-point dependence.** The quantities $p_{i}$, $P$,
$X$, $\rho_{i}$, $V$, $K$, $\mathcal P$ and $W$ are read in the one inertial
frame fixed above, and $J_{o}$, $T_{o}$, $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$, $I$ are read
about the reference curve $o$ in that frame. They are not invariant under a
change of frame or reference point: their transformation laws under a change
of inertial frame are stated and proved in the frame-transformation item of
this page, and every conservation statement involving them names the frame
and the reference point in which it is made.

**(f) Status.** This item is a definition: it introduces symbols, their
domains, regularity, dimensions and frame dependence from the model's data.
It adopts no force law beyond the force branch already fixed, asserts no
balance of any of these quantities and records no measured value.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: Common data: $M=8$, $\mu=\frac32$, $V=\frac{2\cdot3+6\cdot(-1)}{8}=0$, $d^-=-4n$, $\lVert d^-\rVert_2^2=16$, $K^-=12\ \mathrm{J}$.

For each candidate outgoing pair below, define $x_i(t)=t v_i^-$ for $t\le0$ and $x_i(t)=t v_i^+$ for $t>0$. Both position curves are continuous on $I$, affine and hence $C^2$ on either side of $0$, and take values in the declared full domain $Q$. They have precisely the specified one-sided velocities, and $m_ix_i''=0=F_i(t,x,x')$ away from $0$. Thus all trajectory conditions of the isolated reciprocal impulse model hold for both candidates; only the reciprocal jumps remain to check. Moreover $\langle v_2^--v_1^-,n\rangle=-4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}<0$, so the common incoming data approach along $n$.
Outcome (a), sticking: $v_1^+=v_2^+=0$. Then $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=2(0-3)n=-6n$ and $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=6(0+1)n=+6n$; the impulse is $J=-6n\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ and the total momentum is $0=P^-$.
Outcome (b), elastic: $v_1^+=-3n$, $v_2^+=+1n$. Then $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=2(-6)n=-12n$ and $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=6(+2)n=+12n$; the impulse is $J=-12n\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ and the total momentum is $0=P^-$.

Together with the curves of step 1.2, steps 2.1 and 2.2 establish two complete runs of clause (i), with the same incoming data and different impulses ($-6n$ versus $-12n$) and outgoing velocities ($0$ versus $-3n$ and $+1n$). The first also satisfies restitution with $e=0$, and the second with $e=1$. Hence reciprocal impulse accounting alone does not fix the outgoing velocities, and the false statement fails.

Energy: by [L2] the changes are $\Delta K_{(a)}=\frac32\cdot\frac12(0-16)=-12\ \mathrm{J}$ and $\Delta K_{(b)}=\frac32\cdot\frac12(16-16)=0$; the outcomes are therefore also distinguished by their energy accounting, so no choice of impulse can be recovered from the momentum data and the two outcomes are genuinely different model histories.

Consequence: in the collinear isolated-impact model the contact law of [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (ii) (equivalently, the coefficient $e$, or a dynamical contact model producing the impulse) is an independent model datum; the reciprocal impulse equations constrain only the *sum* $m_1\Delta v_1+m_2\Delta v_2=0$. The same conclusion is recorded as clause 5 of [[pthm-cm15-impact-balance]].
